The first two are stated. The third is inferred from "for the v3 design" and should be confirmed against the experiment record before it is accepted. Extraction is wrong in characteristic ways. It invents plausible entities, merges two distinct things with the same name, and misses implicit relationships, so a human review of each batch is not optional.

Typed Links Make the Notes Computable

Notice the shift. A folder lets you find a note you already know exists. A typed graph lets you derive a fact no single note states, by chaining relationships. The question moves from "where did I write that?" to "what follows from what I know?"

Graph querying is the retrieval of answers from a graph by following relationships. In a graph database such as Neo4j the query language Cypher expresses a path as a pattern. Before the example, read the notation: parentheses are nodes, square brackets are relationships, and an arrow gives the direction. The query below asks for every paper that reports an experiment that used a given dataset.

MATCH (p:Paper)-[:REPORTS]->(e:Experiment)-[:USED]->(d:Dataset {name: "Dataset A"})
RETURN p.title, e.name

You do not need a graph database to benefit. A graph can live in your Markdown files as typed links in the frontmatter of each note, and a short script can read them and answer the same question. What matters is that the relationships are explicit and typed, not what stores them.

docs.title: Diagram: Personal Knowledge Graph Query Explorer
docs.text:
Personal Knowledge Graph Query Explorer

Type: graph-model sim-id: pkg-graph-query-explorer Library: vis-network Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/infographics/tree/main/docs/sims/learning-path-explorer Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: solve Learning Objective: The learner will solve five questions about a twelve-edge personal knowledge graph by following typed, directed relationships, and give each answer as the exact set of entities, with at least 4 of 5 correct.

Prerequisites: entity, relationship, typed relationship, graph schema, backlink, and graph querying, all defined in the section "From Files to a Knowledge Graph" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of five questions the learner selects the set of entities that answer it and submits. An answer is correct when the selected set equals the answer set in Content exactly. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Hovering over edges to read their types is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A relationship can be followed in either direction with the same meaning. (2) A question that needs more than one hop cannot be answered from the graph. (3) A paper that is not directly linked to a dataset is unaffected by that dataset.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level work needs the learner to carry out the traversal procedure on a concrete graph. The questions rise from one hop to three, so the learner practices chaining relationships, which is the property that makes a graph more than a folder.

Content:

The graph is invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative" in the sim. Entities and their types:

ID Entity Type E1 Run 07 Experiment E2 Run 08 Experiment D1 Dataset A Dataset D2 Dataset B Dataset S1 ADC Design v2 Design S2 ADC Design v3 Design P1 Paper Alpha Paper P2 Paper Beta Paper C1 ENOB Concept A1 Dr. Rivera Person

Relationships, each directed from the first entity to the second:

# From Relationship To 1 Run 07 TESTED ADC Design v2 2 Run 08 TESTED ADC Design v3 3 Run 07 USED Dataset A 4 Run 08 USED Dataset A 5 Run 08 USED Dataset B 6 ADC Design v3 REVISES ADC Design v2 7 Paper Alpha REPORTS Run 07 8 Paper Beta REPORTS Run 08 9 Paper Beta CITES Paper Alpha 10 Paper Alpha ABOUT ENOB 11 Paper Beta ABOUT ENOB 12 Dr. Rivera AUTHORED Paper Beta

Questions, in this order:

# Question Answer set Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which experiments used Dataset A? Run 07, Run 08 Follow USED edges backward into Dataset A (edges 3 and 4). 2 Which designs were tested in an experiment that used Dataset B? ADC Design v3 Dataset B is used only by Run 08 (edge 5), and Run 08 tested ADC Design v3 (edge 2). 3 Which papers report an experiment that tested the design that ADC Design v3 revises? Paper Alpha ADC Design v3 REVISES ADC Design v2 (edge 6), Run 07 tested ADC Design v2 (edge 1), and Paper Alpha reports Run 07 (edge 7). 4 Which papers are cited by a paper that Dr. Rivera authored? Paper Alpha Dr. Rivera authored Paper Beta (edge 12), and Paper Beta cites Paper Alpha (edge 9). 5 If Dataset A were found to be corrupted, which papers must be rechecked? Paper Alpha, Paper Beta Dataset A is used by Run 07 and Run 08 (edges 3 and 4), which are reported by Paper Alpha and Paper Beta (edges 7 and 8).

Provenance: The traversal procedure and the schema are from the section "From Files to a Knowledge Graph" of this chapter. The entities, names, and relationships are invented for illustration.

Rules: An answer set is computed by following edges only in their stated direction, or against it where the question asks for the "from" side. Each question has exactly one answer set, given above. A selection is correct only if it equals the answer set, with no missing and no extra entities.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the graph and question 1.
  2. The learner clicks the entities that answer the question and submits.
  3. The sim highlights the path that produces the correct answer set and shows the "Why" sentence, then advances.
  4. After question 5, the sim shows the count correct. The learner should notice that question 5 needs a path of two hops and has two answers.

Feedback: Five questions, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the "Why" sentence and the highlighted path. Incorrect: the correct answer set, the highlighted path, and the "Why" sentence. The correct set is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 5 correct" is shown, with whether the mastery threshold of 4 was met.

Starting State: The full graph is shown with edge types visible on hover and question 1 posed. The question on screen is "Which entities answer this, by following the relationships?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that typed, directed relationships let a program answer multi-hop questions, and that the PKG research rule of thumb is about 60 percent of value in nodes and 40 percent in relationships.

docs.title: Grounding a Model With the Graph
docs.text:
Graph retrieval-augmented generation (graph RAG) is retrieval-augmented generation, as introduced in Chapter 3, where the retrieved material is a subgraph of facts selected by following relationships, not a set of text passages ranked by similarity. The question is mapped to entities in the graph, the neighbourhood of those entities is collected, and the resulting facts are placed in the prompt with an instruction to answer from them.

The advantage over passage retrieval is on multi-hop questions. A vector search for "which papers need rechecking if Dataset A is corrupted?" finds passages that mention Dataset A and misses the paper that reports an experiment that used it, because that paper never names the dataset. Following the relationships finds it. A worked example: the question is converted to the entity "Dataset A", the traversal collects two experiments and two papers, and the prompt receives four lines such as "Run 07 USED Dataset A; Paper Alpha REPORTS Run 07", with the instruction "answer only from these facts; if they are insufficient, say so". The model's answer is then both grounded and checkable against named links.

The same caution as in Chapter 4 applies. The graph is only as good as its entities and relationships, an agent-extracted link that nobody reviewed can be wrong, and a graph that exposes private results to a tool must be governed. Chapter 19 returns to the privacy of a personal knowledge graph that an always-on agent can read.

docs.title: The Anatomy of an Agent Skill
docs.text:
Everything so far organizes what is known. The remainder of the chapter concerns what is done repeatedly. An agent skill is a packaged, reusable capability for an agent: a directory containing instructions, and optionally scripts and reference files, that teaches the agent how to carry out one kind of task the same way each time. A prompt you saved is a skill's ancestor. A skill adds a name, a description the agent can use to decide when it applies, and supporting material loaded only when needed.

The skill's central file is SKILL.md, a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter followed by instructions. Its parts have specific jobs.

The skill name is a short identifier, in lowercase with hyphens, that names the capability and typically matches the directory name. It is also how you invoke the skill explicitly.

The skill description is a one- or two-sentence statement of what the skill does and when to use it. It is the most important line in the file, for a reason that comes from how skills are loaded. An agent keeps only the names and descriptions of its available skills in context. It reads the full instructions only when it decides a skill applies.

Skill triggering is that decision: the agent compares the user's request with the descriptions of the available skills and loads the matching skill's instructions. A skill with a vague description, such as "helps with data", will trigger on the wrong requests or not at all. A skill whose description names the task and the situations that call for it will trigger reliably.

Skill instructions are the body of SKILL.md: the numbered procedure, the constraints, and the output format that the agent follows once the skill is loaded. They apply the techniques of Chapters 3 and 4, written once.

Supporting files are the other files in the skill directory: scripts the agent runs, reference documents it reads when needed, and templates it fills in. Keeping them outside SKILL.md keeps the always-loaded text small, because the agent opens a supporting file only when the instructions point to it.

A complete minimal skill for the running project, with illustrative content, has this layout and main file.

enob-report/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/enob.py
├── references/targets.md
└── templates/report.md

---
name: enob-report
description: Compute ENOB from a coherently sampled ADC record and write a one-page report. Use when the user asks for ENOB, SNDR, or an ADC characterization summary.
---

# ENOB Report

1. Read the record file the user names. If none is named, ask for it.
2. Run scripts/enob.py with the sampling rate and the nominal bits.
3. Compare the result with the target in references/targets.md.
4. Write the report using templates/report.md.

Never edit files in data/raw/. Report ENOB in bits to one decimal.

Triggering is easiest to understand with examples. Given the description above, the agent compares each request with it. "What is the ENOB of capture-07.csv?" matches the named task and the cue "ENOB", so the skill loads. "Give me an ADC characterization summary for the new board" matches the cue "characterization summary", so it loads. "Plot the spectrum of capture-07.csv" mentions the same file but asks for a different task, so it should not load, and a description that read "helps with ADC data" would have loaded it wrongly. "Draft the related-work paragraph" has nothing in common with the description, so it does not load.

Read the file as a reader would. The frontmatter is between the two lines of three hyphens and contains exactly two fields. The description does both jobs, saying what the skill does and when to use it. The body is short and procedural, and it points to the script, the reference, and the template by path.

A Vague Description Never Triggers

A common trap is a well-written skill with a description such as "analysis helper". The agent sees only the description when choosing, so the skill is skipped, or fires on requests it cannot handle. State the task and the cues in the description, test it with five realistic requests, and rewrite it until it fires on the right ones.

docs.title: Diagram: Skill Anatomy Labeler
docs.text:
Skill Anatomy Labeler

Type: microsim sim-id: skill-anatomy-labeler Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify, for each of eight lines or files of a skill, whether it is the skill name, the skill description, skill instructions, or a supporting file, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: skill name, skill description, skill instructions, supporting files, and SKILL.md, all defined in the section "The Anatomy of an Agent Skill" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight items the learner commits one of four labels. A label is correct when it equals the label in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Viewing the whole SKILL.md and directory tree is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The description only says what the skill does and not when to use it. (2) Scripts and templates are part of SKILL.md. (3) The name and the description are the same thing.

Instructional Rationale: Remember-level recognition is the base for later design work. Labeling items in a single realistic skill ties each term to a concrete example.

Content:

The skill is the enob-report skill shown in the chapter. The four labels are Skill name, Skill description, Skill instructions, and Supporting file.

# Item shown Correct label Why (shown as feedback) 1 name: enob-report Skill name It is the short identifier of the capability. 2 description: Compute ENOB from a coherently sampled ADC record and write a one-page report. Use when the user asks for ENOB, SNDR, or an ADC characterization summary. Skill description It states what the skill does and when to use it, which is what the agent reads to decide to load it. 3 1. Read the record file the user names. If none is named, ask for it. Skill instructions It is a step of the procedure that is followed once the skill is loaded. 4 Never edit files in data/raw/. Skill instructions It is a constraint in the body of SKILL.md. 5 scripts/enob.py Supporting file It is a script the instructions tell the agent to run, and it lives outside SKILL.md. 6 references/targets.md Supporting file It is a reference document opened only when the instructions point to it. 7 templates/report.md Supporting file It is a template the agent fills in, kept outside SKILL.md. 8 3. Compare the result with the target in references/targets.md. Skill instructions It is a procedural step that points to a supporting file.

Provenance: The skill and its parts are from the section "The Anatomy of an Agent Skill" of this chapter. The file contents are illustrative.

Rules: Each item has exactly one correct label. A line inside SKILL.md below the frontmatter is Skill instructions. A path to a file other than SKILL.md is a Supporting file.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the skill directory tree and SKILL.md with item 1 highlighted.
  2. The learner chooses one of the four labels and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence, then highlights the next item.
  4. After item 8, the sim shows the count correct.

Feedback: Eight items, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "This is a ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct label is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown, with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: The directory tree and SKILL.md are shown with item 1 highlighted. The question on screen is "Which part of the skill is this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that SKILL.md has YAML frontmatter with a name and a description, that the description says what the skill does and when to use it, that instructions are the body, and that scripts, references, and templates are supporting files opened only when pointed to.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
A research project that lasts needs memory that does not live in anyone's head or in a chat window. Plain files of defined types form a knowledge base. Typed links turn it into a graph that can be queried and used to ground an agent. And a skill packages one repeatable task so that it is done the same way, loaded only when it applies.

The main points to carry forward:

  • A knowledge base is built from research notes, specifications, glossaries, decision logs, and session logs, each with one job, joined by cross references.
  • Project memory is the part an agent loads to resume work, and a session log is the bridge between sessions.
  • A knowledge graph stores entities and typed, directed relationships, and a personal knowledge graph applies this to one researcher's own material, governed by a small schema.
  • Backlinks and entity extraction make the graph cheap to grow, and extracted links must be reviewed.
  • Graph querying and graph RAG answer multi-hop questions that text similarity misses.
  • An agent skill is a directory built around SKILL.md: a name, a description that drives triggering, instructions, and supporting files loaded on demand.

Your Project Can Remember

You can now sort project material into notes, specifications, glossary, decisions, and logs, answer a multi-hop question by following typed relationships, and name the four parts of a skill. That is the memory and the packaging the rest of the book builds on.

The next chapter takes the skill from a file you can read to one you can design, test, and share. Round up a task you do at least once a month, and bring it.

docs.title: Designing, Testing, and Sharing Agent Skills
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers the full life of a skill: choosing a scope, writing single-purpose skills, testing and evaluating them, versioning, sharing, installing, and maintaining them. It ends with a research skill template. After this chapter you can turn a repeatable task from your own workflow into a skill that a colleague can install and trust.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 17 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Reference Documents 2 Progressive Disclosure 1 Skill Scope 9 Single Purpose Skill 8 Skill Testing 5 Skill Evaluation 1 Skill Versioning 2 Skill Library 5 Skill Sharing 2 Skill Installation 1 Slash Command 1 Skill Composition 4 Skill Metadata 1 Skill Failure Modes 3 Skill Maintenance 1 Skill Examples 4 Research Skill Template 3

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 2: How Language Models Work
  • Chapter 3: Choosing Models and Writing Clear Prompts
  • Chapter 4: Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting
  • Chapter 5: Markdown Project Files and Version Control
  • Chapter 6: Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill

From a File You Read to a Tool You Trust

Reading a skill is easy. Trusting one is the hard part, and it comes from design choices and tests you run before anyone else relies on it. By the end you will have a procedure for turning a task you repeat into a skill a colleague can install without asking you how it works. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Scoping a Skill
docs.text:
The most consequential decision in a skill's life is made before any instruction is written: what it is for. Skill scope is the boundary of the task a skill covers, stated by what it takes as input, what it produces, and what it explicitly does not do. A single-purpose skill is a skill whose scope is one task with one kind of output. The recommendation of this chapter is to make skills single-purpose, and the reason is practical rather than aesthetic.

A skill that does one thing has a description that can be precise, so it triggers on the right requests. It has instructions short enough that the agent follows all of them. It has an output that can be checked against one set of acceptance criteria. And when it fails, the failure points to one place. A skill that "handles all the analysis for the project" fails all four ways at once: the description is vague, the instructions are long and the agent skips steps, the output is many things, and a failure could be anywhere.

A useful test of scope is the one-sentence rule. Write the skill's purpose as a single sentence of the form "Given X, produce Y, checked by Z." If you need the word "and" to join two different outputs, you probably have two skills. If you cannot name Z, you have not yet defined how anyone would know the skill worked.

Too broad Single purpose One-sentence form "Help with my ADC project" enob-report Given a coherently sampled record, produce a one-page ENOB report, checked by the five acceptance criteria. "Do the literature work" citation-verify Given a list of citations, produce a table of verified, corrected, or unverifiable entries, checked by a database lookup per entry. "Prepare the paper" figure-caption-check Given a figure and its caption, produce a list of missing caption elements, checked against the venue's checklist.

Table 1. Broad requests narrowed into single-purpose skills.

The Skill That Does Everything

A common trap is growing one skill by adding "while you are at it" steps until it does five jobs. It happens because adding a step is cheaper than creating a skill. The result triggers unreliably and fails in ways you cannot localize. When a skill needs a second output, split it, and let the two be composed.

docs.title: Writing the Skill: Progressive Disclosure and Reference Documents
docs.text:
A skill's text competes for the same context window as everything else, and the agent's attention is finite. Progressive disclosure is the design principle that makes a skill's content available in layers, so that only as much is loaded as the task needs. There are three layers. The metadata, that is the name and description, is always in context. The instructions in SKILL.md are loaded when the skill triggers. The supporting files are loaded only when an instruction points to them. A skill with a long reference table, a large template, and a library script pays for none of them until the step that uses them.

Reference documents are the supporting files that hold the knowledge a skill needs but that is too long or too specialized for SKILL.md: a venue's formatting rules, a table of measurement targets, a style guide, a data dictionary. The instruction should name the file and say when to read it: "If the target venue is IEEE, read references/ieee-checklist.md." That sentence is the entire cost of making a large body of knowledge available.

Three habits keep a skill's text effective:

  • Write the description last, and test it. The description decides triggering, so it should name the task, the inputs it recognizes, and the situations that call for it.
  • Keep SKILL.md short. A procedure of five to ten numbered steps, with the constraints stated once. If it grows beyond a page, move material to a reference document.
  • Prefer a script to prose for exact work. If a step is a computation, such as the ENOB formula, put it in a tested script the skill runs, rather than asking the model to do arithmetic from a description.

docs.title: Testing and Evaluating a Skill
docs.text:
A skill is a prompt with a name, and like any prompt it needs tests. Skill testing is running a skill on a fixed set of requests and checking the results against stated expectations. A skill needs two kinds of test, because it can fail in two distinct ways: it can be used when it should not be, or not used when it should.

Trigger tests check the description. Write a short list of realistic requests that should load the skill and a list that should not, including near misses that share vocabulary with the skill but ask for something else. Behavior tests check the output. Give the skill representative inputs, including an edge case and a case where the correct output is "cannot do this", and check each output against the skill's acceptance criteria from the specification.

Skill evaluation goes one step further: it measures. Because model output varies from run to run, a single success proves little. Evaluation runs each test several times, records the pass rate, and compares versions or compares the skill against doing the same task with no skill at all. A skill that improves the pass rate on your test set from 40 percent to 90 percent has earned its place. A skill that makes no measurable difference is overhead that costs context.

A worked example: for the enob-report skill, five trigger tests and five behavior tests are written. Two of the behavior tests are synthetic records with known ENOB values (an ideal 10-bit quantizer, and the same record with added noise), so the expected number is known in advance. The tests run three times each against version 1.0 of the skill and again against version 1.1. The results are tabulated, and a change is accepted only if the pass rate does not fall on any test.

Write the Should-Not-Trigger Tests First

Everyone tests that a skill fires when asked. Few test that it stays quiet when it should. Write four near-miss requests that share a keyword with your skill but ask for something different, and make sure none triggers it. That single list catches most description problems.

docs.title: Diagram: Skill Description Trigger Tester
docs.text:
Skill Description Trigger Tester

Type: microsim sim-id: skill-description-trigger-tester Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish, for each of eight user requests, whether a stated skill description should trigger the skill or not, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: skill description, skill triggering, single-purpose skill, and trigger tests, all defined in the sections "Scoping a Skill" and "Testing and Evaluating a Skill" above and in Chapter 6.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight requests the learner commits "should trigger" or "should not trigger". A choice is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the skill description is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any request that shares a keyword with the description should trigger the skill. (2) A request that is about the same files but for a different task should trigger it. (3) A skill should trigger on any request that mentions its domain.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level work needs the learner to separate the task a request asks for from the vocabulary it uses. Near-miss requests that share keywords force a judgment on the task and not on surface features.

Content:

The skill description shown is: "Check a SPICE netlist for floating nodes, a missing .end card, and unit suffix errors. Use when the user asks to lint, check, or validate a .sp or .cir netlist file."

# User request Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 Lint circuits/ldo.sp for floating nodes. Should trigger It asks for the checking task the description names. 2 Is there anything wrong with this netlist? (a .cir file is attached) Should trigger It asks for a check of a .cir netlist, which the description covers. 3 Run the transient simulation of ldo.sp and plot Vout. Should not trigger It asks for simulation and plotting. It mentions the same file but not the checking task. 4 Write a netlist for a two-stage op-amp. Should not trigger It asks for a netlist to be generated, not checked. 5 Validate that every .sp file under circuits/ ends with a .end card. Should trigger It asks for validation of a property the description names. 6 Explain what a floating node is. Should not trigger It is a concept question and does not ask for a file to be checked. 7 Check my Verilog testbench for syntax errors. Should not trigger It asks for a check, but of a different language than the description covers. 8 My 1M resistor behaves like one milliohm. Check the units in ldo.sp. Should trigger It asks for a check of unit suffixes in a .sp file. In SPICE, M means milli and MEG means mega.

Provenance: The trigger concept is from Chapter 6 and the section "Testing and Evaluating a Skill" of this chapter. The description and requests are invented for illustration, and the sim labels them "illustrative".

Rules: A request should trigger the skill when it asks for a task and an input type that the description names. Shared vocabulary alone does not make a request trigger. Each request has exactly one correct answer.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the skill description and request 1.
  2. The learner chooses "should trigger" or "should not trigger" and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence, then shows the next request.
  4. After request 8, the sim shows the count correct and lists the requests that share a keyword with the description but should not trigger.

Feedback: Eight requests, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: the correct answer plus the "Why" sentence. The correct answer is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: The description and request 1 are shown with no choice made. The question on screen is "Would an agent load this skill for this request?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that triggering is a comparison of the request with the description, that a skill needs tests for both firing and staying quiet, and that near-miss requests that share a keyword are the most useful trigger tests.

docs.title: Failure Modes and Maintenance
docs.text:
Skills fail in a small number of recurring ways. Skill failure modes are those characteristic patterns, and knowing them lets you diagnose a misbehaving skill by symptom instead of by guesswork. The most common are listed here.

  • Undertriggering: the skill is not used when it should be. The cause is almost always the description.
  • Overtriggering: the skill loads on requests it cannot handle. The cause is a description that is too broad.
  • Instruction drift: the skill loads, but the agent skips or reorders steps. The cause is usually a SKILL.md that is too long or a step that is not checkable.
  • Missing dependency: a script needs a library, tool, or file that is not present on the machine where the skill runs.
  • Stale reference: a reference document or a hard-coded path is out of date, so the skill gives a confident but obsolete answer.
  • Scope creep: the skill has accumulated extra jobs and now does none of them reliably.

Skill maintenance is the continuing work of keeping a skill correct as its surroundings change: models update, tools change versions, venues revise requirements, and your own conventions evolve. A skill with no maintenance decays quietly, because nothing breaks loudly. The remedy is routine: rerun the test set whenever the model, the tools, or the skill changes; date every reference document; and record in the skill's metadata when it was last verified.

docs.title: Diagram: Skill Failure Mode Classifier
docs.text:
Skill Failure Mode Classifier

Type: microsim sim-id: skill-failure-mode-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: attribute Learning Objective: The learner will attribute each of eight observed skill problems to one of six failure modes, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: the six skill failure modes (undertriggering, overtriggering, instruction drift, missing dependency, stale reference, scope creep), all defined in the section "Failure Modes and Maintenance" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight observations the learner commits one of six failure modes. A choice is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions list is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any skill problem is a problem with the model. (2) A skill that gives a wrong answer must have bad instructions. (3) A skill that does not run has failed to trigger.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level work needs the learner to trace a symptom to its cause. The observations share surface features, such as "it gave the wrong result", so the learner must reason from what changed or what was skipped.

Content:

# Observation Correct failure mode Why (shown as feedback) 1 The user asked for an ENOB report in plain words and the agent did not use the skill at all. Undertriggering The skill was not loaded for a request it covers, which points to the description. 2 Asked to plot a spectrum, the agent loaded the ENOB skill and produced a report nobody wanted. Overtriggering The skill loaded for a request it does not cover, which points to a description that is too broad. 3 The skill loaded, but the agent never ran the acceptance check in step 4 and reported success. Instruction drift The skill loaded and a step was skipped, which points to long or uncheckable instructions. 4 The skill's script fails with "No module named scipy" on a colleague's machine. Missing dependency The script needs a library that is not installed where the skill runs. 5 The report compares the result with a 9.0-bit target, but the project's target was raised to 9.5 bits last month. Stale reference The reference document was not updated when the requirement changed. 6 The skill now also converts units, drafts the paper's abstract, and files tickets, and its ENOB reports have become unreliable. Scope creep The skill has accumulated extra jobs and does none reliably. 7 A request that says "check the ENOB of this converter" was ignored, but "give me an ENOB report" works. Undertriggering The description names only one phrasing of the task, so a covered request was missed. 8 After a model update the skill runs, but the agent summarizes the procedure instead of executing steps 2 and 3. Instruction drift The skill loaded, and the agent departed from the steps, which points to instructions that need to be shorter or checkable.

Provenance: The six failure modes are from the section "Failure Modes and Maintenance" of this chapter. The observations are invented for illustration, and the sim labels them "illustrative".

Rules: Each observation has exactly one correct mode. A mode is chosen from the symptom of what did not happen (not loaded, loaded wrongly, step skipped, cannot run, outdated content, too many jobs).

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads observation 1 and the six failure modes.
  2. The learner chooses one mode and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence, then moves to the next observation.
  4. After observation 8, the sim shows the count correct and the recommended fix for each mode that was missed.

Feedback: Eight observations, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "This is ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct mode is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: Observation 1 is shown with the six modes listed and none chosen. The question on screen is "Which failure mode explains this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists six failure modes and states that undertriggering and overtriggering trace to the description, that instruction drift traces to long or uncheckable instructions, and that stale references and missing dependencies cause confident but wrong or failed output.

docs.title: Versioning, Sharing, and Installing
docs.text:
A skill is a directory of text files, so everything from Chapter 5 applies: it belongs in a Git repository, with commits that say what changed and why. Skill versioning is giving each released state of a skill an identifier, such as a semantic version number, so that users can tell which one they have and a result can be tied to the version that produced it. Increment the major number when a change alters the skill's output format or behavior in a way that could break a user's pipeline, and the minor and patch numbers for additions and fixes. Keep a short changelog in the repository.

Skill metadata is the descriptive information about a skill beyond its name and description: its version, author, license, the date it was last verified, and the tools or models it was tested with. Some packaging tools validate frontmatter strictly and reject unknown top-level keys, so it is safest to place custom fields under a single metadata map instead of adding new top-level keys.

---
name: enob-report
description: Compute ENOB from a coherently sampled ADC record and write a one-page report. Use when the user asks for ENOB, SNDR, or an ADC characterization summary.
metadata:
  version: "1.1.0"
  last_verified: "2026-10-15"
  tested_with: "NumPy 2.x"
---

Skill sharing is making a skill available to colleagues, and the simplest reliable channel is the Git repository that already holds it. A skill library is a collection of skills kept together, usually one repository with one directory per skill, with a README listing what each does. Skill installation is placing a skill where the agent looks for skills, and for most agents this means copying or linking the skill directory into a known skills folder, either per project or per user. One workable arrangement, used by the author of this book, is a single library repository cloned once, with the user's skills folder holding symbolic links to the directories inside it, so that a git pull updates every skill at once.

A slash command is an explicit way to invoke a skill by typing its name preceded by a slash, such as /enob-report, instead of relying on the agent to decide from the description. Explicit invocation is useful for skills that take action, for skills you want to run at a moment of your choosing, and as a fallback while you are still tuning a description.

Before you share a skill, ask what a new user needs that you carry in your head. Provide a README with a one-paragraph purpose, the install steps, an example request, an example of correct output, and the dependencies. Run the test set on a clean machine, not only on yours, because missing dependencies show up only there.

docs.title: Composing Skills and Studying Examples
docs.text:
Skill composition is combining single-purpose skills into a larger workflow, where each skill's output is the next skill's input. Composition is the reason to keep skills small. A pipeline of five skills, each with its own tests, is easier to debug than one skill that does the same five things, because a failure is localized to the step whose acceptance check fails.

This book is itself the product of a composed skill chain. Its repository's contributor instructions list the order: validate the course description, generate the concept graph, design the chapter structure, write the chapters, build the interactive simulations, and then generate the glossary, FAQ, quizzes, and references. Each step reads the files the previous step wrote, which is the handoff discipline of Chapter 1 with the artifact being a file in the repository.

The best way to learn skill design is to read working skills. Look at three properties in each example you read:

  • Description: does it name the task and the situations that call for it?
  • Procedure: are the steps numbered, short, and checkable?
  • Boundaries: does it say what it will not do and where it stops?

A Pipeline Is Skills Joined by Files

Notice why composing by files works. Each file is an artifact you can open, diff, and test. A skill that hands its work to the next by a file leaves you a checkpoint between every pair of steps, which is exactly where Chapter 9 will ask you to put review.

docs.title: A Research Skill Template
docs.text:
The template below collects the chapter into a starting point. It is a structure, not a rule: delete sections that a particular skill does not need, and keep it short.

---
name: <task-in-lowercase-with-hyphens>
description: <What it does, in one sentence. Use when <the situations and phrasings that call for it>.>
metadata:
  version: "0.1.0"
  last_verified: "<YYYY-MM-DD>"
---

# <Skill title>

## Purpose
Given <input>, produce <output>, checked by <acceptance check>.

## Inputs
- <required input and its format>
- Ask the user if <input> is missing; do not guess.

## Procedure
1. <Step with a checkable result.>
2. Run scripts/<name>.py with <arguments>.
3. If <condition>, read references/<name>.md.

## Output
<Exact format: file name, columns, or fields.>

## Acceptance checks
- <Testable condition 1>
- <Testable condition 2>

## Never
- <Boundary: files not to edit, actions needing approval.>

## When it cannot do the task
State what is missing and stop. Do not produce a partial result that looks complete.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
A skill is worth the effort when a task recurs and when the result can be checked. The practices that make one trustworthy are not exotic: a narrow scope, a precise description, short instructions backed by scripts and references, tests for both firing and staying quiet, versions, and routine maintenance.

The main points to carry forward:

  • Skill scope is set by a one-sentence rule, and a single-purpose skill triggers, executes, and fails more predictably.
  • Progressive disclosure loads the description always, the instructions on triggering, and reference documents only when pointed to.
  • Skill testing needs trigger tests, including near misses, and behavior tests with known answers. Skill evaluation measures pass rate over repeated runs against versions and against no skill.
  • Skill failure modes are undertriggering, overtriggering, instruction drift, missing dependency, stale reference, and scope creep, and each points to a different fix.
  • Versioning, metadata, sharing, installation, and slash commands make a skill portable. A Git repository is the simplest library.
  • Skill composition joins single-purpose skills by files, leaving a checkpoint between steps.
  • Maintenance is routine: rerun the tests whenever the model, tools, or skill change.

A Skill Others Can Trust

You can now scope a skill to one checkable task, write a description that triggers correctly, test it for both firing and staying quiet, and diagnose a misbehaving skill by its failure mode. That is a repeatable task turned into something a colleague can install.

The next chapter gives skills something to act with. Tools, files, shell commands, and subagents are what turn a procedure into an agent that does work. Round up your first skill, and bring it along.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter explains what makes an agent more than a chatbot: the agent loop, tool calls and definitions, file access, shell commands, code execution, and the Model Context Protocol. It covers sandboxing, permissions, and subagents that work in parallel with isolated context. After this chapter you can describe what an agent can reach and set limits on it.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 22 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Tool Use 430 Agent Loop 79 Tool Call 3 Tool Definition 2 File Access 98 Shell Commands 170 Web Search 8 Web Fetch 6 Code Execution 121 Sandboxing 116 Permissions 89 Permission Modes 64 Model Context Protocol 10 MCP Server 9 External Data Sources 2 API Integration 1 Database Access 1 Scripts in Skills 1 Subagent 34 Parallel Agents 1 Agent Memory 2 Agent Hooks 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 2: How Language Models Work
  • Chapter 3: Choosing Models and Writing Clear Prompts
  • Chapter 4: Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting
  • Chapter 6: Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill

Where Words Become Actions

Until now the model has only produced text. In this chapter it starts to read your files, run your scripts, and call other programs, and every one of those abilities is a boundary you set. You will leave able to say exactly what an agent can reach, and to narrow it. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Tool Use and the Agent Loop
docs.text:
A language model by itself can only emit text. Tool use is the mechanism by which a model's text is turned into actions in the world: the model emits a structured request to use a named capability, a surrounding program carries it out, and the result is returned to the model as more text. Reading a file, running a script, searching the web, and querying a database are all tools. Tool use is what separates an agent from an assistant, in the sense defined in Chapter 1.

Two terms describe the two sides of the mechanism. A tool definition is the description of a tool given to the model: its name, a plain-language statement of what it does, and a schema of the arguments it accepts. A tool call is the model's structured request to use a tool, with specific argument values. It is essential to see who does what. The model never executes anything. It writes a tool call, a program called the harness runs the tool, and the harness puts the result into the context.

A tool definition and a tool call, in a common JSON form, make this concrete. In the definition, name identifies the tool, description is what the model reads to decide when to use it, and input_schema states the arguments and their types. In the call, input supplies the values for one use.

{
  "name": "read_file",
  "description": "Read a text file from the project and return its contents.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": { "path": { "type": "string", "description": "Path relative to the project root" } },
    "required": ["path"]
  }
}

{ "tool": "read_file", "input": { "path": "results/enob-sweep-2026-10-15.csv" } }

The agent loop is the cycle that these pieces form. The model receives the task and the tool definitions, decides on the next action, and emits a tool call. The harness runs it and returns the result. The model reads the result and decides again, and the loop repeats until the model judges the task complete, an error stops it, or a limit is reached. Each pass through the loop adds the call and its result to the context, so a long loop uses the window faster than a long conversation would.

Step Who acts What happens 1. Decide Model Reads the task, the context, and the tool definitions, then chooses an action 2. Call Model Emits a tool call with arguments, or a final answer 3. Run Harness Executes the tool, subject to permissions 4. Observe Harness to model The result is added to the context 5. Repeat or stop Model Loops to step 1, or stops when done or when a limit is reached

Table 1. One pass through the agent loop and who performs each step.

The loop is why an agent can solve problems that a single prompt cannot. It can try something, see an error, and correct itself. It is also why errors compound: a wrong early observation shapes every later decision. The first MicroSim steps through a short loop so that you can predict the decision at each turn.

docs.title: Diagram: Agent Loop Stepper
docs.text:
Agent Loop Stepper

Type: microsim sim-id: agent-loop-stepper Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: infer Learning Objective: The learner will infer the agent's next tool call at each of five steps of a loop that diagnoses a low ENOB result, given the task and the results observed so far, with at least 4 of 5 correct.

Prerequisites: tool use, tool definition, tool call, agent loop, and the roles of the model and the harness, all defined in the section "Tool Use and the Agent Loop" above.

Evidence of Mastery: At each of five steps the learner commits one of three candidate next actions before the agent's actual choice is shown. A prediction is correct when it equals the action marked correct in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct. Stepping forward after the reveal is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The model runs the tools itself. (2) The agent decides everything in one planning step and then executes. (3) An error result ends the loop.

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level inference needs the learner to predict from the observed results, so that the dependence of each action on the previous observation becomes visible. Committing before the reveal makes the learner's mental model testable.

Content:

Task shown at the start: "The ENOB of capture-07.csv is 6.1 bits but the converter should give about 9. Find out why." Tools available: read_file, run_python, list_files. The data are invented and labeled "illustrative".

Step Result observed so far Candidate A Candidate B Candidate C Correct Why (shown as feedback) 1 Nothing yet. list_files on the project root run_python to recompute ENOB with a different formula read_file on the paper draft A The agent knows nothing about the project, so it looks at what exists before acting. 2 Files: data/raw/capture-07.csv, scripts/enob.py, docs/spec.md. read_file scripts/enob.py read_file data/raw/capture-07.csv list_files on data/raw A The result is computed by the script, so the method is the first thing to inspect. 3 enob.py computes SNDR over all FFT bins, including bin 0 (DC). run_python to print the DC bin magnitude of capture-07.csv rewrite enob.py without being asked read_file docs/spec.md A A hypothesis has appeared (DC counted as noise), and a cheap measurement tests it before anything is changed. 4 DC bin magnitude is 40 times larger than the next-largest non-signal bin. run_python to compute ENOB with the DC bin excluded, without editing the file edit enob.py and overwrite the old result report success A The agent tests the fix on a copy and compares, so the original file and result stay intact. 5 ENOB with DC excluded is 9.1 bits. report the cause and the evidence, and propose the change for approval silently apply the change to enob.py rerun the capture A The task was to find why, and a change to the project file is the researcher's decision.

Provenance: The loop structure is from the section "Tool Use and the Agent Loop" of this chapter. The files, results, and numbers are invented for illustration.

Rules: At each step exactly one candidate is correct, as marked. The correct candidate is the one that follows from the results observed so far and does not exceed the scope of the task.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the task, the tools, and the results observed so far.
  2. The learner chooses one of the three candidate next actions and submits.
  3. The sim reveals the agent's actual action, then shows the harness executing it and the result being added to the context.
  4. After step 5 the sim shows the count correct and the full loop as a list of calls and results.

Feedback: Five steps, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: the correct action and the "Why" sentence. The correct action is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 5 correct" is shown.

Starting State: The task and the three tools are shown with no results yet. The question on screen is "What should the agent do first?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the model emits a tool call and the harness executes it, that results are returned to the context, and that the loop repeats until the task is complete or a limit is reached.

docs.title: Reaching Files, Shells, and Code
docs.text:
Most useful tools for research fall into a few families, and each one carries its own risk. It is worth taking each in turn, because the risk of an agent is the sum of what its tools can do.

File access is the ability to read, create, edit, and delete files. Reading is the most common and usually the safest. Writing changes the project and should be covered by version control, which turns an unwanted edit into a one-command undo. The scope matters: an agent confined to the project directory can do far less damage than one that can write anywhere your user account can.

Shell commands are commands run in your command line environment: ls, grep, python, git, and anything else installed. A shell tool is the most general and therefore the most dangerous tool, because it is an open door to everything the account can do. The same shell that runs grep runs rm -rf, git push --force, and a command that downloads and executes a script from the internet.

Code execution is the running of code that the agent itself wrote, such as a Python script that analyzes a dataset. It is the capability that makes an agent useful for data work, and it multiplies the risk of the shell, because the code is new and unreviewed when it runs. An agent-written script might delete a directory it was meant to clean, send data to a service, or run for hours.

A worked example of how to read a shell command before approving it: ask what it changes, whether the change can be undone, and who else is affected. Five commands that an agent might propose in the ADC project illustrate the range.

Command What it changes Undoable? Reasonable response ls results/ Nothing, it only lists Not applicable Allow by pattern python scripts/enob.py data/processed/run07.csv Writes an output file Yes, if results are in version control Allow for scripts in the project rm -r results/old/ Deletes a directory Only from version control or backup Ask, and check the path git push --force origin main Rewrites the shared history Hard, and affects collaborators Deny, or ask with a warning curl https://example.com/setup.sh \| sh Executes downloaded code No Deny

Table 2. Reading shell commands by their effect, reversibility, and reach.

Code execution deserves a worked example of its own, because the code in question did not exist a minute ago. Suppose an agent proposes the following cleanup script. First, what it does: it visits every directory under results/ and, if the directory name begins with tmp, deletes it and everything inside it.

import shutil, pathlib

for d in pathlib.Path("results").iterdir():
    if d.is_dir() and d.name.startswith("tmp"):
        shutil.rmtree(d)

Reading it with the three questions above shows the problem. A directory named tmp-final-figures, which you kept deliberately, matches the pattern and is deleted without a trace, because shutil.rmtree does not use the trash. The fix is not to ban the script but to make it reviewable: print the list of directories it would delete first, require confirmation, and run it only on a clean working tree so that anything lost can be restored. A review of thirty seconds before the first run is the cheapest control in this chapter.

Family Typical use Characteristic risk Standard control File reading Load data, read notes Exposing sensitive files to the context Limit scope to the project File writing Edit scripts, save results Overwriting good work Version control, protect raw data Shell commands Run tools, inspect state Destructive or irreversible commands Permissions, command allow-lists Code execution Analysis, simulation Unreviewed code with side effects Sandbox, review before first run Web search and fetch Find and read pages Prompt injection, unreliable sources Treat results as untrusted

Table 3. Tool families, their risks, and the usual controls.

Web search is a tool that submits a query and returns a ranked list of results, and web fetch is a tool that retrieves the content of a specific page. Together they extend an agent past its knowledge cutoff, which is their main value for research. They also bring in the untrusted text discussed under prompt injection in Chapter 4. A fetched page is data, and nothing in it is an instruction. Citations that come from a search should be verified against the source, as in Chapter 2.

docs.title: Sandboxing and Permissions
docs.text:
Two complementary controls decide what an agent may actually do. They answer different questions, and a sound setup uses both.

Sandboxing is the technical restriction of what a running process can reach, enforced by the operating system or a container, so that even a misbehaving command cannot exceed it. A sandbox limits the filesystem the process can see or write, the network it can connect to, and the resources it can consume. Its strength is that it does not depend on the agent's cooperation: a command that tries to read outside the allowed directory simply fails. Typical sandboxes are containers, virtual machines, and operating-system sandboxes built into the agent tool.

Permissions are the rules that decide whether a given tool call is allowed, requires your approval, or is denied. They work at the level of the harness: before running a call, the harness checks it against the rules. A permission rule can match a tool, a command pattern, or a path. Permissions are policy and sandboxing is enforcement, so permissions without a sandbox rely on the harness being configured correctly, and a sandbox without permissions gives you no say over actions that are permitted but unwise.

A permission policy is usually a short list of rules that match a tool and a pattern. The generic form below is illustrative, and each tool has its own syntax. Read the rules first as plain statements: reading anything in the project is allowed, running scripts from scripts/ is allowed, deleting and pushing ask, and credentials and raw data are denied.

allow  read   ./**
allow  edit   ./scripts/** ./docs/**
allow  run    python scripts/*
ask    run    rm *   pip install *   git push *
deny   read   ~/.ssh/**   ./.env
deny   edit   ./data/raw/**
deny   run    curl * | sh   sudo *

The sandbox then enforces what the policy cannot guarantee. Suppose the agent writes a script that tries to open a file in your home directory. Permissions might have missed it, because the command was python scripts/helper.py, which the rules allow. A sandbox that limits the process to the project directory makes the open fail regardless of what the policy said. The two controls catch different mistakes, which is why you want both.

Permission modes are preset overall postures for how much the agent may do without asking. Names differ between tools, but the pattern is consistent:

  • Ask for everything: every file edit and command waits for your approval. Safest, and slow enough that people stop reading what they approve.
  • Auto-accept edits: file edits inside the project proceed, while commands still ask.
  • Plan or read-only: the agent may read and think but may not change anything, which is a good mode for the first look at an unfamiliar project.
  • Bypass: all checks are disabled. Appropriate only inside a sandbox that has nothing of value to lose, and never on a machine that holds credentials.

A good working pattern is to pair a tight mode with a permissive allow-list for the safe, frequent commands, so that the approvals you are asked for are rare and therefore read. Approval fatigue is a real hazard: an agent that asks fifty times an hour trains you to click yes without reading.

Bypass Is Not a Productivity Setting

A common trap is turning off all permission checks because the prompts are tedious. It happens because approval fatigue is real, and the cost of one destructive command is invisible until it lands. Fix the tedium instead: allow the safe, repeated commands by pattern, run in a sandbox, and keep the project under version control.

docs.title: Diagram: Agent Permission Boundary Judge
docs.text:
Agent Permission Boundary Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: agent-permission-boundary-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-persona-testing/tree/main/docs/sims/agent-autonomy-boundary Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge, for each of ten proposed agent actions, whether a stated permission policy allows it, requires approval, or denies it, with at least 8 of 10 correct.

Prerequisites: file access, shell commands, code execution, sandboxing, permissions, and permission modes, all defined in the sections "Reaching Files, Shells, and Code" and "Sandboxing and Permissions" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of ten actions the learner commits one of three outcomes. An outcome is correct when it equals the outcome in Content under the stated policy. Mastery is at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the policy is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any action inside the project directory is safe. (2) A command is safe if it is common. (3) Approval is needed for everything that changes a file.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work needs the learner to apply stated criteria to cases. The policy has three outcomes so that the learner must weigh reversibility and scope and not choose between allow and deny only.

Content:

The policy shown is illustrative. Rules apply in this order, and the first match decides.

Rule Condition Outcome 1 Reads or writes any path outside the project directory, or reads credentials or key files Deny 2 Any command that downloads and executes code, or uses elevated privileges Deny 3 Writes to data/raw/ Deny 4 Deletes files, installs packages, pushes to a remote, or sends data over the network Ask 5 Reads files in the project, or edits files in scripts/ or docs/, or runs a Python script from scripts/ Allow # Proposed action Correct outcome Why (shown as feedback) 1 Read docs/spec.md Allow Rule 5: a read inside the project. 2 Edit scripts/enob.py to fix a bug Allow Rule 5: an edit in scripts/. 3 Run python scripts/enob.py data/processed/run07.csv Allow Rule 5: a script from scripts/. 4 Overwrite data/raw/capture-07.csv with a cleaned version Deny Rule 3: raw data is never written. 5 Run rm -r results/old/ Ask Rule 4: deletion is irreversible without version control, so it needs approval. 6 Run pip install scipy Ask Rule 4: installing a package changes the environment. 7 Run curl https://example.com/setup.sh | sh Deny Rule 2: it downloads and executes unreviewed code. 8 Read ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 Deny Rule 1: it reads a credential file outside the project. 9 Run git push origin main Ask Rule 4: it sends project contents to a remote. 10 Edit ../other-project/notes.md Deny Rule 1: it writes outside the project directory.

Provenance: The permission concepts are from the sections "Reaching Files, Shells, and Code" and "Sandboxing and Permissions" of this chapter. The policy and actions are invented for illustration, and the sim labels them "illustrative policy". The domain example.com is reserved for documentation.

Rules: Rules are evaluated in numeric order and the first matching rule decides the outcome. Each action matches exactly one rule as given.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the policy and action 1.
  2. The learner chooses Allow, Ask, or Deny and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct, the matching rule number, and the "Why" sentence, then shows the next action.
  4. After action 10, the sim shows the count correct and the actions that were Ask, and states that these are the approvals the researcher would see.

Feedback: Ten actions, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the rule number and the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "The policy gives ." plus the rule number and the "Why" sentence. The correct outcome is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 10 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 8 was met.

Starting State: The policy and action 1 are shown with no choice made. The question on screen is "What does the policy say about this action?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that permissions are policy and sandboxing is enforcement, that actions outside the project, credentials, and downloaded code should be denied, that irreversible or outward-bound actions should need approval, and that raw data should be protected.

docs.title: Reaching Outside: MCP, Data Sources, and Skills With Scripts
docs.text:
An agent's built-in tools cover files, a shell, and the web. Research needs more: a lab database, a reference manager, a ticket tracker, a simulator's job queue. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that defines how an agent connects to external tools and data in a uniform way, so that a capability written once can be used by any agent that speaks the protocol. An MCP server is a program that exposes a set of tools, and sometimes data, over this protocol. The agent, as the client, discovers the server's tools and their definitions and then calls them like any other tool.

The benefit is reuse. Rather than building a custom integration for each agent, you run or install an MCP server for the service, and the tool definitions arrive in the standard form. The cost is a larger attack surface: every connected server is code that runs with some access, and its tool descriptions and results flow into the model's context. Treat a server like any dependency. Prefer ones you can read, give each the narrowest credentials that work, and know what it can reach.

Three kinds of connection are common in research. External data sources are read-only collections of information: a paper index, a standards database, a lab wiki. API integration is a connection to a service with an interface: a reference manager, a repository host, a job scheduler. Database access is the ability to query a database directly. For all three, the rule is least privilege. Give the agent a read-only credential unless the task requires writing, and scope it to the one schema or one project it needs.

Scripts in skills are the same idea inside the skill package of Chapters 6 and 7: a skill can include a script that the agent runs instead of doing a computation in its head. An exact calculation such as ENOB belongs in a tested script. The script is reviewed once, and the agent's job is to call it with the right arguments, which is a much smaller thing to get wrong.

docs.title: Subagents, Parallel Work, Memory, and Hooks
docs.text:
A subagent is a separate agent instance that a main agent starts to carry out one part of a task, with its own context window, and often with its own restricted set of tools. When it finishes, it returns a result, normally a summary, to the main agent. Two properties make subagents valuable. They isolate context: the five papers a subagent reads do not fill the main agent's window, and only the findings return. And they can run at the same time.

Parallel agents are subagents run concurrently on independent parts of a job. A worked example: you ask for a comparison of five SAR ADC papers. The main agent starts five subagents, each reading one paper and returning its design parameters and the sentences that support them. The main agent then merges the five results into a table. The wall-clock time is about that of one paper rather than five, and the main context holds five short results instead of five papers.

The costs are real. Each subagent consumes its own tokens, so total cost goes up even as time goes down. The summary a subagent returns is lossy, and an error inside a subagent is invisible unless the result is checked. Parallel agents that write to the same file can overwrite each other, so assign each its own output file, or keep parallel work read-only. These are the problems of orchestration, which Chapters 9 and 10 develop.

Agent memory is whatever persists across the agent's sessions. A model has none of its own, so memory is implemented as files: the project instruction file of Chapter 5, the knowledge base and session logs of Chapter 6, and files the agent writes to remember what it has learned. Memory in files is good for a researcher, because it is inspectable and editable. You can read what the agent remembers, correct it, and put it under version control.

Agent hooks are scripts that the harness runs automatically at defined moments, such as before a tool is used, after a file is edited, or when the agent stops. A hook is deterministic: unlike an instruction in a prompt, which the model may or may not follow, a hook always runs. This makes hooks the right tool for rules that must never be skipped, such as running the test suite after an edit, blocking any command that matches a dangerous pattern, or committing the work to version control when a session ends.

Instructions Are Suggestions, Hooks Are Rules

Notice the difference in kind. A line in an instruction file asks the model to behave. A hook makes the harness behave, whatever the model decides. When a rule matters enough that you would be unhappy to see it skipped once, move it from the prompt to a hook or a permission.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
An agent is a model plus tools plus a loop, and its power and its risk are the same quantity: what its tools can reach. Setting limits is not a barrier to using agents; it is what lets you use them with confidence.

The main points to carry forward:

  • Tool use turns the model's text into actions. The model writes a tool call against a tool definition, and the harness executes it.
  • The agent loop decides, calls, observes, and repeats, so early errors compound.
  • File access, shell commands, and code execution are increasingly powerful and increasingly risky, and version control is the safety net for them.
  • Web search and fetch extend knowledge, and their results are untrusted data.
  • Sandboxing enforces limits technically, permissions set policy, and permission modes are presets, and none of them should be bypassed for convenience.
  • MCP servers, data sources, APIs, and databases connect agents to research systems, with least-privilege credentials.
  • Subagents and parallel agents isolate context and save time at a token cost, and their results must be checked.
  • Agent memory lives in files you can inspect, and hooks enforce rules deterministically.

You Can Draw the Boundary

You can now describe the loop an agent runs, name what its tools can reach, and set permissions so that irreversible and outward-bound actions need your approval. That is the control surface for everything an agent does in the chapters ahead.

The next chapter moves from what a single agent can reach to how you supervise it and divide work among agents with defined roles. Round up the limits you would set, and bring them.

docs.title: Supervising Agents and Defining Agent Roles
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers how to supervise agents that act on your behalf: autonomy levels, logging, failure modes, runaway behavior, cost control, scheduling, and trust boundaries. It then defines the specialized roles in an agent team, such as planning, execution, reviewer, research, coding, and writing agents. After this chapter you can assign roles and decide how much autonomy each agent gets.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 2: How Language Models Work
  • Chapter 3: Choosing Models and Writing Clear Prompts
  • Chapter 4: Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting
  • Chapter 6: Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill
  • Chapter 8: Agents, Tool Use, and Subagents

A Flock Needs a Shepherd

One agent you can watch. Several agents, running while you work on something else, need rules you wrote in advance: how much each may do on its own, what it must log, and when it must stop. This chapter gives you those rules and the roles that make a team of agents legible. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Autonomy and Supervision
docs.text:
Agent autonomy is the degree to which an agent acts without a human decision at each step. It is a dial, not a switch, and the right setting is different for each task. An agent that may only suggest has no autonomy and no risk, and delivers a fraction of the benefit. An agent that acts unattended delivers the full benefit and carries the full risk. The art is to set the dial per task from the properties of the task and not from your confidence in the model.

Three properties of a task determine how far the dial can safely turn. Reversibility is whether the effect can be undone: an edit to a file in version control can, and an email that has been sent cannot. Reach is whether the result leaves your control, by being sent, published, or written to a shared system. Verifiability is whether you or a script can check the result quickly and objectively: a program that must pass tests is verifiable, and a paragraph of related work is not, without reading the cited papers.

A small ladder of levels makes the choice concrete. The levels are a convention of this book and not a standard.

Level Name The agent may Typical use 0 Suggest only Propose; you perform the action Anything that leaves your control and cannot be checked 1 Approve each step Act after you approve each action Irreversible or outward-bound actions that can be checked 2 Act within a boundary Act freely inside a defined scope, and stop at gates for your approval Reversible work whose quality needs a human read 3 Act and report Act unattended and report afterwards Reversible, local, automatically verifiable work

Table 1. Autonomy levels and where each fits.

The assignment rule used in this chapter's exercise follows from the three properties. If the result leaves your control and cannot be verified, the agent suggests only. If it leaves your control and can be verified, each step needs approval. If it stays local but cannot be undone, each step needs approval. If it is local and reversible but cannot be checked quickly, the agent acts within a boundary and stops at gates. If it is local, reversible, and verifiable, it can act and report.

Agent supervision is the set of practices by which you keep a deployed agent honest while it works: watching what it does, bounding what it may do, sampling its output, and stopping it when it departs from the task. Supervision is not the same as reading everything. It is the design of where a human looks, so that attention goes where the risk is.

Autonomy Follows the Task, Not the Model

Notice what the three properties are about: the effect and not the agent. A very capable model should still not send email unreviewed, and a modest one can safely reformat a bibliography. Set autonomy by asking what the worst result of the action would cost and whether you could tell.

docs.title: Diagram: Agent Autonomy Level Assigner
docs.text:
Agent Autonomy Level Assigner

Type: microsim sim-id: agent-autonomy-level-assigner Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-persona-testing/tree/main/docs/sims/agent-autonomy-boundary Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: recommend Learning Objective: The learner will recommend an autonomy level from 0 to 3 for each of eight research tasks from its reversibility, reach, and verifiability, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: agent autonomy, reversibility, reach, verifiability, and the four autonomy levels, all defined in the section "Autonomy and Supervision" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight tasks the learner commits one of four levels. A level is correct when it equals the level in Content, which follows from the assignment rule in Rules. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the task attributes is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A capable model deserves more autonomy on every task. (2) Anything local is safe to run unattended. (3) If a result is outward-bound, a quick look at it is enough.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work needs the learner to apply criteria to cases and defend a choice. The attributes are given for each task, so the decision is about weighing them and not about guessing facts.

Correct level Why (shown as feedback) 1 Reformat the entries of refs.bib to a venue's style Yes, in version control No Yes, the document compiles and entries can be diffed 3 Local, reversible, and verifiable, so it can act and report. 2 Draft a related-work paragraph for your paper Yes No No, claims need reading the cited papers 2 Local and reversible, but quality needs a human read, so it works within a boundary and stops at a gate. 3 Email a summary of the results to a collaborator No Yes No 0 It leaves your control and cannot be checked, so the agent suggests and you send. 4 Push the analysis branch to the group's shared repository No Yes Yes, the diff and test results can be checked 1 It leaves your control, so each step needs your approval, though it is checkable. 5 Delete intermediate files under results/tmp/ No No Yes, a dry run lists them 1 It is local but cannot be undone, so each step needs approval. 6 Run the nightly parameter sweep and save results to a new folder Yes No Yes, a check script validates the output 3 Local, reversible, and verifiable, so it can act and report. 7 Refactor an analysis script that has no tests Yes No No 2 Reversible and local, but without tests the result cannot be checked quickly, so a human read is needed. 8 Submit a job that spends the lab's shared compute quota No Yes Yes, the job's parameters can be reviewed 1 It leaves your control, so each step needs approval.

If Leaves your control is Yes and Verifiable is Yes, the level is 1. If Leaves your control is No and Reversible is No, the level is 1. If Leaves your control is No, Reversible is Yes, and Verifiable is No, the level is 2. If Leaves your control is No, Reversible is Yes, and Verifiable is Yes, the level is 3.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees task 1 with its three attributes.
  2. The learner chooses a level from 0 to 3 and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether the level was correct and the "Why" sentence, with the rule that applied.
  4. After task 8, the sim shows the count correct, and a summary of how many tasks fell at each level.

The correct level is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.
