Chapter Anchors: The chapter states four levels from 0 to 3, three properties (reversibility, reach, verifiability), and the assignment rule above, and that autonomy is set by the task and not by the model's capability.

docs.title: Logging, Failure Modes, and Runaway Agents
docs.text:
Agent logging is the recording of what an agent did, in a form you can read afterward. A useful log has, for each step, the time, the tool called and its arguments, the result or an excerpt of it, the files changed, the tokens used, and the model and settings in force. Logs serve three purposes: they let you audit what happened overnight, they let you debug a failure by finding the step at which things went wrong, and they let you reproduce a result. Keep them as plain files in or beside the project, so that they are searchable and, where appropriate, versioned.

Agents fail in recognizable ways, and naming the patterns is the first step to catching them. Agent failure modes commonly include the following.

  • Premature completion: the agent reports success without having run the check that defines success.
  • Hallucinated result: the agent reports a number or file that no tool produced.
  • Scope drift: the agent fixes something nobody asked it to touch.
  • Test weakening: faced with a failing test, the agent edits the test and not the code.
  • Wrong arguments: the agent calls the right tool with the wrong path, parameter, or units.
  • Runaway loop: the agent repeats an action without progress.

A runaway agent is an agent that continues acting beyond the point it should have stopped, by looping, spawning further work, or consuming resources without converging. The usual cause is a loop with no termination limit and a model that interprets each failure as a reason to try again. The defenses are mechanical: set a maximum number of steps, a time limit, and a budget on tokens or money; require that the agent stop and report when the same error recurs; and make destructive actions require approval.

Done Is a Claim, Not a Fact

A common trap is accepting an agent's statement that a task is complete. It happens because the report is fluent and the check is tedious. Make the check part of the task: require the output of the acceptance check in the report, and treat a "done" without it as unfinished.

Cost control is the set of limits and habits that keep agent spending predictable. Agents are expensive in a particular way. Each pass through the agent loop resends the growing context, so cost grows faster than the number of steps. A worked example with illustrative numbers shows the effect. The task starts with a 10,000-token context, and each iteration adds 2,000 tokens of tool results. At iteration \( i \) the input is \( 10{,}000 + 2{,}000(i-1) \) tokens. Over 10 iterations the total input is \( 10 \times 10{,}000 + 2{,}000 \times (0+1+\dots+9) = 190{,}000 \) tokens. Over 20 iterations it is \( 20 \times 10{,}000 + 2{,}000 \times (0+1+\dots+19) = 580{,}000 \) tokens. Doubling the steps roughly tripled the cost. At 3 dollars per million input tokens, the figures are about 0.57 and 1.74 dollars, small for one run and not small for a team of agents running all night.

The controls follow from the arithmetic. Set a step limit and a spending cap. Summarize or reset the context between phases. Use a smaller, cheaper model for routine steps and a stronger one only where it matters. Watch usage as a metric, and read the first few runs of any new workflow closely, since cost surprises appear at the beginning.

Failure mode What you would see in the log Mechanical defense Premature completion "Done" with no check output Require check output in the report Hallucinated result A number with no producing tool call Trace every reported value to a call Scope drift Edits to files outside the request Path permissions; review the diff Test weakening Test file changed with a failing code change Protect tests, or review test diffs first Wrong arguments Tool errors, or results from the wrong file Read the first calls of a new workflow Runaway loop The same call repeated many times Step limit, repeat detector, spending cap

Table 2. Failure modes, how they appear in a log, and a mechanical defense for each.

docs.title: Scheduling, Background Work, and Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
Task scheduling is arranging for an agent task to run at a set time or interval, such as a nightly literature sweep or a weekly rerun of an analysis when new data arrive. Background tasks are tasks an agent runs while you do other work, whether started now or by a schedule. The two share one hazard: nobody is watching. Before an agent runs unattended, four things should be true.

  1. The scope is narrow and written down: which files and tools it may use.
  2. The task is idempotent, which means running it twice gives the same result as running it once, so a repeated or interrupted run does no harm.
  3. It writes a log, and the log is where you look first the next morning.
  4. It has limits on steps, time, and spending, and it stops and reports when it hits them.

Agent evaluation is measuring how well an agent performs a task, as skill evaluation measured a skill in Chapter 7. The method is the same at a larger scale: a fixed set of tasks with known good outcomes, repeated runs because behavior varies, and a record of success rate, cost, and time. Evaluate an agent before you give it autonomy, and again after you change its model, tools, or instructions.

A trust boundary is a line between components or sources you trust and those you do not, across which data must be checked before it is acted on. For an agent, the content of a web page, an email, a downloaded paper, and the output of a third-party tool are all outside the boundary. The practical consequence is that text crossing the boundary is treated as data and not as instructions, and that the agent holding the most dangerous capabilities should read the least trusted text. Chapter 4 introduced prompt injection as the attack that exploits a missing boundary.

Credential handling is the discipline of managing secrets such as passwords, API keys, and tokens so that an agent can use a service without exposing the secret. The rules are short. Never put a secret in a prompt, an instruction file, a skill, or a repository. Provide secrets through environment variables or a secrets manager. Issue the narrowest credential that works: read-only where reading is enough, scoped to one project, and short-lived where the service allows it. Where possible, have the harness inject the credential at the moment of use, so that the model never sees it. Rotate any credential that may have entered a log or a context.

docs.title: Defining Agent Roles
docs.text:
Supervising a single agent is a problem of attention. Supervising several is a problem of legibility: you must be able to say what each is for, what it may touch, and what it hands on. Agent roles are named responsibilities that divide work among agents, each with a defined purpose, inputs, outputs, tools, and autonomy level. A role is written once, as an agent specification file, and reused. Giving each agent one role has the same benefits as single-purpose skills: a narrow instruction set, a checkable output, and failures that localize.

Two roles frame the book's model of a team. A planning agent reads, explores, and decomposes: it surveys literature, breaks a problem into tasks, drafts specifications and acceptance criteria. Its output is a plan or a document, usually reversible and cheap to discard, so it can be given high autonomy and run in volume. An execution agent carries out a defined task: it writes code, runs analyses, builds simulations, prepares figures. Its output changes files and consumes resources, so it is bounded by its specification and its permissions, and its results are checked.

The planner-executor pattern is the arrangement in which a planning agent produces a specification and an execution agent carries it out, with the specification serving as the handoff. The pattern is effective for a reason that goes back to Chapter 4: the plan is a document you can read and correct before any execution happens, and the execution agent has an unambiguous task and acceptance criteria. It also reduces cost, because the strong, expensive model can plan and a smaller one can execute routine steps.

A reviewer agent is an agent whose job is to check another agent's output against stated criteria and report defects. It earns its keep because it works from the criteria and not from the producer's intentions, and it can be run by a different model, which gives some independence. It does not replace a human or a script. A reviewer shares the weaknesses of language models in general, so it complements tests and your own sampling instead of substituting for them.

Domain agents specialize an execution or planning role for one kind of research work:

  • A literature agent searches, triages, and summarizes papers, and its output is a reading list with extracted claims. A research agent is the broader form that gathers and organizes information for a question.
  • An analysis agent loads data, runs statistical and signal-processing steps, and produces tables and plots.
  • A coding agent writes, runs, and debugs code, including simulation scripts and tests.
  • A writing agent drafts and revises prose from notes and results, within the author's voice and the venue's conventions.

An agent handoff is the transfer of work from one agent to another. A handoff is where information is lost, so it is worth designing explicitly. A good handoff artifact states the goal, the inputs with their locations, the constraints, the acceptance criteria, what has been done, and what questions remain. It is a file, as in Chapter 1's workflow, so that you can read it. Context isolation is the practice of giving each agent only the context its role needs, and not the whole history, so that an agent is not distracted, cannot leak what it should not see, and cannot be misled by another agent's tangents.

Role Main job Typical output Typical autonomy Typical check Planning agent Decompose, survey, specify Plan, specification 2 or 3 Human read of the plan Execution agent Carry out a specified task Files, results 1 or 2 Acceptance criteria, tests Reviewer agent Check output against criteria Defect list 3 Sample of its findings Literature agent Search and summarize papers Annotated list 2 Citation lookup Analysis agent Run analysis Tables, plots 2 Known-answer tests Coding agent Write and test code Scripts, tests 2 Tests, diff review Writing agent Draft and revise text Section drafts 2 Author read; claim check

Table 3. Agent roles and their usual outputs, autonomy levels, and checks. The levels refer to Table 1 and are starting points, not rules.

Write the Role as a Job Description

For each agent, write five lines: purpose, inputs, outputs, tools it may use, and when it must stop and ask. If you cannot fill in the last line, you have not decided its autonomy yet, and the agent will decide for you.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Agents can be given real work only when you can see what they do and bound what they can do. Autonomy is set per task, from reversibility, reach, and verifiability. Logs, limits, and checks make failures visible and bounded. Roles make a group of agents legible.

The main points to carry forward:

  • Agent autonomy is a dial set per task by reversibility, reach, and verifiability, not by the model's capability.
  • Supervision is the design of where a human looks. Logging makes the work auditable and reproducible.
  • Agent failure modes, including premature completion, hallucinated results, scope drift, test weakening, wrong arguments, and runaway loops, each have a mechanical defense.
  • Cost control uses step limits, spending caps, and context resets, because loop cost grows faster than the number of steps.
  • Scheduled and background tasks need narrow scope, idempotence, logs, and limits before they run unattended.
  • Trust boundaries and credential handling keep untrusted text as data and secrets out of the model's context.
  • Roles such as planning, execution, reviewer, literature, analysis, coding, and writing agents divide work. The planner-executor pattern makes the plan a readable handoff.
  • Handoffs and context isolation keep information from being lost or leaked between agents.

A Team You Can Read

You can now set an autonomy level from reversibility, reach, and verifiability, name the failure that a log line shows, and write a role as a job description with a stopping rule. That makes a group of agents something you can supervise.

The next chapter assembles these roles into coordinated teams, with task queues, handoff protocols, review checkpoints, and a candid look at when adding agents stops paying off. Round up the roles you would need for your project, and bring the list.

Summary
docs.text: This chapter develops orchestration: breaking work into tasks, queuing and prioritizing them, defining handoff protocols, and placing review checkpoints and human approval gates. It explains span of control, delegation, and the 20-planning-agent, 10-execution-agent model. After this chapter you can design a coordinated agent team and judge when scaling it stops paying off.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 4: Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting
  • Chapter 6: Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill
  • Chapter 8: Agents, Tool Use, and Subagents
  • Chapter 9: Supervising Agents and Defining Agent Roles

Conducting, Not Typing

Launching thirty agents is easy. Knowing what they should do, in what order, and how you will review thirty outputs is the actual work. This chapter gives you the arithmetic and the structure to do it. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: The Team and the Orchestrator
docs.text:
An agent team is a set of agents with defined roles that work toward one shared goal through explicit handoffs. Orchestration is the coordination of that work: deciding what is done, by which agent, in what order, with what checks, and what happens when something goes wrong. The orchestrator is whoever performs this coordination. In this book it is the researcher, who may be helped by an orchestrating agent that keeps the queue and drafts status reports, but who remains accountable for the result.

The book's working model divides the team into two groups. A planning agent team is a group of planning agents that explore, decompose, and specify: they survey literature, propose approaches, draft specifications and acceptance criteria, and critique each other's plans. An execution agent team is a group of execution agents that carry out specified tasks: they write code, run simulations and analyses, and prepare figures and text. The agent ratio is the number of agents in each group. The model used throughout this book is roughly 20 planning agents to 10 execution agents.

The reason for the two-to-one ratio is a property of the outputs, not a rule of nature. Planning output is cheap and reversible: a plan that turns out to be wrong costs a few minutes of reading and is discarded. It is therefore sensible to produce many plans in parallel and let you choose. Execution output changes files, consumes compute, and must be verified, and each unit of it costs more of your attention to check. So the execution side is kept smaller. The numbers are a design target and not a law. They should move with how much attention you have and how checkable your tasks are, as the arithmetic later in the chapter shows.

Attention Is the Scarce Resource

Notice that nothing in the team's size is limited by compute or by the number of agents you may launch. The limit is the number of outputs you can responsibly read in a day. Everything in orchestration is a way of spending that attention where it prevents the most damage.

docs.title: Breaking Work Down
docs.text:
Work breakdown is the decomposition of a goal into tasks that are small enough to specify and to check, as in the task decomposition of Chapter 1. Each task in a breakdown should have an owner role, an input, an output, and an acceptance check. Task dependencies are the relations among tasks that say which must finish before another can start, because one needs the other's output. A task queue is the ordered list of tasks waiting to be done, with their status, usually kept as a plain file in the project so that agents and the researcher read the same record.

Dependencies determine how much a team can parallelize. A worked example uses nine tasks from the running ADC project, with illustrative durations in hours. Each task and its prerequisites:

Task Name Duration (h) Needs T1 Literature survey 3 none T2 Measurement procedure draft 2 T1 T3 ENOB script 3 T2 T4 Test suite 2 T2 T5 Simulation run 4 T3, T4 T6 Analysis 2 T5 T7 Figures 1 T6 T8 Report draft 3 T6 T9 Final assembly 1 T7, T8

Table 1. A task queue with durations and dependencies.

The tasks add up to 21 hours of work. With as many agents as you like, the project still cannot finish before the longest chain of dependent tasks, called the critical path. Here the chain T1, T2, T3, T5, T6, T8, T9 takes 3 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 18 hours. The test suite T4 can slip by one hour without delaying anything, and the figures T7 by two hours. Adding agents cannot shorten 18 hours. Only shortening a task on the critical path can, and even then the next-longest chain takes over: reducing T3 from 3 hours to 1 hour moves the finish to 17 hours, not 16, because the path through T4 then becomes critical.

docs.title: Diagram: Task Dependency Critical Path Scheduler
docs.text:
Task Dependency Critical Path Scheduler

Type: graph-model sim-id: task-dependency-critical-path Library: vis-network Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/statistics-course/tree/main/docs/sims/view-task-graph Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the earliest finish time, the critical path, and the slack of tasks in a nine-task dependency graph, and recalculate the project duration after one duration changes, with at least 4 of 5 answers correct.

Prerequisites: task dependencies, task queue, critical path, earliest finish, and slack, all defined in the section "Breaking Work Down" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of five questions the learner enters a value or selects a path. An answer is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Dragging nodes or reading a task's details is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The project duration is the sum of all task durations. (2) Adding agents shortens any schedule. (3) Shortening a critical task always shortens the project by the same amount.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level work needs the learner to carry out the forward-pass calculation on a real graph and then see how changing one duration moves the critical path.

Content:

The tasks, durations in hours, and prerequisites are those in the chapter's Table 1: T1 (3, none), T2 (2, T1), T3 (3, T2), T4 (2, T2), T5 (4, T3 and T4), T6 (2, T5), T7 (1, T6), T8 (3, T6), T9 (1, T7 and T8). The numbers are illustrative and labeled "illustrative" in the sim.

# Question Answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 What is the earliest finish time of T5, in hours? 12 T3 finishes at 8 and T4 at 7. T5 starts at the later, 8, and runs 4 hours. 2 Which tasks form the critical path? T1, T2, T3, T5, T6, T8, T9 The longest chain is 3 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 18 hours. 3 What is the slack of T4, in hours? 1 T4 could finish at 8 without delaying T5, which starts at 8. T4 finishes at 7, so its slack is 1 hour. 4 What is the project duration, in hours? 18 T9 starts when T8 finishes at 17, and takes 1 hour. 5 If T3 is reduced from 3 hours to 1 hour, what is the new project duration, in hours? 17 T3 then finishes at 6, but T4 finishes at 7, so T5 starts at 7 and the project ends at 17.

Provenance: The method and the task table are from the section "Breaking Work Down" of this chapter. The durations are invented for illustration.

Rules: Earliest start of a task = the maximum earliest finish of its prerequisites, or 0 if none. Earliest finish = earliest start + duration. The project duration is the maximum earliest finish over all tasks. A task is on the critical path when its slack is 0, where slack = latest finish - earliest finish and the latest finish does not delay the project duration. Durations are whole hours.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the graph with durations on the nodes and question 1.
  2. The learner enters the number or selects the tasks and submits.
  3. The sim shows the correct answer and highlights the relevant tasks and the forward pass of earliest start and finish times.
  4. For question 5, the sim lets the learner change T3's duration and shows the new critical path.
  5. After question 5, the sim shows the count correct. The learner should notice that cutting 2 hours from a critical task saved only 1 hour.

Feedback: Five questions, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: the correct answer and the "Why" sentence. The correct answer is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 5 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 4 was met.

Starting State: The graph is shown with durations on the nodes and no times computed. The question on screen is "When can T5 finish?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's task table lists nine tasks totalling 21 hours, a critical path of 18 hours through T1, T2, T3, T5, T6, T8, and T9, and a project duration of 17 hours if T3 is reduced to 1 hour.

docs.title: Handoffs, Shared Workspaces, and Conflicts
docs.text:
A handoff protocol is the agreed form in which work passes from one agent to the next. Chapter 9 listed what a handoff must contain: the goal, the inputs, the constraints, the acceptance criteria, the work done, and the open questions. The protocol makes this uniform: one file format, one location, and a small fixed set of status values. A minimal protocol uses five statuses: queued, running, needs-review, accepted, and rejected. An agent never marks its own work accepted. That status belongs to a reviewer agent, a script, or you.

A shared workspace is the common area where the team's files live. Because several agents may act at once, structure prevents collisions. Give each agent its own output directory, or its own Git branch, so that two agents never write the same file. Keep inputs read-only. Make merging an explicit step that goes through review, instead of letting agents write into the main line directly. The Git practices of Chapter 5 provide exactly this.

Conflict resolution is deciding what to do when two agents produce incompatible results, such as two analysis agents reporting different ENOB values for the same record, or two planning agents recommending different architectures. Averaging is rarely right. A sound procedure follows. Establish whether the disagreement is about facts or about judgment. For facts, trace each result to its inputs and method, and find the first point of divergence, which is usually a different assumption, window function, or file version. For judgment, ask a reviewer agent for the evidence on each side, then decide yourself. Whatever the outcome, record the decision and the reason in the decision log of Chapter 6, so that the conflict is not silently reopened.

Make the First Divergence Visible

When two agents disagree, do not ask which is right. Ask each to list its inputs, settings, and file versions in a table, then compare the tables line by line. The disagreement almost always sits on one row, and finding it takes minutes.

docs.title: Review, Approval, and Researcher Attention
docs.text:
A review checkpoint is a defined point in the workflow at which output is examined before the next step uses it. A human approval gate is a review checkpoint at which a person must say yes before work continues. Checkpoints can be automated, for example a test suite or a check script, or performed by a reviewer agent. A gate requires you. The difference matters, because gates consume the scarce resource.

Researcher attention is the time and concentration you can give to reviewing in a day, and it is the binding constraint on the size of a team. It can be treated quantitatively. If a planning agent produces \( k_p \) outputs a day and each takes \( r_p \) minutes to review, and an execution agent produces \( k_e \) outputs taking \( r_e \) minutes, then for \( n_p \) planning agents and \( n_e \) execution agents the daily review load, with \( c \) minutes for resolving conflicts, is

\[ L = n_p\, k_p\, r_p + n_e\, k_e\, r_e + c. \]

A worked example with illustrative numbers: 20 planning agents each give one output a day at 6 minutes each, 10 execution agents each give one output a day at 15 minutes each, and conflicts take 30 minutes. The load is \( 120 + 150 + 30 = 300 \) minutes, which is 5 hours. If you have 4 hours of attention, the team is too large for the attention available. Three remedies exist. Reduce the team. Increase the share of review handled by scripts and reviewer agents. Or review a sample of the cheapest, most reversible outputs and not all of them. Reviewing half of the planning outputs brings the load to \( 60 + 150 + 30 = 240 \) minutes, which is exactly 4 hours.

Span of control is the number of agents one orchestrator can supervise effectively. It is the attention budget divided by the review cost per agent. It is not fixed. A team of agents with machine-checkable outputs has a much wider span than a team whose outputs need a careful read.

docs.title: Diagram: Orchestrator Review Load Calculator
docs.text:
Orchestrator Review Load Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: orchestrator-review-load-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the daily review load of an agent team from its size and per-output review times, and adjust the team or the review fraction to fit a stated attention budget, in three challenges.

Prerequisites: researcher attention, span of control, review checkpoint, and the load formula \( L = n_p k_p r_p + n_e k_e r_e + c \), all defined in the section "Review, Approval, and Researcher Attention" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of three challenges the learner types a value and submits. A value is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Changing the quantities in exploration mode is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Review load grows only with the number of execution agents. (2) More agents always means more done. (3) Sampling review is the same as skipping review.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level work needs the learner to carry out the load calculation and then use it to make a design decision, so that the formula becomes a planning tool.

Content:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Planning agents n_p 0 40 1 20 agents Execution agents n_e 0 20 1 10 agents Planning outputs per agent per day k_p 1 4 1 1 outputs Execution outputs per agent per day k_e 1 4 1 1 outputs Review time per planning output r_p 2 15 1 6 minutes Review time per execution output r_e 5 30 1 15 minutes Conflict resolution c 0 120 10 30 minutes per day Attention available 1 8 0.5 4 hours per day Fraction of planning outputs reviewed 0.25 1.0 0.25 1.0 fraction

The review load is L = (planning fraction reviewed) x n_p x k_p x r_p + n_e x k_e x r_e + c, in minutes.

Challenges, in this order. All use the default values except where stated.

# Challenge Answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 What is the daily review load in hours for the default team? 5.0 20 x 1 x 6 = 120, plus 10 x 1 x 15 = 150, plus 30 is 300 minutes, which is 5.0 hours. 2 With attention fixed at 4 hours, 10 execution agents, and every planning output reviewed, what is the largest number of planning agents that fits? 10 240 minutes minus 150 minus 30 leaves 60 minutes, and 60 / 6 = 10 planning agents. 3 With 20 planning agents and attention fixed at 4 hours, what is the largest fraction of planning outputs, from 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, that can be reviewed? 0.5 At 0.5 the load is 60 + 150 + 30 = 240 minutes, which equals 4 hours. At 0.75 it is 270 minutes, which exceeds it.

Provenance: The formula and the default numbers are from the section "Review, Approval, and Researcher Attention" of this chapter. All values are illustrative and labeled "illustrative" in the sim.

Rules: Load in minutes = fraction x n_p x k_p x r_p + n_e x k_e x r_e + c. The load fits when load <= attention x 60. All arithmetic is exact. Fractions of agents are not allowed.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 and enters the load in hours.
  2. After each submission the sim shows the worked calculation and a bar comparing the load with the attention available.
  3. After the three challenges, exploration opens: the learner changes any of the nine quantities and watches the bar. The learner should notice that halving review time on execution outputs has more effect than halving it on planning outputs.

Feedback: Three challenges, two attempts each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the worked calculation. Incorrect on the first attempt: "Check that each term is agents x outputs x minutes." Incorrect on the second attempt: the worked calculation is shown and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "n of 3 correct" is shown.

Starting State: The default team and attention of 4 hours are shown with the bar, and challenge 1 is posed. The question on screen is "How many hours of review does this team need each day?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states 20 planning agents and 10 execution agents, 6 and 15 minutes of review, 30 minutes of conflict resolution, a load of 300 minutes (5 hours) against 4 hours of attention, and a load of 240 minutes when half of the planning outputs are reviewed.

docs.title: Specifying, Prioritizing, and Reporting
docs.text:
An agent specification is the written definition of one agent: its role, purpose, inputs, outputs, tools and permissions, autonomy level, stopping conditions, and the handoff format. It is the file that makes an agent reproducible, and it is where the roles of Chapter 9 become concrete. A compact specification for a planning agent, with illustrative content:

# Agent: literature-planner
Role: planning agent
Purpose: propose a search strategy and a candidate reading list for a stated question.
Inputs: question statement (docs/question.md), glossary (docs/glossary.md).
Outputs: docs/plans/search-strategy.md, docs/plans/reading-list.md (status: needs-review).
Tools: web search, read files. No file writes outside docs/plans/.
Autonomy: level 2. Stops and asks when the question is ambiguous.
Handoff: acceptance criteria listed at the top of each output file.

Plan review is the examination of a plan before any execution begins. It is the highest-leverage review in the workflow, because a defect found in a plan costs minutes, while the same defect found after execution costs a rerun. Check a plan against the question: does it address the stated metric, are the tasks checkable, are the dependencies right, and is anything out of scope? Plan revision is the controlled change of a plan when new findings arrive. Revise by editing the plan file, noting what changed and why in the decision log, and re-queuing only the tasks whose inputs changed, which the dependency structure identifies.

Task prioritization is the choice of what goes first in the queue. Three considerations dominate: tasks on the critical path come first, tasks that unblock many others come early, and tasks that reduce uncertainty about the plan, such as a quick feasibility check, come before expensive ones that depend on it.

Progress tracking is the recording of each task's status in the queue, and status reporting is the periodic summary of that record for the researcher. A useful report is short and answers four questions: what finished, what is blocked and why, what needs your decision, and what has been spent. Ask an orchestrating agent to produce it from the queue and the logs each morning, and read it before you read anything else.

Delegation is handing a task to an agent along with the authority to carry it out. Delegate tasks that are well specified and checkable. Keep the framing of the question, the choice among approaches, and the final judgment of what is true. These are the parts of research that the agents' outputs only inform.

docs.title: Cost, Benefit, and the Limits of Scaling
docs.text:
Cost and benefit analysis for an agent team compares what the team saves with what it costs. The benefit is the work you would otherwise do by hand, expressed in hours. The costs are the review time, which is the dominant one and is paid in your attention, the compute and subscription cost of the agents, the setup effort to write specifications, and the cost of errors that escape review. A team is worth running when the saving, net of review, is large and the escape rate is low and known.

Scaling agent teams is adding agents to do more at once, and it pays off only while three limits are not binding. The first is attention: past the span of control, the added output is not reviewed, so it adds risk and not value. The second is dependencies: past the width of the dependency graph, added agents sit idle, as the critical-path example showed, where 21 hours of work still took 18. The third is coordination: more agents mean more handoffs, more potential conflicts, and more shared state to keep consistent. A reasonable discipline is to grow a team one role at a time, measure the review load and the escape rate at each size, and stop when an additional agent adds more review than it removes work.

More Agents Is Not More Done

A common trap is launching a large team because launching is cheap. It happens because the cost shows up later, as a pile of unreviewed output. Size the team to your review budget first, and add an agent only when the queue shows idle capacity that review can absorb.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Orchestration is the design of how work, checks, and decisions flow through a team of agents so that your attention goes where it prevents the most damage. The number of agents is the least important parameter. Dependencies, review cost, and the quality of handoffs set what the team can actually deliver.

The main points to carry forward:

  • An agent team has planning and execution groups, and the 20-to-10 agent ratio reflects that plans are cheap to discard and executions are expensive to check.
  • Work breakdown produces tasks with owners, outputs, and checks. Task dependencies set the critical path, which parallelism cannot shorten.
  • Handoff protocols, shared workspaces, and conflict resolution use files, separate outputs, and a trace to the first divergence.
  • Review checkpoints can be automated. Human approval gates consume your attention and belong where actions are irreversible or outward-bound.
  • Researcher attention is quantifiable. Review load grows with team size and sets the span of control.
  • Agent specifications, plan review, and plan revision make agents reproducible and catch defects when they are cheapest.
  • Prioritization, progress tracking, and status reporting keep the queue and the researcher in step.
  • Scaling is limited by attention, by dependencies, and by coordination, and you should stop adding agents when they add more review than they remove work.

You Can Size a Team

You can now compute a critical path and the slack on a task, estimate the daily review load of a team and fit it to your attention, and say why 20 planning agents and 10 execution agents is a design target and not a law. That is the arithmetic of orchestration.

The following chapters apply this machinery to the everyday tasks of research, starting with the literature. Round up the question you would give a planning team, and bring it.

docs.text: This chapter applies agents to the literature workflow: building a search strategy, generating keywords, triaging and summarizing papers, chaining citations, and managing references. It stresses verifying citations and synthesizing evidence from sources of known quality. After this chapter you can produce an annotated reading list with verified citations.

docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 2: How Language Models Work
  • Chapter 4: Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting

The Literature, Without Drowning

Everyone in a fast field falls behind the literature, and agents can read faster than you can. They also invent references with a straight face. This chapter shows how to use their speed while keeping every citation you rely on checked. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Searching: Strategy, Keywords, and Sources
docs.text:
A literature review is a structured account of what is known about a question, built from a systematic search and a critical reading of the sources found. The quality of a review is bounded by the quality of the search that feeds it, and a search is a procedure that can be written down and repeated. A search strategy is that written procedure: the question, the concepts it contains, the terms for each concept, the databases searched, the date range, and the filters applied. Writing it down is what separates a literature search from browsing.

The first step is the question, framed as in Chapter 1 with a metric and a threshold. The second is to split the question into its concepts. For the running example, a question about calibration of a SAR ADC has three concepts: the architecture, the converter, and the technique. The third step is keyword generation: listing for each concept the terms under which authors might have written about it. This is a task that an assistant does well, because it requires breadth and no verification of facts: synonyms, abbreviations, spelling variants, and neighboring terms. Ask for them, then read the list critically and remove the terms that would pull in a different field.

Concept Terms to search Architecture "successive approximation", "successive-approximation register", SAR Converter ADC, "analog-to-digital converter", "A/D converter" Technique calibrat*, "offset correction", "mismatch correction", "foreground calibration"

Table 1. Keyword generation for one question: terms for each concept.

Terms within one concept are joined with OR, because any of them identifies the concept. Concepts are joined with AND, because a paper must be about all of them. Quotation marks match an exact phrase, and an asterisk matches word endings. The resulting query for the example is ("successive approximation" OR SAR) AND (ADC OR "analog-to-digital converter") AND (calibrat* OR "offset correction"), and the syntax differs slightly between databases, so check each database's help page.

Scholarly databases are the indexes in which you run the query. For electrical engineering and computer design the main ones are publisher platforms such as IEEE Xplore and the ACM Digital Library, citation indexes such as Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, and open indexes such as Semantic Scholar and DBLP. A preprint server is a repository where authors post manuscripts before or alongside peer review. arXiv is the large general one, and TechRxiv serves the IEEE community. Preprints give you results months earlier, and they have not been through peer review, which matters for the source-quality question below. Search at least two databases, because their coverage differs, and record for each the query, the date, and the number of results.

Log the Query Like an Experiment

Save every query with the database, the date, and the result count in a file in your project. When a reviewer asks how you found the related work, or when you rerun the search in six months to find what is new, that file is the whole answer.

Two numbers describe how well a query performs. Precision is the fraction of the results returned that are relevant, and recall is the fraction of all the relevant papers that were returned. With \( TP \) relevant results returned, \( FP \) irrelevant ones returned, and \( FN \) relevant ones missed,

\[ \text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}, \qquad \text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}. \]

Broadening a query raises recall and lowers precision, and narrowing does the opposite. A scoping search, where missing a key paper is costly, should favor recall. A search for a short list of the best papers on a subtopic can favor precision.

docs.title: Diagram: Search Query Precision and Recall Explorer
docs.text:
Search Query Precision and Recall Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: search-precision-recall-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/search-microsims/tree/main/docs/sims/keyword-search-flow Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the precision and recall of three search queries run on a corpus of twenty papers with eight known relevant papers, and choose the query that suits a stated purpose.

Prerequisites: search strategy, precision, recall, true positive, false positive, and false negative, all defined in the section "Searching: Strategy, Keywords, and Sources" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of three queries the learner enters precision and recall, each to two decimal places, and then chooses the query for a stated purpose. A value is correct when it is within 0.01 of the value in Content. The choice is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 values correct and the choice correct. Browsing the corpus is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A query that returns many results is a good query. (2) High precision means the search found everything relevant. (3) Precision and recall always move together.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level work needs the learner to compute the two measures on concrete result sets and then use them in a decision. A query with high recall and low precision, and one with the reverse, make the trade-off visible in numbers.

The corpus is synthetic and labeled "synthetic, invented for this exercise". It has 20 papers, P1 to P20. The relevant papers are P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P6, P7, and P8. The other twelve, P9 to P20, are not relevant.

Query Description Papers returned A A narrow query using the exact phrase "foreground calibration" P1, P2, P3, P4, P9, P10 B A broad query using OR across many synonyms P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P6, P7, P8, P9, P10, P11, P12, P13, P14, P15, P16 C A balanced query combining architecture and technique terms P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P6, P7, P9

Query Returned TP FP FN Precision Recall A 6 4 2 4 0.67 0.50 B 16 8 8 0 0.50 1.00 C 8 7 1 1 0.88 0.88

The correct answer is Query B, because it has recall 1.00, and the reason shown is "Recall is the priority when a missed paper is costly, and the extra irrelevant results can be removed in triage."

Provenance: The definitions of precision and recall are from the section "Searching: Strategy, Keywords, and Sources" of this chapter. The corpus and queries are synthetic and invented for this exercise.

Rules: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) and recall = TP / (TP + FN). Values are displayed to two decimal places. Returned papers are counted from the sets above. A relevant paper is one of P1 to P8.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the 20 papers with the relevant set hidden, and query A's result set.
  2. The learner marks which returned papers are relevant after the relevant set is revealed, then enters precision and recall.
  3. The learner repeats for queries B and C.
  4. The learner chooses the query for the stated purpose and submits. The sim shows the worked values and the reason.

Feedback: Three queries, two attempts each for the numbers, then one attempt for the choice. Correct: "Correct." plus the worked counts. Incorrect on the first attempt: "Count the relevant papers returned and divide by the number returned for precision, and by 8 for recall." Incorrect on the second attempt: the worked counts are shown. The correct choice is revealed after the single attempt.

Starting State: The corpus is shown with query A's results highlighted. The question on screen is "What fraction of the results are relevant, and what fraction of the relevant papers were found?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states the two formulas and that broadening a query raises recall and lowers precision. The chapter does not state the corpus numbers.

docs.title: Triage, Summarization, and Claim Extraction
docs.text:
A successful search returns more papers than you can read. Paper triage is the fast sorting of results into those to read closely, those to skim, and those to set aside, using only the title, abstract, and figures. An agent can do first-pass triage from a rubric you supply: relevance to the question, whether the work is measured or simulated, the process node or technology, the year, and the venue. The rubric matters more than the model. A triage prompt that says only "rate relevance from 1 to 5" returns inconsistent scores, and one that names the criteria and requires a one-line reason for each is auditable.

Paper summarization is producing a short account of a paper. It is among the strongest uses of a language model, and it has one characteristic failure: the summary may be built from the abstract and the model's expectations about the field, and not from the paper's body. A summary that sounds right can state a result the paper does not contain. The defenses are those of Chapter 4: supply the full text, ask for a structured summary with the section for each statement, and spot-check.

Claim extraction makes this concrete. It is the extraction of specific, checkable statements from a paper, each with its supporting evidence and location. Instead of "what is the paper about?", the task is "list each quantitative claim, with the value, units, conditions, and the sentence and table it comes from." A worked example for one paper, with illustrative values:

Claim Value Conditions Where stated ENOB 9.2 bits 1 MS/s, input at Nyquist, 1.0 V supply Section IV, Table II Power 45 µW Same as above Section IV, Table II Process 65 nm CMOS Not applicable Section II Measured or simulated Measured 12 samples of the chip Section IV

Table 2. Extracted claims, each with conditions and a location.

Each row can be checked in under a minute by going to the stated location. This is the output to ask agents for, because it converts a summary you would have to trust into a set of facts you can confirm.

A Summary of a Paper You Did Not Read

A common trap is citing a paper from a model-written summary. It happens because the summary reads like the paper. It may have been built from the abstract and the model's priors. Before you cite a claim, open the paper and find the sentence, and ask the agent for the location with every claim so that this takes seconds.

docs.title: Following Citations
docs.text: Citation chaining is finding papers by following the citation links of a paper you already have. Backward chaining follows a paper's reference list to the work it builds on. Forward chaining follows the papers that cite it, which are found in the citation indexes, to the work that builds on it. Chaining finds papers that keyword searches miss, because it follows influence and not vocabulary. A paper cited by many of your seed papers' references is usually foundational, and a recent paper that cites several of your seeds is usually relevant to the current state of the art.

docs.title: Diagram: Citation Chaining Explorer
docs.text:
Citation Chaining Explorer

Type: graph-model sim-id: citation-chaining-explorer Library: vis-network Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: solve Learning Objective: The learner will solve five citation-chaining questions on a graph of eight papers by following references backward and citations forward, with at least 4 of 5 correct.

Prerequisites: citation chaining, backward chaining, forward chaining, and the meaning of a citation edge, all defined in the section "Following Citations" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of five questions the learner selects the set of papers that answer it and submits. An answer is correct when the selected set equals the answer in Content exactly. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Dragging nodes and reading paper details is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Forward and backward chaining find the same papers. (2) Only papers with matching keywords are relevant. (3) The most recent paper is the most foundational.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level work needs the learner to carry out the two chaining procedures on a concrete graph. The final questions combine the two directions, which is how the technique is used in practice.

Content:

The papers are invented and labeled "illustrative". An edge "X cites Y" points from X to Y.

Paper Year Role S 2022 Seed paper A 2018 Cited by S B 2019 Cited by S C 2020 Cited by S F 2017 Cited by B and by C D 2023 Cites S E 2024 Cites S and C G 2025 Cites D

Edges: S cites A, S cites B, S cites C, B cites F, C cites F, D cites S, E cites S, E cites C, G cites D.

# Question Answer set Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which papers are found by backward chaining one step from S? A, B, C These are the papers S cites. 2 Which papers are found by forward chaining one step from S? D, E These are the papers that cite S. 3 Which paper is cited by two of S's references? F B and C both cite F, so F is likely foundational. 4 Which paper is found by forward chaining two steps from S? G G cites D, and D cites S. 5 Which paper cites both S and C? E E cites S and also C, so it is closely tied to this line of work.

Provenance: The chaining procedures are from the section "Following Citations" of this chapter. The papers, years, and edges are invented for illustration.

Rules: Backward chaining follows an edge from the citing paper to the cited paper. Forward chaining follows an edge from the cited paper back to the citing paper. An answer set excludes the seed paper S.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the graph with S highlighted and question 1.
  2. The learner selects the papers that answer the question and submits.
  3. The sim highlights the edges followed and shows the "Why" sentence, then shows the next question.
  4. After question 5, the sim shows the count correct. The learner should notice that forward chaining reaches newer papers and backward chaining reaches older ones.

Feedback: Five questions, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: the correct set and the "Why" sentence. The correct set is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 5 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 4 was met.

Starting State: The graph is shown with S highlighted and the direction of each citation edge visible. The question on screen is "Which papers does this procedure find?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that backward chaining follows references to earlier work and forward chaining follows citations to later work, and that a paper cited by several references of a seed paper is likely foundational.

docs.title: References, Verification, and Quality
docs.text:
A reference manager is a program that stores bibliographic records, attaches PDFs, and formats citations for a document. Zotero, Mendeley, and JabRef are common examples. The record format that matters most in engineering is BibTeX, a plain-text format for bibliographic entries that LaTeX uses to build reference lists. Each entry has a type, a key, and fields. The entry below is the book's primary reference, which is the first entry on the References page.

@inproceedings{ketter2008advocate,
  author    = {Ketter, Wolfgang and Batchu, Arun and Berosik, Gary and McCreary, Dan},
  title     = {A semantic web architecture for advocate agents to determine preferences and facilitate decision making},
  booktitle = {Proceedings of the 10th International Conference on Electronic Commerce (ICEC '08)},
  year      = {2008},
  doi       = {10.1145/1409540.1409554}
}

Because BibTeX is plain text, it fits the version-controlled project of Chapter 5, and an agent can edit it. It is also where fabricated references enter a manuscript, since a model can write a perfectly formatted entry for a paper that does not exist.

DOI lookup is the retrieval of a paper's metadata from its digital object identifier by asking a registry. The DOI resolver at doi.org redirects to the publisher's page, and the Crossref registry returns the record as data. Citation verification is the use of that lookup, and of a title search, to confirm that each entry exists and that its authors, venue, year, and title match, as in the four-outcome classification of Chapter 2. A short script that reads a BibTeX file, resolves every DOI, and flags entries with no DOI or a mismatch automates most of the check, and an agent can write it. The one step that cannot be automated is confirming that the paper supports the sentence it is cited for.

Source quality is the trustworthiness of a source as evidence. It is not a single score. For engineering results, the questions that matter are whether the paper is peer reviewed or a preprint, whether the results are measured on silicon or only simulated, whether the experimental conditions are stated completely, whether data or code are available, and whether independent groups have replicated or cited the result as confirmed. A preprint can be excellent and a journal paper can be weak. What matters is to record what kind of source each claim rests on, so that your synthesis can state it.

docs.title: Synthesis
docs.text:
A comparison table puts the extracted claims of several papers side by side, with a row per paper and a column per attribute, with the conditions in the columns. It is the working tool of synthesis. Its columns are the attributes on which the papers can be compared: architecture, process, supply, sampling rate, ENOB, power, and whether measured. Empty cells are informative. A cell that is blank for most papers shows what the field has not measured.

Evidence synthesis is the combination of findings from several sources into a statement about what is known, with the strength of the evidence. For engineering literature the central care is to compare like with like. Two papers that report ENOB at different input frequencies, supply voltages, or process nodes are not comparable by their headline numbers, and averaging them produces a number that describes neither. A comparison table with conditions as columns makes such mismatches visible, and a synthesis states them.

A research gap is a question the literature does not answer, or answers only under conditions that do not cover yours. Gaps are found by reading the comparison table: a combination of attributes with no entries, a result reported only in simulation, a claim supported by a single group. Related work is the section of a paper that positions your contribution against the literature, and a good one follows from the comparison table. It groups papers by approach, states what each achieves under what conditions, and ends with the gap. An annotated bibliography is a reference list with a short note for each entry on what it claims, the quality of the evidence, and its relevance. A reading list is the prioritized subset to read in full, in order.

The Table Is the Argument

Notice that once the claims sit in a table with conditions, much of the synthesis is already done. You see which results can be compared, where the field agrees, and which cells are empty. A related-work section written from that table has a spine, and one written from memory has a list.

docs.title: Putting It Together: A Literature Pipeline
docs.text:
The pieces form a pipeline that fits the planning and execution model of Chapter 10. Each stage has an output you can check.

  1. Question and strategy: you write the question and the concepts, and an agent generates terms. You approve the strategy. Output: search-strategy.md.
  2. Search: an agent runs the queries and records each query, database, date, and count. Output: a results file of BibTeX.
  3. Triage: an agent applies your rubric to each result with a one-line reason. Output: a sorted list. You review the borderline cases.
  4. Extraction: an agent extracts claims with locations from the papers you chose. Output: a comparison table.
  5. Verification: a script resolves every DOI and flags mismatches, and you confirm that each cited claim is in the paper.
  6. Synthesis: a writing agent drafts the related-work section from the table, and you revise it in your own voice (Chapter 15).

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
AI assistance changes the speed of every stage of the literature workflow and none of the standards. A written search strategy, verified references, and claims tied to locations are what turn faster reading into trustworthy synthesis.

The main points to carry forward:

  • A search strategy is a written, repeatable procedure. Use keyword generation for breadth, and log queries, databases, and dates.
  • Precision and recall trade off, and a scoping search should favor recall.
  • Scholarly databases and preprint servers differ in coverage and in peer review, so search more than one and record the source type.
  • Triage by rubric, structured summarization, and claim extraction with locations make agent output auditable.
  • Citation chaining, backward and forward, finds what keyword search misses.
  • BibTeX in version control, DOI lookup, and citation verification guard the reference list against fabricated entries.
  • Source quality is recorded per claim. Comparison tables put conditions in columns so that evidence synthesis compares like with like and shows research gaps.

A Reading List You Can Stand Behind

You can now write a search strategy, compute the precision and recall of a query, chain citations in both directions, and build a comparison table in which every claim has a location and every reference has been looked up. That is an annotated reading list with verified citations.

The next chapter turns from papers to data, where the same discipline of keeping errors visible applies to the numbers you measure yourself. Round up one dataset, and bring it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter applies AI to the data side of research: choosing data formats, cleaning measurement data, exploring and visualizing it, and writing analysis scripts and notebooks in Python. It emphasizes keeping errors visible rather than hidden. After this chapter you can prompt an agent to write, run, and debug an analysis on a real dataset.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 5: Markdown Project Files and Version Control
  • Chapter 8: Agents, Tool Use, and Subagents

Let the Agent Write It, Let the Data Check It

An agent will write an analysis script in a minute that would take you an hour. What it cannot know is whether your data are clean or whether the answer is plausible. This chapter is about arranging the work so that wrong results announce themselves. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Data and Its Formats
docs.text:
Measurement data are the numbers recorded from an instrument, a simulator, or a sensor: captured ADC codes, waveform samples, sweep results, power readings. They have properties that generic datasets do not. They carry noise and quantization. They depend on instrument settings that must be recorded with them. They can contain artifacts: saturation, dropped samples, a probe that slipped. And they are the one thing in a project that you cannot regenerate with a prompt, so they must be protected.

A data format is the file layout in which data are stored. The choice affects what agents and scripts can do with them.

CSV and JSON are the two plain-text formats to prefer. CSV, comma-separated values, stores a table with one row per record and one column per quantity. It is simple, readable in any editor, and diffable. Its weakness is that it has no types or units, so the meaning of a column must be recorded elsewhere. JSON stores nested key-value structures, which suits metadata: instrument, settings, date, operator, and units. A reliable pattern is a CSV of values with a JSON sidecar file of the same name that describes them.

Format Strength Weakness Use for CSV Simple, readable, diffable No units or types; large files are slow Tables of measured values JSON Nested, self-describing Verbose for large arrays Settings and metadata NumPy .npy or HDF5 Compact, fast, typed arrays Binary, not diffable Large waveform records Vendor instrument format Complete instrument state Opaque, tool-specific Archive, then convert to an open format

Table 1. Common data formats and what they suit.

A worked example shows a capture with its sidecar. Everything the analysis needs to interpret the numbers is in the two files, and nothing depends on remembering.

# data/raw/capture-07.csv  (one ADC output code per line)
512
531
...

{
  "file": "capture-07.csv",
  "instrument": "bench-ADC-board",
  "sampling_rate_hz": 1000000,
  "input_frequency_hz": 499000,
  "nominal_bits": 10,
  "supply_v": 1.0,
  "captured": "2026-10-09",
  "samples": 4096
}

Raw Is Read-Only, Always

Put captured files in data/raw/, make them read-only, and never write to that directory from a script. Everything downstream is generated into data/processed/. Then a bad cleaning step can be rerun from the original, and an agent has a boundary it can obey.

docs.title: Cleaning Without Hiding
docs.text:
Data cleaning is preparing data for analysis by dealing with missing values, duplicates, unit mismatches, and artifacts. Done carelessly it is the quietest source of wrong results in research, because every choice changes the answer and nothing marks that a choice was made. Three rules keep it honest.

First, cleaning is a script, not an edit. The raw file is never changed. A script reads it, applies named steps, and writes a new file. Second, every change is logged: how many rows were dropped, which, and why. Third, remove only for a documented cause. A point is removed because the notebook says the probe slipped, not because it is inconvenient. A point that is merely an outlier is information about the distribution, and removing it is a claim about the system.

A worked example with illustrative numbers: a batch of 40 devices has measured offsets between 0.5 and 2.1 mV, with one device at 12 mV and one at 6.8 mV. The 12 mV device has a lab-notebook entry reading "probe slipped, remeasure". Excluding it is justified, and the exclusion is recorded with the reason. The 6.8 mV device has no such entry and is a valid part. It stays in the data, is reported, and is investigated, because a real tail in the distribution is exactly what a yield analysis is meant to find.

Action When it applies What to record Keep Variation is physical or consistent with expected noise Nothing, or a note that it was examined Exclude with log A documented cause, such as a duplicate, a missing-value code, or a known fault Row identifiers, count, and reason Correct and log A documented systematic error, such as a unit mismatch The conversion, its justification, and the rows Remeasure The data cannot support the analysis, such as a stuck or missing channel Which measurements and why

Table 2. Four responses to an anomaly, and what to record for each.

docs.title: Diagram: Measurement Data Cleaning Decision Simulator
docs.text:
Measurement Data Cleaning Decision Simulator

Type: microsim sim-id: data-cleaning-decision-simulator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge, for each of eight anomalies in a batch of measurements, whether to keep, exclude with a log, correct and log, or remeasure, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: data cleaning, the three rules of honest cleaning, and the four responses in the section "Cleaning Without Hiding" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight anomalies the learner commits one of four actions. An action is correct when it equals the action in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the lab notebook excerpt is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) An outlier should be removed because it is an outlier. (2) A suspicious value can be edited in the raw file. (3) Any problem with the data can be fixed by cleaning.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work needs the learner to apply a stated criterion, the documented cause, to concrete cases. The cases include two where the right answer is to keep a surprising value and two where cleaning is the wrong response.
