The batch is synthetic, labeled "synthetic, invented for this exercise". It is 40 devices with offset voltages measured in millivolts, and the lab notebook is available for each anomaly.

# Anomaly Notebook excerpt Correct action Why (shown as feedback) 1 Device 17 reads 12 mV, while the other devices read 0.5 to 2.1 mV. "Device 17: probe slipped during measurement, remeasure." Exclude with log There is a documented cause, so exclusion is justified and the reason is recorded. 2 Device 31 reads 6.8 mV, while the other devices read 0.5 to 2.1 mV. No entry. Keep There is no documented fault, so the value is data. It is reported and investigated. 3 The temperature column reads 0.0 for devices 8 to 12. "Logger cable disconnected for devices 8 to 12." Remeasure The values are missing and cannot be recovered or inferred. 4 Rows for devices 22 and 23 appear twice in the merged file. "Merged files A and B; overlap at 22 and 23." Exclude with log The duplicates are artifacts of the merge, and one copy of each is kept. 5 All values in lot B are about one thousand times smaller than in lot A. "Lot A exported in mV; lot B exported in V." Correct and log A documented unit mismatch is converted, and the conversion is recorded. 6 The value -999 appears in three rows of the offset column. "Instrument writes -999 when a reading fails." Exclude with log -999 is the instrument's missing-value code, so those rows have no measurement. 7 Six devices from one wafer edge read about three times higher than the rest. No entry. Keep A systematic spatial pattern is a finding about the process and is not an artifact. 8 In capture 12 the ADC output is the same code for all 4,096 samples. "Input cable not connected for capture 12." Remeasure The record contains no information about the converter.

Provenance: The four actions and the honest-cleaning rules are from the section "Cleaning Without Hiding" of this chapter. The batch and the notebook excerpts are synthetic.

Rules: Each anomaly has exactly one correct action. Exclusion requires a documented cause. A value with no documented cause is kept. Missing or unusable measurements require remeasurement and are not cleaned.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads anomaly 1 with its notebook excerpt.
  2. The learner chooses one of the four actions and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence, and what would be recorded in the cleaning log.
  4. After anomaly 8, the sim shows the count correct and a summary of how many rows were kept, excluded, corrected, and sent for remeasurement.

Feedback: Eight anomalies, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "The better response is ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct action is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: Anomaly 1 is shown with the four actions and no choice made. The question on screen is "What should happen to this data?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states four actions (keep, exclude with log, correct and log, remeasure), that removal needs a documented cause, that an undocumented outlier is kept and investigated, and that raw files are never edited.

docs.title: Exploring, Analyzing, and Plotting
docs.text:
Exploratory analysis is looking at the data before computing anything on it: its size, ranges, distributions, and shape. For a captured ADC record that means the number of samples, the minimum and maximum code, the fraction of samples at full scale, a plot of the codes against time, and a plot of the spectrum. These steps are cheap, and they catch the problems that make a downstream number meaningless: a clipped waveform, a record that is too short, a signal at the wrong frequency.

Statistical analysis is the quantification of what the data show and how sure you can be. For measurements the basics are enough to start: the mean and standard deviation across repeated runs, a confidence interval, and the number of independent samples behind a claim. State the sample size beside every statistic. A mean of nine chips and a mean of three hundred are different claims, and an agent will happily write both in the same sentence.

Data visualization is the graphical display of data, and plotting is the act of producing a plot, in Python typically with the Matplotlib library. A plot that supports a claim has labeled axes with units, a legend where there is more than one series, a visible indication of uncertainty or spread, and the raw data shown and not only a fit. When an agent writes the plot, read it as a reviewer would: are the units on the axes, is the scale honest, is anything cropped, and does it show what the text says it shows?

Cleaning That Improves the Result

A common trap is a cleaning step that happens to make the number better. It happens because an agent asked to "get a clean result" has an incentive to remove what hurts it. Whenever a cleaning step changes a headline number, report the result both with and without it, and ask what documented cause justified the step.

docs.title: Analysis Scripts in Python
docs.text:
Python is the language in which most research analysis is now written, and an agent writes it fluently. An analysis script is a program that reads data, applies a defined procedure, and writes results, and it is the unit of reproducible analysis: the script, run on the raw data, produces the figure and the table. Analysis that exists only as a sequence of manual steps cannot be repeated.

Before the example, the key ideas of the code in plain terms. The script loads codes from a file. It computes the fraction of samples at the minimum or maximum code, which signals clipping. It windows the record with a Hann window, a smooth taper that reduces spectral leakage when the signal is not exactly periodic in the record. It computes the power spectrum, excludes the DC bin explicitly, takes the fundamental as the largest remaining bin and its neighbors, treats everything else as noise and distortion, and converts the ratio to ENOB with the formula of Chapter 4. Notice that failures are loud: a short record raises an error, and clipping is printed.

import numpy as np

def load_codes(path, n_bits):
    codes = np.loadtxt(path, dtype=int)
    if codes.size < 64:
        raise ValueError(f"record too short: {codes.size} samples")
    clipped = np.mean((codes <= 0) | (codes >= 2**n_bits - 1))
    print(f"samples={codes.size}  clipped={clipped:.4%}")
    return codes, clipped

def enob(codes):
    x = codes - codes.mean()
    spec = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x * np.hanning(x.size))) ** 2
    spec[0] = 0.0                      # exclude DC explicitly
    k = int(np.argmax(spec))
    lo, hi = max(k - 3, 1), k + 4      # fundamental plus leakage bins
    signal = spec[lo:hi].sum()
    noise = spec.sum() - signal        # noise and distortion
    sndr_db = 10 * np.log10(signal / noise)
    return (sndr_db - 1.76) / 6.02

To have an agent write something like this, give it the specification and acceptance criteria of Chapter 4, point it at one raw file and its sidecar, require loud failure, and ask it to print the quantities it used. Then run it on the synthetic known-answer record from the acceptance criteria before you run it on real data. A script that cannot reproduce a known answer is not ready for an unknown one.

docs.title: Reading Error Messages
docs.text:
An error message is the program's report that something went wrong. In Python it appears as a traceback: a stack of lines, each naming a file, a line number, and the function being executed, ending with the exception type and a message. Read it from the bottom. The last line names the kind of failure and the reason. The line just above it shows the statement that failed. The lines above that show the chain of calls that led there, and the entry nearest the bottom that is in your code is where to look first.

Error messages are the most useful information an agent has, and agents sometimes hide them: a try block that catches every exception and carries on, a default value substituted silently, a warning filtered out. These make a script appear to work while it computes the wrong thing. A rule that serves well is to let the script fail, and to treat any catch-all handler an agent adds as a defect to remove unless it logs the error and stops.

docs.title: Diagram: Python Traceback Reader
docs.text:
Python Traceback Reader

Type: microsim sim-id: python-traceback-reader Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine five Python tracebacks and identify the cause of each from the exception type, message, and failing line, with at least 4 of 5 correct.

Prerequisites: error message, traceback, exception type, and the rule of reading a traceback from the bottom, all defined in the section "Reading Error Messages" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of five tracebacks the learner chooses one of three diagnoses. A diagnosis is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Expanding the full traceback is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The first line of a traceback shows the problem. (2) A ValueError that the code raised on purpose is a bug in the code. (3) Every error is a code defect.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level work needs the learner to attribute an error to its source from the evidence in the traceback. Options include a plausible but wrong cause for each item, so that the learner must read the message and not only the exception type.

Content:

Each traceback is invented and labeled "illustrative".

# Traceback (condensed) Option A Option B Option C Correct Why (shown as feedback) 1 File "scripts/enob.py", line 12, in load_codes: FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'data/raw/capture-7.csv' The file path is wrong; the file is named capture-07.csv The CSV file is corrupted NumPy is not installed A The message names a file that does not exist, and the data directory holds capture-07.csv. 2 File "scripts/enob.py", line 8, in load_codes: ValueError: record too short: 12 samples A bug in np.loadtxt The input record is too short, and the script rejected it as designed The window function is wrong B The script raised this error deliberately, so the input is the problem and not the code. 3 File "scripts/plot.py", line 1, in : ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'scipy' The environment does not have scipy installed The script has a typo in a variable name The data file is empty A The import failed before any other code ran, which points to the environment. 4 File "scripts/enob.py", line 17, in enob: IndexError: index 4096 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 4096 The CSV has too many columns An off-by-one in an index or slice that reaches one past the end The sampling rate is wrong B An index equal to the array size is one past the last valid index, which is 4095. 5 File "scripts/enob.py", line 14, in enob: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for -: 'str' and 'float' The data were loaded as text because a header line was not skipped The FFT length is not a power of two The Hann window is missing A A string cannot be subtracted from a float, which suggests the codes were read as strings, often because of a header row.

Provenance: The reading rule is from the section "Reading Error Messages" of this chapter. The tracebacks, file names, and messages are invented for illustration.

Rules: Each traceback has exactly one correct diagnosis, given above. The sim must shuffle the option order independently for each learner.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees traceback 1, condensed to the file, line, function, and message.
  2. The learner chooses one of the three diagnoses and submits.
  3. The sim reveals the correct diagnosis and the "Why" sentence, and highlights the part of the traceback that determines it.
  4. After traceback 5, the sim shows the count correct.

Feedback: Five tracebacks, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: the correct diagnosis and the "Why" sentence. The correct answer is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 5 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 4 was met.

Starting State: Traceback 1 is shown with three diagnoses and none chosen. The question on screen is "What does this error tell you about the cause?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a traceback is read from the bottom, that the last line names the failure, that the nearest line of your own code is where to look first, and that a deliberately raised error points to the input.

docs.title: Environments and Notebooks
docs.text:
Dependency management is recording and controlling the libraries a script needs, so that it runs the same way tomorrow and on another machine. The minimum is a virtual environment, an isolated set of installed packages for one project, and a file listing the packages and their versions, for example a requirements.txt generated with pip freeze. Without this, a script that worked in March fails in October because a library changed, and the failure looks like a bug in your analysis.

A notebook environment is an interactive document that mixes code, results, and text, with the code run in cells. A Jupyter notebook is the standard form: a file of cells that run in a live session. Notebooks are excellent for exploration, because you see each result as you build it. They have two weaknesses that matter for research. The state of a session depends on the order in which cells were run, so a notebook can show results that its own code cannot reproduce. And the file format mixes code and output, which makes diffs hard to read.

Notebook to script is the move from exploration to reproducibility: once the analysis is settled, the code is extracted from the notebook into a script or module, which is then run from the top on the raw data. A reliable check before you trust any notebook is to restart the kernel and run all cells in order. If the results change, the notebook was lying. A good habit is to keep the notebook as the narrative and figure producer, with real logic in tested functions in a script that the notebook imports.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
An agent changes how fast analysis code is written and nothing about what makes an analysis trustworthy. The practices are those of a careful experimentalist: record the context of every number, protect the raw data, make every change visible, check the code on a known answer, and let errors stop the work.

The main points to carry forward:

  • Measurement data need their settings recorded. Prefer CSV and JSON with a sidecar, and keep raw files read-only.
  • Data cleaning is a logged script, and removal needs a documented cause. Outliers are information.
  • Exploratory analysis comes before computation and catches clipping, short records, and wrong frequencies.
  • Statistics and plots state sample size, units, and spread, and show the raw data.
  • An analysis script fails loudly, prints the quantities it used, and is checked on a known-answer record first.
  • Error messages are read from the bottom, and a catch-all handler that hides them is a defect.
  • Dependency management and a notebook-to-script discipline make results reproducible, and restart-and-run-all is the test.

An Analysis That Argues Back

You can now keep raw data untouched, clean with a logged and justified script, read a traceback from the bottom, and test an analysis script on a known answer before real data. That makes wrong results visible, which is the point.

The next chapter extends the same discipline to code that simulates and tests circuits and systems, where silent errors are the main danger. Round up one script an agent has written for you, and bring it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter focuses on trusting AI-written research code: unit tests, code review, debugging, silent errors, and numerical sanity checks. It covers simulation scripts, parameter sweeps, signal processing, circuit simulation, HDL code and testbenches, and reproducible environments. After this chapter you can test and document code an agent wrote before relying on its results.

This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 4: Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting
  • Chapter 5: Markdown Project Files and Version Control
  • Chapter 12: AI-Assisted Data Analysis and Scripting

Code That Runs Is Not Code That Is Right

An agent's code almost always runs. The danger is the code that runs and returns a plausible, wrong number. This chapter gives you the tests and sanity checks that turn "it ran" into "it is right". Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Why Tests, and Which Ones
docs.text:
The central difficulty with AI-written research code is that it fails quietly. A syntax error announces itself. A unit mistake, a wrong index, or a formula that is nearly right produces a clean run and a number that looks reasonable. Silent errors are exactly these: defects that cause no exception and no warning and change the result. Research code is especially exposed because the right answer is not known in advance, so nothing signals that the answer is wrong.

A worked example makes the point. Suppose the signal and noise are powers, and the code converts their ratio to decibels with the voltage formula, 20 * log10(ratio), instead of the power formula, 10 * log10(ratio). For a power ratio of about 316,000 the correct figure is 55.0 dB. The buggy code returns 110.0 dB. The ENOB formula of Chapter 4 then gives \( (110.0 - 1.76) / 6.02 \approx 18.0 \) bits for a 10-bit converter. The code ran and printed a number to two decimal places. Only a person who knows that a converter cannot exceed its nominal resolution would notice.

Three defenses work together, and none is sufficient alone. Unit tests check that code returns known answers on chosen inputs. Numerical sanity checks test results against physical and definitional limits. Code review has a person or another agent read the code, and especially the diff, for what it does.

A unit test is a small automated check that calls one function with a chosen input and compares the output with an expected value. In Python the usual tool is pytest, which runs every function whose name begins with test_. A good test of a research function has a known answer, and it is best to build the known answer independently of the code. Before the example: the test generates an ideal 10-bit quantization of a full-scale sine wave, for which the ENOB is, by construction, 10, and checks that the function agrees within 0.1 bit.

import numpy as np
from enob import enob            # the function under test

def ideal_record(n_bits=10, n=4096, cycles=127):
    t = np.arange(n)
    x = 0.5 + 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * cycles * t / n)   # full-scale sine, 0..1
    return np.round(x * (2**n_bits - 1)).astype(int)

def test_ideal_quantizer_gives_nominal_bits():
    assert abs(enob(ideal_record()) - 10.0) < 0.1

def test_added_noise_lowers_enob():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)               # fixed seed: repeatable
    noisy = ideal_record() + rng.normal(0, 2, 4096)   # 2 LSB of noise
    assert 7.0 < enob(noisy) < 7.5

def test_short_record_is_rejected():
    import pytest
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        enob(np.arange(10))

The second test shows a useful habit: the expected range follows from a hand calculation (noise of 2 LSB with quantization noise of 0.29 LSB lowers the ENOB by about 2.8 bits). The test therefore encodes understanding, and not just whatever the code currently returns.

Ask the Agent for the Tests First

Before an agent writes the function, have it write the tests from your acceptance criteria, and read them. A test file is shorter than the code and exposes the agent's understanding of the problem. If a test encodes the wrong expectation, you will find it in two minutes instead of after a week of results.

docs.title: Numerical Sanity Checks
docs.text:
A numerical sanity check tests a result against something that must be true regardless of the details of the computation. It does not prove that a value is right. It can prove that it is wrong, which is often all you need. Five kinds of check cover most research code.

  • Definitional limits: an ADC's ENOB cannot exceed its nominal resolution by more than a small margin, and a probability lies between 0 and 1.
  • Physical limits: efficiency is at most 100 percent, power dissipated in a passive circuit is not negative, and a causal system does not respond before its input.
  • Hand calculation: an order-of-magnitude result that you can compute on paper. For an RC low-pass filter the cutoff is \( f_c = 1 / (2\pi R C) \). With R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF that is about 1.59 kHz, so a simulation that reports 15.9 kHz has a unit or parameter error.
  • Scaling: a linear system doubles its output when the input is doubled, and a quantity that should scale as the square of amplitude should quadruple.
  • Limit cases: a zero input produces zero output, and a very large resistor draws almost no current.

docs.title: Diagram: Numerical Sanity Check Judge
docs.text:
Numerical Sanity Check Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: numerical-sanity-check-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge each of eight reported results as plausible or as violating one of four kinds of sanity check, with at least 7 of 8 judged correctly.

Prerequisites: numerical sanity check and its four failing kinds (exceeds a limit, disagrees with a hand calculation, violates scaling, impossible value), all defined in the section "Numerical Sanity Checks" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight results the learner commits one of five verdicts. A verdict is correct when it equals the verdict in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the hint about each check is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A result printed to many digits is precise and therefore right. (2) A result that is merely different from expectation is an error. (3) A simulation result can be trusted because the simulator is well known.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work needs the learner to apply criteria to a result and name which criterion it fails. Three of the items are plausible, so that the learner does not treat every result as suspect.

Content:

All results are invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative".

# Reported result Correct verdict Why (shown as feedback) 1 A 10-bit ADC is reported to have an ENOB of 17.98 bits. Exceeds a limit ENOB cannot exceed the nominal resolution by more than a small margin. This is the 10 versus 20 log10 error. 2 A 10-bit ADC is reported to have an ENOB of 9.2 bits at 1 MS/s. Plausible It is below the nominal resolution by a typical amount. 3 A low-dropout regulator is reported to have a power efficiency of 104 percent. Exceeds a limit Efficiency cannot exceed 100 percent. 4 An RC low-pass filter with R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF is simulated and the -3 dB frequency is 1.59 kHz. Plausible It agrees with 1 / (2 pi R C) = 1.59 kHz. 5 An RC low-pass filter with R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF is simulated and the -3 dB frequency is 15.9 kHz. Disagrees with a hand calculation It is ten times the hand calculation of 1.59 kHz, which suggests a wrong parameter or unit. 6 A sweep of 64 points reports 64 different supply power values, all between 41 and 49 µW. Plausible The values are positive, bounded, and vary with the swept parameter as expected. 7 A linear filter gives an output of 0.05 V for a 0.1 V input and 0.15 V for a 0.2 V input. Violates scaling Doubling the input of a linear system must double the output, which would be 0.10 V. 8 The noise standard deviation of a record is reported as -0.8 LSB. Impossible value A standard deviation is never negative.

Verdict options: Plausible, Exceeds a limit, Disagrees with a hand calculation, Violates scaling, Impossible value.

Provenance: The five kinds of check and the RC formula are from the section "Numerical Sanity Checks" of this chapter. The results are invented for illustration.

Rules: Each result has exactly one correct verdict. A result is Plausible when it violates none of the five kinds of check. The RC cutoff is f_c = 1 / (2 pi R C), and the result is judged to disagree when it differs from the hand value by a factor of 2 or more.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads result 1.
  2. The learner chooses one of the five verdicts and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct, the "Why" sentence, and the quick calculation that exposes the problem if there is one.
  4. After result 8, the sim shows the count correct.

Feedback: Eight results, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "The verdict is ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct verdict is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: Result 1 is shown with five verdicts and none chosen. The question on screen is "Is this result plausible, and if not, which check does it fail?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states the five kinds of check, the RC cutoff of 1.59 kHz for 1 kΩ and 100 nF, and the 17.98-bit ENOB that results from using 20 log10 on a power ratio.

docs.title: Debugging and Code Review
docs.text:
Debugging is finding and fixing the cause of a defect. A reliable procedure has four steps: reproduce the failure reliably, isolate it to the smallest input and the smallest piece of code that still fails, form a hypothesis about the cause and test it, and fix it with a new test that fails before the fix and passes after. An agent is good at the mechanical part of this. Your job is to insist on the test, because an agent that "fixes" a bug without a failing test has no evidence that the bug was the thing it changed. Version control helps here, since the Git history can show which commit made the result change.

Code review is the reading of code and its changes by someone other than the author. Reviewing an agent's code is easiest as a review of its diff. Look first at what the change touches, then at numbers and constants, then at deleted lines, and last at the logic. Four questions cover most defects: does it do what the specification says, what happens on the boundary input, is every unit stated, and is there anything in the diff you were not asking for? A second agent can do a first pass against a checklist. Treat its findings as leads and not as a verdict.

docs.title: Simulation Code
docs.text:
A simulation script is a program that sets up a model, runs it, and records the outputs, whether the model is a Python system model or a driver for a circuit simulator. It has a standard shape: read parameters, build the model, run, validate the output, and write results with their parameters. Keeping the parameters in a file, not scattered in code, is the habit that makes later changes safe.

A parameter sweep repeats a simulation over a grid of parameter values to see how a result depends on them. Sweeps are where agents are most useful and where cost grows fastest. Four parameters at eight values each is \( 8^4 = 4{,}096 \) runs. At 30 seconds per run that is about 34 hours sequentially, or about 4 hours on eight cores. Before launching, estimate the cost, run a coarse grid first, and make the sweep resumable by writing each result as it finishes with its parameters.

Signal processing code, such as filtering, FFTs, and windowing, is a frequent source of silent errors because the result depends on subtle choices: the window, the number of samples per cycle, whether the input is coherent. The remedy is the known-answer test: a synthetic sine at a known frequency and amplitude must appear at the expected bin with the expected magnitude.

Circuit simulation is the use of a simulator such as ngspice to compute a circuit's behavior from a netlist, and it is a task where an agent can write a netlist in seconds. A netlist is easy to write plausibly and wrongly. The standard remedies are a lint pass for floating nodes and missing end cards, attention to unit suffixes (in SPICE, M means milli and MEG means mega), and, above all, a hand calculation to compare with the simulated result, as with the RC filter.

HDL code is code in a hardware description language such as Verilog or VHDL. An agent can write it, and it is the area where a model's training data is thinnest and its errors most subtle, such as latches inferred by accident or mismatched widths. A testbench is the HDL code that drives a design with inputs and checks its outputs. Testbench generation by an agent saves work, with one important caveat. An agent writes tests for the cases it imagined, so a testbench is only as complete as the agent's reading of the specification. Make it self-checking, with expected values computed independently, and review its coverage against the specification, not against the design.

The Test That Mirrors the Code

A common trap is asking the same agent to write the code and its tests in one step. It happens because the agent derives both from the same understanding, so a misreading appears in both and the test passes. Give the tests an independent source of truth: a hand calculation, a published value, or your own reading of the specification.

docs.title: Diagram: Unit Test Selector for Seeded Bugs
docs.text:
Unit Test Selector for Seeded Bugs

Type: microsim sim-id: unit-test-selector-seeded-bugs Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the idea of a known-answer test by selecting, from eight candidate unit tests, a set of at most four that exposes all three seeded bugs in a function.

Prerequisites: unit test, known-answer test, silent error, and boundary input, all defined in the sections "Why Tests, and Which Ones" and "Debugging and Code Review" above.

Evidence of Mastery: The learner selects up to four tests and presses Run. The selection is correct when every one of the three bugs is exposed by at least one selected test and no more than four tests are selected. Mastery is a correct selection on the first run. Reading the function source is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A test that passes proves the function is correct. (2) More tests are always better than well-chosen ones. (3) Tests of typical values catch boundary bugs.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level work needs the learner to use the known-answer idea on a concrete function. The limit of four tests forces the learner to choose tests for what they would reveal and not to pick them all.

Content:

The function under test, written in Python with NumPy, computes a signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio in decibels from signal and noise powers, and its specification states: "Return 10 times the base-10 logarithm of signal power divided by noise power. Raise ValueError if either power is not positive." The buggy implementation is:

def sndr_db(signal, noise): return 20 * np.log10(signal / noise)

It has three seeded bugs, which the sim labels as follows.

Bug Description A Uses 20 times the logarithm instead of 10 times. B Does not raise ValueError when the noise power is 0. C Does not raise ValueError when the signal power is negative or 0.

Candidate tests, each with the expected result under the specification and the bug it exposes:

# Test call Expected under the specification Exposes bug Why (shown as feedback) 1 sndr_db(100, 1) 20.0 dB A The buggy code returns 40.0. 2 sndr_db(1, 1) 0.0 dB none log10(1) is 0, so every version returns 0.0. 3 sndr_db(10, 0) raises ValueError B The buggy code does not raise ValueError for a zero noise power. 4 sndr_db(-5, 1) raises ValueError C The buggy code returns NaN and does not raise ValueError. 5 sndr_db(1000, 1) 30.0 dB A The buggy code returns 60.0. 6 sndr_db(2, 1) 3.01 dB, within 0.01 A The buggy code returns 6.02. 7 sndr_db(4, 1) 6.02 dB, within 0.01 A The buggy code returns 12.04. 8 sndr_db(0, 1) raises ValueError C The buggy code returns negative infinity and does not raise ValueError.

Provenance: The function and specification are invented for this exercise and mirror the dB error of the chapter's worked example.

Rules: A bug is exposed by a test when the buggy implementation's result differs from the expected result. The three bugs are exposed only by the tests listed against them. A selection exposes all three bugs when it contains at least one of tests 1, 5, 6, 7 (bug A), test 3 (bug B), and at least one of tests 4, 8 (bug C). The minimum correct selection has three tests.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the specification and the buggy implementation, and the eight candidate tests with their expected results.
  2. The learner selects up to four tests and presses Run.
  3. The sim runs the selected tests against the buggy function and reports which pass and which fail, and which bugs remain hidden.
  4. The learner may change the selection and run again. The sim then reveals the minimum set and the reason each test exposes its bug.

Feedback: The learner may run any number of times, and the first run is the one that counts as evidence. After each run: "Bugs exposed: . Bugs hidden: ." If more than four tests are selected the sim refuses with "Choose at most four tests." The "Why" sentence for each selected test is shown after the run.

Starting State: The eight tests are shown with none selected. The question on screen is "Which tests would reveal what is wrong?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the 10 versus 20 log10 error is a silent error, that a test needs an independently known answer, and that boundary inputs expose bugs that typical values hide.

docs.title: Reproducible Code
docs.text:
Test data are the inputs used to exercise code. Three kinds are valuable: synthetic data with a known answer, such as the ideal quantizer record; edge cases, such as an empty record, a constant record, or a record at full scale; and a small golden file, a real captured record whose correct result was verified independently and is stored with the tests, so that a change that alters the result is caught.

A reproducible environment is a recorded and recoverable set of conditions under which code ran: the language version, the library versions, the tool versions (including the simulator and its version), the operating system if it matters, and the random seeds. Pin library versions in a requirements file, seed every random number generator, and record the simulator version in the output. For work that must be reproduced years later, a container image captures the environment more completely.

Data provenance is the record of where a result came from: which input files, which code version, which parameters, which environment, and when. A simple and effective form is a run manifest written beside each result.

{
  "result": "results/enob-sweep-2026-10-15.csv",
  "inputs": ["data/raw/capture-07.csv"],
  "code_commit": "5cc5016",
  "parameters": {"window": "hann", "fundamental_bins": 7},
  "environment": "requirements.txt@5cc5016",
  "seed": 1,
  "run_at": "2026-10-15T11:40:00"
}

Code documentation is the written explanation of what code does, for the next reader. For research functions the part that matters most is the contract: what the inputs are, in what units, what is returned, what raises an error, and the equation or source it implements. An agent writes serviceable docstrings quickly, and you should check that the units and the formula it states are the ones the code uses.

Refactoring is changing the structure of code without changing its behavior, to make it clearer or easier to extend. It is a safe task for an agent only when tests already exist, because the tests are the definition of "without changing behavior". Run the tests before and after, and review the diff. Performance profiling is measuring where a program spends its time, usually with a profiler such as Python's cProfile, before optimizing. Intuition about the bottleneck is frequently wrong, and an agent's guess is no better. Profile first, change the dominant cost, and rerun the tests.

Plausible Is Not a Property of the Number

Notice that every check in this chapter compares a result with something outside the code that produced it: a known answer, a physical limit, a hand calculation. A number cannot vouch for itself. Verification always needs a second source that does not share the first one's mistakes.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Code from an agent is a hypothesis about how to compute a result, and the practices of this chapter are how you test that hypothesis. They are inexpensive when built in at the start and very expensive to retrofit after a number has appeared in a draft.

The main points to carry forward:

  • Silent errors run cleanly and return wrong numbers. A 10 versus 20 log10 mistake turned a 10-bit converter into an 18-bit one.
  • Unit tests use known answers built independently of the code, and are best written before the code.
  • Numerical sanity checks compare results with definitional and physical limits, hand calculations, scaling, and limit cases.
  • Debugging reproduces, isolates, hypothesizes, and fixes with a failing test, and code review reads the diff.
  • Simulation scripts and parameter sweeps keep parameters in files, estimate cost first, and write results as they finish.
  • Signal processing, circuit simulation, HDL code, and testbenches each need an independent check, because an agent tests what it imagined.
  • Test data, reproducible environments, and data provenance make a result recoverable, and documentation, refactoring, and profiling keep code maintainable.

Code You Can Defend

You can now write a known-answer unit test, name the sanity check that a bad result fails, pick tests that expose seeded bugs, and write a run manifest that ties a result to its code and data. That is the evidence that lets an AI-written script into a paper.

The next chapter moves from verifying results to producing ideas, using agents as thinking partners without surrendering your judgment. Round up a half-formed research topic, and bring it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter shows how to use AI as a thinking partner without surrendering judgment: framing a problem, generating and ranking ideas, developing hypotheses, designing experiments, and checking novelty. It includes techniques such as devil's advocate prompts and analogical thinking. After this chapter you can move from a vague topic to a feasible research roadmap.

Concept Concept Impact Score Problem Framing 7 Idea Generation 11 Hypothesis Development 6 Devils Advocate Prompt 1 Analogical Thinking 1 Experiment Design 3 Feasibility Assessment 2 Research Roadmap 1 Idea Ranking 1 Novelty Check 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 3: Choosing Models and Writing Clear Prompts
  • Chapter 4: Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting
  • Chapter 10: Orchestrating Teams of Planning and Execution Agents
  • Chapter 11: AI-Assisted Literature Search and Synthesis

A Partner That Never Tires of Your Bad Ideas

A model will produce forty ideas in a minute and never get bored of your thirty-ninth revision. What it cannot do is decide which idea is worth two years of your life. This chapter is about using its volume and keeping the choice. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Framing the Problem
docs.text:
Problem framing is the work of turning a topic into a question that can be investigated: deciding what the problem is, which quantity matters, under what constraints, and what would count as progress. It happens before any solution is sought, and it is where most of a project's leverage lies. A well-framed problem makes an average method look good, and a badly framed one defeats an excellent method.

A vague topic such as "low-power ADCs for sensor nodes" can be framed in many ways, and each framing implies different work. An assistant is useful here because it can produce framings quickly. Ask it for five distinct framings, and for each, the quantity to optimize, the constraint that binds, and what would have to be true for it to be worth doing. Then apply the question tests of Chapter 1: is each specific, measurable, bounded, and falsifiable?

Framing Quantity Binding constraint What it would take Minimize energy per conversion fJ per conversion step Fixed ENOB of 9.5 bits A new comparator or DAC scheme Maximize ENOB at fixed power bits 50 µW budget Better calibration Minimize area mm² Fixed ENOB and energy Denser capacitor array Tolerate process variation yield, percent Fixed spec across corners Robust or self-calibrating design Operate from a harvested supply functioning voltage range Supply from 0.6 V to 1.0 V Wide-range design

Table 1. Five framings of one topic. Each implies a different project. Values are illustrative.

Reframe by Changing One Thing

To get past a stuck framing, ask the model to restate your problem four times, changing exactly one element each time: the metric, the constraint, the scale, or the stakeholder. A change of one thing at a time shows you which element the problem is really about.

docs.title: Generating and Challenging Ideas
docs.text:
Idea generation is the production of candidate approaches to a framed problem. It has two phases that are best kept apart. The divergent phase aims at quantity and range, with no judgment. The convergent phase evaluates and selects. Mixing them kills both: judging ideas while generating them stops the supply, and generating while judging blurs the criteria.

A language model is well suited to the divergent phase. It has absorbed a very wide literature, and it produces variations without social cost. Two prompting habits raise the quality of what it produces. Ask for ideas that differ along named axes, so that the list spans the space and does not cluster. And ask for the ideas in a table with a column for the key assumption, so that you can see what each one depends on. An example prompt, in the structure of Chapter 3:

Problem: reduce the energy per conversion of a 10-bit SAR ADC at fixed ENOB of 9.5 bits in 65 nm CMOS.
Task: propose 10 distinct approaches. Each must differ from the others in at least one of:
architecture, calibration method, circuit technique, or algorithm.
Output: a table with columns: idea (one line), mechanism (one sentence),
key assumption, what would make it fail.
Constraint: do not repeat the same mechanism in different words.

Analogical thinking is borrowing structure from another field. The question is: what other field has solved a problem with the same shape? Sparse sampling from compressive sensing, error-correcting codes from communications, and adaptive filtering from control are examples of ideas that moved into circuit design that way. An assistant can list candidate analogies from fields you do not know, and that is a real advantage, since it has read in more areas than you have. The mapping must then be checked: an analogy carries over a structure only if the constraints correspond, and a plausible-sounding analogy with a broken mapping is a common source of ideas that fail on contact with physics.

A devil's advocate prompt is a request that the model argue against an idea: list the strongest reasons it will fail, the assumptions it depends on, and the result that would show it to be wrong. Models tend to agree with the person they are talking to, so a neutral request such as "what do you think of this idea?" returns encouragement. An explicit request for specific objections returns something useful. Ask for objections ranked by severity, and for the cheapest experiment that would test the most serious one.

The Model Likes Your Idea

A common trap is reading the model's enthusiasm as evidence that an idea is good. It happens because the model is inclined to agree with you and to elaborate. Always run the idea past an explicit devil's advocate prompt, and treat a response with no specific objections as a sign that the prompt, and not the idea, was weak.

docs.title: From Idea to Hypothesis and Experiment
docs.text: Hypothesis development turns an idea into a statement that an experiment could show to be wrong. A research hypothesis has a form that makes this explicit: under stated conditions, a stated change produces a stated effect of at least a stated size. "Foreground calibration of the comparator offset raises the ENOB of the 10-bit SAR ADC from 8.6 to at least 9.5 bits at 1 MS/s and 1.0 V, in 65 nm CMOS" is a hypothesis. "Calibration makes the ADC better" is not, because no result could contradict it.

docs.title: Diagram: Falsifiable Hypothesis Sorter
docs.text:
Falsifiable Hypothesis Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: falsifiable-hypothesis-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish falsifiable hypotheses from statements that no experiment could contradict, among eight statements, with at least 7 of 8 classified correctly.

Prerequisites: hypothesis, falsifiable, metric, and condition, all defined in the section "From Idea to Hypothesis and Experiment" above and in Chapter 1.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight statements the learner commits "falsifiable" or "not falsifiable". A classification is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the checklist of properties is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A statement with a number in it is falsifiable. (2) A confident, technical-sounding statement is a hypothesis. (3) A statement that cannot fail is the strongest claim.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level work needs the learner to decompose a statement into its parts, metric, condition, and threshold, and to see which part is missing. Non-falsifiable items fail in different ways so that no single cue is enough.

Content:

All statements are invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative".

# Statement Correct classification Why (shown as feedback) 1 A 10-bit SAR ADC with foreground offset calibration reaches an ENOB of at least 9.5 bits at 1 MS/s in 65 nm CMOS while drawing under 50 µW. Falsifiable It names a metric, a threshold, and the conditions, and a measurement could contradict it. 2 Calibration makes the ADC better. Not falsifiable It has no metric and no threshold, so no result can contradict it. 3 The ADC will perform well under suitable conditions. Not falsifiable The conditions are unspecified, so any failure can be blamed on unsuitable conditions. 4 Either the offset improves or it does not. Not falsifiable It is true whatever happens, so it says nothing about the circuit. 5 Adding a 4-bit redundant capacitor array reduces the standard deviation of DNL by at least 30 percent relative to the baseline layout in a 200-run Monte Carlo simulation. Falsifiable It names the change, the size of the effect, the baseline, and the test. 6 Machine learning will eventually make analog design obsolete. Not falsifiable It has no time bound and no measurable criterion, so no observation could contradict it. 7 A surrogate model trained on 5,000 simulated samples predicts the op-amp gain within 1 dB on held-out designs. Falsifiable It names the training size, the tolerance, and a held-out test. 8 Any result that disagrees with the theory was caused by measurement error. Not falsifiable It explains away every disagreement in advance, so no result can count against the theory.

Provenance: The form of a hypothesis is from the section "From Idea to Hypothesis and Experiment" of this chapter. The statements are invented for illustration.

Rules: A statement is falsifiable when it names a measurable quantity, a threshold or direction and size of effect, and conditions under which it is tested, so that some possible observation would contradict it. A statement missing any of these, or that is true under every outcome, is not falsifiable.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads statement 1.
  2. The learner chooses "falsifiable" or "not falsifiable" and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence, with the missing element named for a not-falsifiable statement.
  4. After statement 8, the sim shows the count correct.

Feedback: Eight statements, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "This statement is ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct classification is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: Statement 1 is shown with two choices. The question on screen is "Could any measurement show this to be wrong?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a hypothesis names a stated change, a stated effect size, and stated conditions, and gives "calibration makes the ADC better" as an example of a statement that is not falsifiable.

Experiment design is the planning of the measurements or simulations that will test a hypothesis, and it is where a hypothesis becomes work. An experiment needs a defined independent variable that you change, a dependent variable that you measure, the controlled variables that you hold fixed, a baseline against which the effect is compared, enough repetitions to separate the effect from noise, and, decided before the data are seen, the criterion that will count as support or refutation. Writing the criterion in advance is the protection against fitting the interpretation to the result. An agent can draft a protocol quickly. Your contribution is the domain knowledge it lacks: confounds such as temperature drift, the corner cases that matter, and the limits of the instrument.

docs.title: Judging Feasibility, Ranking, and Novelty
docs.text:
Feasibility assessment estimates whether an idea can be carried through with the time, tools, skills, and data you have. A quick feasibility estimate uses a back-of-envelope calculation and a short list of requirements: is the process available, does the needed tool license exist, how long does fabrication or a measurement take, and does the result need data you do not have? Ask an agent to enumerate what the idea requires and to mark each requirement as in hand, obtainable, or missing, then check the list yourself for what only you know about your lab.

Idea ranking is ordering candidate ideas by weighted criteria. The usual criteria are impact, feasibility, novelty, and risk. The rank depends on the weights, and so the weights are the real decision. A student whose thesis rests on a novel contribution and a researcher with a deadline in three months should weight the same four scores differently and will pick different projects from the same list. Make the scoring explicit in a table, let an agent propose scores, correct them, and then vary the weights to see whether the ranking is stable.

The second MicroSim practices this on a small set of ideas. The weighted score of an idea is \( S = \sum_i w_i s_i \), where \( s_i \) is its score on criterion \( i \) from 1 to 5 and \( w_i \) is the weight, with the weights summing to 1.

docs.title: Diagram: Research Idea Ranking Matrix
docs.text:
Research Idea Ranking Matrix

Type: microsim sim-id: research-idea-ranking-matrix Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the weighted score of research ideas under two weighting profiles and state which idea ranks first under each, with all five answers correct.

Prerequisites: idea ranking, weighted score, impact, feasibility, novelty, and risk, all defined in the section "Judging Feasibility, Ranking, and Novelty" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of five questions the learner enters a number or chooses an answer. A number is correct when it is within 0.05 of the value in Content, and a choice is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is 5 of 5 correct. Changing the weights in exploration mode is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The best idea is the best under every weighting. (2) A high score on one criterion makes an idea rank first. (3) The weights are a technicality and not part of the decision.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level work needs the learner to carry out the weighted-sum calculation and then see the ranking change with the weights, which makes the weighting the visible decision.

Content:

Scores from 1 to 5, where 5 is best. "Low risk" is scored so that a higher number means lower risk. The ideas and scores are invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative".

Idea Impact Feasibility Novelty Low risk I1: Foreground calibration of comparator offset 3 5 2 5 I2: Learned redundancy to reduce mismatch 4 2 5 2 I3: New capacitor array layout 3 4 3 4 I4: Time-interleaved SAR with background calibration 5 2 4 2

Weighting profiles, each summing to 1.0:

Profile Impact Feasibility Novelty Low risk P1: Exploratory thesis 0.3 0.1 0.4 0.2 P2: Deadline in three months 0.2 0.5 0.1 0.2

Reference scores:

Idea P1 score P2 score I1 3.2 4.3 I2 3.8 2.7 I3 3.3 3.7 I4 3.7 2.8

Questions, in this order:

# Question Answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 What is the weighted score of I4 under P1? 3.7 5 x 0.3 + 2 x 0.1 + 4 x 0.4 + 2 x 0.2 = 1.5 + 0.2 + 1.6 + 0.4 = 3.7. 2 What is the weighted score of I1 under P2? 4.3 3 x 0.2 + 5 x 0.5 + 2 x 0.1 + 5 x 0.2 = 0.6 + 2.5 + 0.2 + 1.0 = 4.3. 3 Which idea ranks first under P1? I2 Its score of 3.8 is the highest under P1. 4 Which idea ranks first under P2? I1 Its score of 4.3 is the highest under P2. 5 Is there an idea that ranks first under both profiles? No I2 leads under P1 and I1 leads under P2, so the weights decide the choice.

Provenance: The weighted-sum formula is from the section "Judging Feasibility, Ranking, and Novelty" of this chapter. All scores and weights are invented for illustration.

Rules: Score S = sum over criteria of weight x score. Scores are displayed to one decimal place. Weights in exploration mode must sum to 1.0 in steps of 0.05, with a minimum of 0.0 and a maximum of 1.0. Ties are reported as tied.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the score matrix and the two weighting profiles, and question 1.
  2. The learner enters the number or chooses the answer and submits.
  3. The sim shows the worked calculation and the full ranking under both profiles.
  4. After question 5, exploration opens: the learner sets their own weights and watches the ranking change. The learner should notice that the ranking can be reversed by moving a small amount of weight.

Feedback: Five questions, two attempts each for the numeric answers and one for the choices, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the worked calculation. Incorrect on the first numeric attempt: "Multiply each score by its weight and add the four products." Incorrect on the second attempt, or on a choice: the worked calculation and the correct answer. A running count "n of 5 correct" is shown.

Starting State: The score matrix and profile P1 are shown with question 1. The question on screen is "Which idea wins when novelty matters most?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that ranking depends on the weights, that a thesis with a novelty emphasis and a deadline-driven project weight the same scores differently, and that the weighted score is the sum of weight times score.

Novelty check is the verification that an idea has not already been done. It is a point where a model is unreliable in a particular way: a model's statement that an idea is novel is not evidence, because it reflects what the model does not remember, not what the literature contains. Run the search pipeline of Chapter 11 on the core of your idea, with several phrasings, and in more than one database. Record the five closest prior works, and for each write in one sentence what you would do differently. A novelty claim that rests on that table is a claim you can defend to a reviewer.

docs.title: The Research Roadmap
docs.text:
A research roadmap is the plan that connects the framed problem to a sequence of work: the hypotheses to be tested, the experiments that test them, the order, the dependencies, and, importantly, the decision points. At each decision point the roadmap states what result would lead to continuing, to changing direction, or to stopping. A roadmap with explicit go and no-go criteria is the research version of the acceptance criteria of Chapter 4, and it protects against the common failure of continuing a line of work because of the effort already spent.

Stage Question Output Go criterion If not 1. Feasibility Can the offset be measured to 0.1 mV? Measurement note Repeatability within 0.1 mV on 10 devices Change the instrument or the method 2. Prototype Does calibration raise ENOB on one device? Simulated and measured ENOB At least 9.0 bits on 5 of 5 devices Revisit the calibration algorithm 3. Characterization Does it hold across corners and 40 devices? Result table with spread At least 9.5 bits at typical and no worse than 9.0 at corners Narrow the claim to what holds 4. Write up What is the contribution relative to prior work? Draft paper Novelty table complete and verified Reframe the contribution

Table 2. A roadmap fragment with go criteria. The numbers are illustrative.

An agent can draft a roadmap from the hypothesis and the feasibility list. Treat the draft as a plan to review (Chapter 10), and add the thing agents cannot supply: your knowledge of how long measurements and fabrication really take in your lab.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
An agent's strength in this phase of research is volume and range, and its weakness is agreement. The techniques of the chapter use the first and guard against the second, while leaving the choices that matter with you.

The main points to carry forward:

  • Problem framing precedes solutions, and a framing is a choice of quantity, constraint, and scale. Ask for several and test each against the question criteria.
  • Idea generation separates divergent and convergent phases, and a table with assumptions and failure conditions makes ideas comparable.
  • Analogical thinking extends your reach, and the mapping must be checked. A devil's advocate prompt counters the model's tendency to agree.
  • A hypothesis states a change, an effect size, and conditions, and so it can be wrong.
  • Experiment design fixes the variables, the baseline, and the support criterion before the data are seen.
  • Feasibility assessment, idea ranking, and novelty checks make the selection explicit. The weights are the decision, and a novelty claim rests on a search.
  • A research roadmap has decision points with go criteria.

From Topic to Roadmap

You can now frame a topic as several testable questions, tell a falsifiable hypothesis from one no result could contradict, compute how the ranking of ideas changes with your priorities, and lay out a roadmap with go criteria. The choices stay yours, and the volume is the agent's.

The next chapter takes a result that has survived this process and follows it into a manuscript. Round up your strongest hypothesis, and bring it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter follows a paper from structure to submission: outlining, drafting, revision, author voice, LaTeX, figures and captions, reference formatting, venue requirements, peer review responses, and arXiv submission. It also covers authorship and co-author review. After this chapter you can draft a section from notes and revise it into your own voice.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 19 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Paper Structure 15 Abstract Writing 2 Outline Generation 9 Drafting 8 Revision 7 Author Voice 1 LaTeX 6 Figure Preparation 4 Figure Captions 1 Reference Formatting 3 arXiv Submission 2 Peer Review Response 1 Technical Editing 3 Style Consistency 1 Grammar and Clarity 1 Authorship 3 Co-Author Review 1 Venue Requirements 3 Cover Letter 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 3: Choosing Models and Writing Clear Prompts
  • Chapter 4: Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting
  • Chapter 5: Markdown Project Files and Version Control
  • Chapter 6: Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill
  • Chapter 9: Supervising Agents and Defining Agent Roles
  • Chapter 11: AI-Assisted Literature Search and Synthesis
  • Chapter 12: AI-Assisted Data Analysis and Scripting

The Paper Is Yours

A model can turn notes into prose faster than you can type, and prose that has not passed through your judgment is not your paper. This chapter shows how to let an agent draft and polish while every claim, every number, and the voice stay yours. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Structure, Outline, and Abstract
docs.text:
Paper structure is the standard arrangement of a research paper into sections that each answer one reader question. For an engineering paper the arrangement is usually an abstract, an introduction, related work, the method or design, the experiments and results, a discussion, and a conclusion. Readers rely on this: they go to the results for the numbers and to the discussion for the limits. A paper that follows the convention is read faster and judged more fairly.

Section The reader's question Typical contents Abstract Should I read this? Context, gap, contribution, headline result, significance Introduction Why does this matter? Problem, why it is hard, contribution, roadmap Related work What is already known? Grouped prior work and the remaining gap Method What exactly was done? Design, algorithm, setup, enough to reproduce Results What was found? Data, tables, figures, with conditions Discussion What does it mean, and what are the limits? Interpretation, limitations, comparison Conclusion What should I take away? Summary and future work

Table 1. The sections of a typical engineering paper and the question each answers.

Outline generation is producing the skeleton of the paper, section by section, with the claim each paragraph will make. It is the stage at which an agent saves the most effort and the one at which your control matters most, because the outline fixes the argument. A good outline is a list of claims, each tied to the evidence that supports it, such as a result file, a figure, or a reference. Give the agent your notes and results, ask for an outline in which every bullet is a claim and names its evidence, and ask it to mark any bullet for which no evidence was supplied. Those marks are the work still to be done.

Abstract writing is the compression of the whole paper into about 150 to 250 words. An abstract has a fixed anatomy, and it is useful to check a draft against it: one sentence of context, one stating the gap or problem, one stating what the paper contributes, one or two giving the key result with its numbers and conditions, and one on significance. The most common defect is a result stated without a number. Write the abstract last, from the finished paper, and make sure every number in it appears in the body.

docs.title: Drafting and Revising
docs.text:
Drafting is writing the first version of a section. A dependable method for working with an agent is to draft from claims, not from a topic. For each paragraph, supply the claim, the evidence, and the intended reader, and instruct the agent to use only the supplied material and to insert a marker such as [NO EVIDENCE] wherever it would have to assert something not supplied. The marker is what keeps a fluent draft from smuggling in claims you cannot support.

Revision is the repeated improvement of a draft, and it benefits most from a human eye on the argument and a machine's help on the sentences. The sequence that works is to revise the structure first (order of sections and paragraphs), then the argument within paragraphs, then the sentences, and last the surface. A model asked to "improve this" at the start works on the surface and leaves a structural problem in place.

Author voice is the consistent personality and phrasing of your writing, and it is what makes a paper read as written by one person. Left alone, models drift toward a generic register: long lists of three, stock transitions, and claims of significance larger than the evidence. Three practices protect your voice. Draft the sections that carry the argument yourself, such as the introduction and discussion, and use the agent for the more routine ones. When you ask for edits, supply a paragraph of your own earlier writing as a style sample and an instruction to edit and not to rewrite. And read the result aloud. If a sentence sounds like no one you know, change it.

Revision by an agent has a specific hazard, which is that numbers and claims change without notice while the prose improves. The check is mechanical and cheap. The script below, with its logic explained first, extracts every number from the text before and after an edit and reports any number that appears in only one of them. The regular expression matches optional signs, digits, decimal points, and thousands separators.

import re, sys

def numbers(text):
    return set(re.findall(r"[-+]?\d[\d,]*\.?\d*", text))

before = open(sys.argv[1]).read()
after = open(sys.argv[2]).read()
b, a = numbers(before), numbers(after)
print("only in original:", sorted(b - a))
print("only in revision:", sorted(a - b))

Run on a revised paragraph, it takes a second and flags a changed ENOB figure that no amount of reading fluent prose would have caught. A clean report does not prove that the claims are unchanged, since a qualifier could have been deleted, but a report with differences is always worth reading.

Edit, Do Not Rewrite, and Diff the Numbers

Tell the agent to preserve every number, unit, and claim, and to change only the wording. Then run the number check and read git diff on the paper source. A revision that changes a number or removes a qualifier is not a revision.

docs.title: Diagram: Paper Section Sorter
docs.text:
Paper Section Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: paper-section-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of ten sentences from an engineering paper into the section where it belongs, with at least 8 of 10 classified correctly.

Prerequisites: the sections of a paper and the reader question each answers, defined in the section "Structure, Outline, and Abstract" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of ten sentences the learner commits one of six sections. A classification is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the table of sections is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any sentence with a number is a result. (2) A contribution statement belongs only in the abstract. (3) A limitation belongs in the conclusion and not in the discussion.

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level classification needs the learner to explain a sentence's function by the reader question it answers. The sentences are drawn from one invented paper so that the sections can be compared in context.

Content:

All sentences are invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative". The six sections are Abstract, Introduction, Related work, Method, Results, and Discussion.

# Sentence Correct section Why (shown as feedback) 1 Successive-approximation converters dominate low-power sensor interfaces, yet their accuracy is limited by capacitor mismatch. Introduction It states the problem and why it matters. 2 Prior calibration schemes either require a dedicated reference or converge slowly [3], [7]. Related work It positions earlier work and points to the gap. 3 The comparator offset is measured by shorting its inputs and averaging 256 decisions. Method It states what was done, in enough detail to reproduce. 4 The calibrated converter reaches an ENOB of 9.4 bits at 1 MS/s. Results It reports a measured finding. 5 The residual error is consistent with the thermal noise of the comparator, which suggests that a larger input pair would give a further gain. Discussion It interprets a result and points to a consequence. 6 Measurements were taken on 12 devices from one wafer at 25 °C with a 4,096-sample record. Method It describes the experimental setup. 7 We present a foreground offset calibration for SAR ADCs that raises measured ENOB from 8.6 to 9.4 bits at 1 MS/s in 65 nm CMOS using 45 µW. Abstract It compresses context, contribution, and key result with numbers into one sentence. 8 Table II lists the ENOB of the 12 devices before and after calibration. Results It presents the data. 9 The gain is limited to chips with an offset below 15 mV, since larger offsets saturate the correction range. Discussion It states a limitation. 10 Section III describes the calibration algorithm and Section IV the measurement setup. Introduction It is the roadmap paragraph that ends an introduction.

Provenance: The sections and their questions are from the section "Structure, Outline, and Abstract" of this chapter. The sentences and values are invented for illustration.

Rules: Each sentence has exactly one correct section. A sentence is classified by the reader question it answers.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads sentence 1.
  2. The learner chooses one of the six sections and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence.
  4. After sentence 10, the sim shows the count correct and the sentences grouped by section.

Feedback: Ten sentences, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "This belongs in ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct section is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 10 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 8 was met.

Starting State: Sentence 1 is shown with six sections and none chosen. The question on screen is "Which reader question does this sentence answer?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists the sections and the reader question each answers, states that an abstract compresses context, gap, contribution, and result, and that the introduction ends with a roadmap.

docs.title: Figures, LaTeX, and References
docs.text:
LaTeX is the typesetting system that most engineering venues use, and it is plain text. That makes it a good fit for the version-controlled project of Chapter 5 and for agents, which write LaTeX fluently. The cautions are practical. An agent may use packages your venue's template does not allow, produce markup that compiles with warnings, or silently alter a macro. Keep the venue's class file and template unchanged, compile after every substantial edit, and read the log for warnings, since a wrong cross-reference shows up there as ?? in the output.

Figure preparation is making the figures that carry the results, and the standards are those of Chapter 12: labeled axes with units, a legible size at the column width, visible spread, and a consistent style across figures. Generate every figure from a script that reads the processed data, so that the figure can be regenerated when the data change. A figure drawn by hand in an editor cannot be reproduced and tends to go stale.

Figure captions are the text that makes a figure readable without searching the body for its context. A good caption states what is plotted, the conditions under which the data were obtained, how to read any markers or error bars, and, where it helps, the one observation the reader should take. The standard to apply is that the figure and caption together can be understood without the body text.

docs.title: Diagram: Figure Caption Critic
docs.text:
Figure Caption Critic

Type: microsim sim-id: figure-caption-critic Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: critique Learning Objective: The learner will critique each of six figure captions by naming its main defect, or that it has none, with at least 5 of 6 judged correctly.

Prerequisites: figure caption and the four properties of a good caption (what is plotted, conditions, how to read it, no unsupported claim), all defined in the section "Figures, LaTeX, and References" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of six captions the learner commits one of five judgments. A judgment is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the checklist is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A short caption is a good caption. (2) A caption can rely on the body text for its conditions. (3) A caption should state the paper's main claim.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work needs the learner to apply a checklist to a caption and name the failing criterion. One item has a caption that is long but has no defect, and one has a short caption that fails, so that length is not a cue.

Content:

All captions are invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative". Judgment options: Vague, Missing conditions, Undefined symbols, Overclaims, No defect.

# Caption Correct judgment Why (shown as feedback) 1 Figure 3. ENOB results. Vague It does not say what is plotted against what, so the reader cannot tell what the figure shows. 2 Figure 4. Measured ENOB versus input frequency for 12 devices at 1 MS/s, 1.0 V, and 25 °C. Markers show the mean and error bars show one standard deviation. No defect It states the quantity, the conditions, and how to read the markers. 3 Figure 5. Measured ENOB versus input frequency. Missing conditions The sampling rate, supply, temperature, and number of devices are not stated. 4 Figure 6. SNDR versus input frequency, showing that our design is the best known SAR ADC. Overclaims A single figure of SNDR versus frequency cannot establish that the design is the best known. 5 Figure 7. FoM_W versus fs for ADC1 to ADC9 (measured, 65 nm). Undefined symbols FoM_W, fs, and ADC1 to ADC9 are not defined in the caption. 6 Figure 8. Power breakdown of the converter at 1 MS/s and 1.0 V (simulated, typical corner): comparator 38 percent, DAC 27 percent, logic 25 percent, clock 10 percent. No defect It states the conditions, that the data are simulated, and the breakdown, which sums to 100 percent.

Provenance: The caption properties are from the section "Figures, LaTeX, and References" of this chapter. The captions and values are invented for illustration.

Rules: Each caption has exactly one correct judgment. A caption is judged by the first failing property, in this order: Vague, Missing conditions, Undefined symbols, Overclaims. A caption with none of these defects is judged No defect.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads caption 1 and the checklist.
  2. The learner chooses one of the five judgments and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence, and offers a corrected caption where there is a defect.
  4. After caption 6, the sim shows the count correct.

Feedback: Six captions, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "The main issue is ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct judgment is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 6 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 5 was met.

Starting State: Caption 1 is shown with five judgments. The question on screen is "Could a reader understand this figure from the caption alone?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a caption says what is plotted, the conditions, how to read the markers, and the observation to take, and that figure and caption together should be understandable without the body.

Reference formatting is producing the reference list in the style a venue requires. With BibTeX and a venue's style file the formatting is automatic, so the job is to keep the BibTeX entries correct and complete: verified as in Chapter 11, with the venue name, year, volume, pages, and DOI present. Never let an agent retype a reference by hand into the text, since that is where fabricated and corrupted entries enter.

Venue requirements are the rules a particular journal or conference sets: the template, the page limit, whether review is anonymous, the reference style, the required statements such as data availability, ethics, and use of AI tools, and the file formats for submission. Read them before drafting, not after. A common and avoidable waste is a paper written to one length and then cut to another, and an agent can check a manuscript against a pasted copy of the requirements.

docs.title: Editing, Consistency, and Co-Authors
docs.text:
Technical editing is the line-by-line check for correctness of terminology, symbols, units, and cross-references. Style consistency is the uniform treatment of the same thing throughout the paper: one abbreviation for each term, one convention for units and number formatting, one notation for each symbol, one spelling variant. Grammar and clarity are the sentence-level correctness and readability of the prose. These three are tasks in which an agent is strong and in which you should still ask for a list of proposed changes and not a silent rewrite, so that each change can be accepted or rejected in the diff. A useful instruction is "list inconsistencies in notation and terminology and propose one resolution for each, without editing the text".

Authorship is the question of who is credited for the work and who is accountable for it. The widely used criteria require substantial contribution, drafting or critical revision, approval of the final version, and accountability for the work. Those criteria cannot be satisfied by a language model, and major publishers, including IEEE and ACM, state that AI systems may not be listed as authors and that substantive use of AI tools must be disclosed. Policies change, so read the current policy of your venue. Chapter 18 treats disclosure in detail.

Co-author review is the circulation of the draft to the people who share responsibility for it. Send them a version that is complete enough to read, with the claims, the evidence, and the open questions marked, and ask for specific things: check the numbers in Table II, confirm the description of the method, read Section 5 for fairness to prior work. Every co-author should know which parts were drafted with AI assistance.

docs.title: Submission and Response
docs.text:
arXiv submission is the posting of a manuscript to the arXiv preprint server, which makes a paper available before or alongside peer review. The practical points are these. You submit the LaTeX source and its figures, and arXiv compiles it, so the source must build cleanly from a clean directory. Include the compiled bibliography file (the .bbl), since arXiv's guidance is to submit that file and not to rely on BibTeX running during processing. Choose the subject category with care, and check the current submission guidelines, including the endorsement rules for first-time submitters. Check the compiled PDF that arXiv produces before announcing, because it is the version readers get.
