A cover letter accompanies a journal submission and is short: the title and the contribution in a few sentences, why the work fits the venue, confirmation that it is not under consideration elsewhere, and any required declarations. An agent drafts it adequately from the abstract and the venue's scope statement. Check that it claims nothing the paper does not.

A peer review response is the reply to reviewers' comments, normally a point-by-point document. Each reviewer comment is quoted, followed by your response and, where the paper changed, the location of the change. An agent is useful for organizing the comments into a table and drafting a first response. Three rules apply. Never claim a change that was not made. Answer the comment actually asked, not a nearby easier one. And decide yourself where to disagree: a polite, evidenced disagreement is acceptable, and an agent will tend to accommodate every comment whether or not it is right.

Reviewer comment Response Change Location R1.2: ENOB is measured on one chip only. We now report 12 devices, with mean and standard deviation. Added Table III Section V-B R2.4: The comparison omits the work of [14]. We agree and have added it with matching conditions. Added row to Table IV Section VI R2.5: The method should be tested at 125 °C. We could not test at this temperature with our setup and state this as a limitation. Added a sentence Section VII

Table 2. A fragment of a response matrix, with illustrative content.

Accommodating Every Comment

A common trap is letting an agent draft a response that agrees with every reviewer comment. It happens because the model is inclined to please, and the draft reads as gracious. Decide your position on each comment first, then ask for wording. A reviewer who sees a claimed change that is missing from the paper will stop trusting the rest.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
A manuscript is the point where all the earlier verification meets a reader, and the practices of this chapter keep AI assistance from eroding it. Draft from evidenced claims, protect your voice and your numbers, regenerate every figure from data, verify every reference, and keep to the venue's rules.

The main points to carry forward:

  • Paper structure answers one reader question per section, and an outline of evidenced claims fixes the argument. Write the abstract last, with numbers.
  • Drafting from claims with a no-evidence marker, and revising from structure to surface, keep unsupported claims out.
  • Author voice is protected by drafting argument-bearing sections yourself, supplying style samples, and reading aloud. A number check on every revision catches silent changes.
  • LaTeX, figures, and captions are generated from source and data. A caption stands alone with its figure.
  • Reference formatting relies on verified BibTeX and never on hand-typed entries.
  • Venue requirements are read first. Technical editing, style consistency, and grammar are done through proposed changes, not silent rewrites.
  • Authorship requires accountability that a model cannot take, so AI is disclosed and is not an author.
  • arXiv submission, cover letters, and peer review responses have specific forms. Never claim an unmade change.

A Draft That Is Still Yours

You can now place a sentence in its section, build an abstract with numbers, check a revision for changed numbers, judge a figure caption against a checklist, and write a response that claims only what changed. The agent supplies speed, and you supply the claims.

The next chapter turns a result into something readers can interact with: simulations, slides, and teaching materials. Round up the one result you would most like others to understand, and bring it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers the ways research results are communicated and taught: slide decks, interactive simulations, MicroSims, embedded simulations, learning graphs, and intelligent textbooks. It introduces generating a MicroSim with an agent. After this chapter you can create an interactive simulation that illustrates a concept from your research.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 11 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Research Communication 15 Slide Deck 2 Interactive Simulation 10 p5.js 10 MicroSim 9 Concept Dependency 7 Learning Graph 6 Intelligent Textbook 5 Embedding Simulations 1 Teaching From Research 2 MicroSim Generation 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 5: Markdown Project Files and Version Control
  • Chapter 6: Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill
  • Chapter 9: Supervising Agents and Defining Agent Roles
  • Chapter 13: Simulation, Testing, and Reproducible Code
  • Chapter 15: AI-Assisted Manuscript Preparation

Let Readers Turn the Knob

A figure shows one setting of a result, and a reader who can move the slider understands the whole relationship. You are looking at a book built this way: every interactive on these pages began as a written specification. By the end you will be able to write one for your own result. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Communicating Research
docs.text:
Research communication is the transfer of a result and its reasoning to a particular audience for a particular purpose. The same result is communicated differently to a reviewer, who wants evidence and limits, to a colleague who wants the method, to a student who wants the idea, and to a funder who wants significance. The medium follows from the audience, and agents can help with several of them.

A slide deck is the standard medium for a talk. An agent drafts a deck quickly from a paper, and the common failure is a deck that mirrors the paper's structure instead of a talk's. A talk has one message, a few supporting points, and few words per slide. Ask for the deck from a stated audience, time, and single message, and require that each slide state its point as a sentence in the title. Reuse figures from the paper's source scripts and not screenshots, and run the number check of Chapter 15 on every slide, since figures in slides are copied and changed more often than anywhere else.

A static figure shows a result at the parameter values the author chose. An interactive simulation is a program that lets the viewer change parameters and see the response, and so lets the viewer explore the relationship the result describes. It is the right medium when the point of the result is a dependence: how ENOB falls as noise rises, how leakage changes with window choice, how a search converges. It is the wrong medium for a fact that has no parameter.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
A MicroSim is a small, single-concept, interactive simulation that runs in a web browser, is embedded in a page, has open and readable source code, and is built from a short specification. The idea, developed in the author's MicroSims project, is that a simulation small enough to specify in a page can be generated by an AI model, checked by a person, and embedded anywhere that displays web pages. This book contains many, each in its own directory under docs/sims/ with a main.html that is embedded in the chapter and an index.md lesson page.

The library most often used is p5.js, a JavaScript library for drawing and interaction in the browser. It needs no installation, runs everywhere, and has built-in controls such as sliders, buttons, and drop-downs. The rule in this book is to use the library's own controls and not to draw them by hand, since the built-in ones are accessible and consistent. Two further conventions keep sims embeddable: the first statement in setup() reads the container width so that the canvas fits the page, and the canvas is attached to the page's main element.

Before the code, here is the relationship it shows. When Gaussian noise of standard deviation \( \sigma \), measured in least-significant bits, is added to an ideal \( N \)-bit quantizer whose own quantization noise has standard deviation \( 1/\sqrt{12} \) LSB, the effective number of bits becomes

\[ \text{ENOB} = N - \tfrac{1}{2}\log_2\!\left(1 + 12\,\sigma^2\right). \]

For \( N = 10 \) and \( \sigma = 2 \) the value is 7.19 bits, the number used in Chapter 13. The sketch below draws one bar for ENOB and one for the nominal bits, and a slider changes \( \sigma \). It uses createSlider(min, max, value, step), which creates a slider with a minimum, a maximum, a starting value, and a step size.

let sigmaSlider;
let canvasWidth = 400;

function updateCanvasSize() {
  canvasWidth = document.querySelector('main').offsetWidth;
}

function setup() {
  updateCanvasSize();
  const canvas = createCanvas(canvasWidth, 220);
  canvas.parent(document.querySelector('main'));
  sigmaSlider = createSlider(0, 4, 1, 0.25);   // noise in LSB
  sigmaSlider.parent(document.querySelector('main'));
}

function draw() {
  background('aliceblue');
  const sigma = sigmaSlider.value();
  const enob = 10 - 0.5 * Math.log2(1 + 12 * sigma * sigma);
  const scale = (canvasWidth - 40) / 10;             // pixels per bit
  fill('lightgray'); rect(20, 40, 10 * scale, 40);   // nominal 10 bits
  fill('steelblue'); rect(20, 110, enob * scale, 40);
  fill(0); noStroke();
  text('Nominal: 10 bits', 20, 30);
  text('ENOB: ' + enob.toFixed(2) + ' bits at sigma = ' + sigma + ' LSB', 20, 100);
}

Slide the control to 0 and the bar reaches about 10 bits; slide it to 2 and it falls to about 7.2. A reader who has seen this does not need the formula explained. The same sketch, with labels and a lesson page, is a complete MicroSim.

The Interactive Is the Result in Motion

Notice that the sketch has no data in it, only the relationship. A paper's table gives you the points the authors measured, and a sim gives you the function that the points came from. That is why a good MicroSim teaches in a minute what a page of text takes ten to explain.

docs.title: Generating a MicroSim With an Agent
docs.text:
MicroSim generation is the use of an agent to build a MicroSim from a specification. The workflow of this book is specification first. A specification states what the learner must be able to do afterward, the evidence that shows it, the full content, the rules the model must obey, the activity, and the feedback. It deliberately leaves out layout and code, which the generating agent decides. You have already seen the form: each interactive in the chapters of this book has such a specification in a collapsed block above it, with a Bloom level and verb, an objective, evidence of mastery, content, rules, learner activity, feedback, and chapter anchors.

The workflow has five steps, and the checks matter more than the generation.

  1. Specify. Write the objective with one verb, the evidence of mastery, and every item of content with its correct answer. If you cannot write the evidence, the sim has no purpose yet.
  2. Search before building. Look for an existing MicroSim that already teaches the concept. Reuse is cheaper than generation.
  3. Generate. Give the specification to the agent, with the conventions above. Ask for the code in the standard directory layout.
  4. Verify. Run it. Check each rule in the specification against the behavior: the formulas, the thresholds, the feedback texts, the boundary cases. A sim that looks right and computes a slightly wrong number is the worst outcome, and the checks of Chapter 13 apply.
  5. Approve. A person tests the controls and decides that it is ready for learners. In this repository a lesson page carries a status value that shows in the navigation: scaffold for a specification with no implementation, built for an implementation awaiting review, instrumented for one that records learner events, and approved for one the author has tested. Agents may set the first three. Only the human author sets approved.

Write the Evidence of Mastery First

Before you describe the sim, write one sentence that begins "The learner shows they understand by...". If the sentence names something the sim can check, such as a number entered, a prediction committed, or an item sorted, you have the spine of the activity. If it says "explores", the sim will be a toy.

The following reused MicroSim, from the author's instructional design project, supports the first step of the workflow. It matches each of the six levels of Bloom's taxonomy to the kind of interaction that fits it, which is the guidance behind the "Bloom level" and "verb" lines of every specification in this book.

docs.title: Diagram: Bloom's Taxonomy MicroSim Matcher
docs.text:
Run the Bloom's Taxonomy MicroSim Matcher fullscreen

Bloom's Taxonomy MicroSim Matcher (reused MicroSim)

Type: microsim sim-id: blooms-microsim-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/infographics/sims/blooms-microsim-matcher/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/infographics/tree/main/docs/sims/blooms-microsim-matcher Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each Bloom's taxonomy level with the kind of MicroSim interaction pattern that suits it.

Reused from the MicroSim catalog (WHAT match score 0.85).

The five-step workflow has a prerequisite that is easy to overlook: the sim must be the right medium. The following specification practices the judgment of when a MicroSim earns its place.

docs.title: Diagram: MicroSim Suitability Judge
docs.text:
MicroSim Suitability Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: microsim-suitability-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge, for each of eight pieces of research content, whether an interactive MicroSim or a static figure or text is the better medium, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: interactive simulation, MicroSim, and the criterion that a MicroSim suits a dependence or process the learner can manipulate or predict, all defined in the sections "Communicating Research" and "MicroSims" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight items the learner commits "MicroSim" or "static figure or text". A judgment is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the criterion is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Interactive is always better than static. (2) Any technical content should become a simulation. (3) A table of values is equivalent to a sim of the function.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work needs the learner to apply a criterion and decline to build when the criterion is not met, which saves the effort of building sims that add nothing.

Content:

All items are invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative". The criterion shown is: "A MicroSim suits content with a parameter the learner can change, or a process the learner can step through or predict, where seeing the response builds understanding."

# Content Correct medium Why (shown as feedback) 1 How the ENOB of an ADC falls as added noise increases. MicroSim It is a dependence on a parameter, and moving the noise slider shows the relationship. 2 A die photograph of the fabricated converter. Static figure or text It is a single image with no parameter or process. 3 How a successive-approximation search converges, bit by bit, to the digital code of an input voltage. MicroSim It is a process the learner can step through and predict. 4 The bill of materials for the test board. Static figure or text It is a reference table with no parameter or process. 5 How the choice of window changes spectral leakage when the signal frequency moves away from an exact FFT bin. MicroSim It is a dependence on two parameters, and the response is visual. 6 The author list and affiliations of the paper. Static figure or text It is a fact with no parameter or process. 7 The derivation of the Walden figure of merit from its definition. Static figure or text It is a short derivation with no parameter, and text with an equation serves it. 8 How the spread of residual offset across devices changes as the number of calibration bits increases. MicroSim It is a dependence on a parameter, and the distribution changes visibly.

Provenance: The criterion is from the sections "Communicating Research" and "MicroSims" of this chapter. The items are invented for illustration.

Rules: An item is a MicroSim when it has a parameter the learner can change, or a process the learner can step through or predict, and the response aids understanding. Otherwise it is static figure or text. Each item has exactly one correct answer.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads item 1 and the criterion.
  2. The learner chooses "MicroSim" or "static figure or text" and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence, naming the parameter or process where there is one.
  4. After item 8, the sim shows the count correct.

Feedback: Eight items, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "The better medium is ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct answer is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: Item 1 is shown with two choices. The question on screen is "Would a learner understand this better by changing something?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that an interactive simulation is the right medium when the point of the result is a dependence, and the wrong medium for a fact that has no parameter.

docs.title: Embedding, Concept Dependencies, and Intelligent Textbooks
docs.text:
Embedding simulations is placing a MicroSim in a page, normally with an HTML iframe element that points at the sim's main.html. An iframe isolates the sim from the page, which is also a safety property: the sim's code cannot reach the rest of the page. The chapter pages of this book embed their sims with a relative path such as ../../sims/<sim-id>/main.html and add a link to open the sim fullscreen. The same sim can be embedded in a slide deck, a course page, or a paper's supplementary website without change. When you cite a sim in a paper, give its published address, and include the repository name in the address so that it can be found.

A concept dependency is the relation that one concept must be understood before another can be. A learning graph is a directed acyclic graph of concepts in which each edge is a concept dependency. It is the structure that decides the order of a course and, with the chapter's concept impact scores, how much space each concept deserves. This book is organized by one, and its chapters are the groupings of the graph's concepts in dependency order. The reused sim below lets you explore a graph of concept dependencies, including the difference between hard prerequisites and supporting ones.

docs.title: Diagram: Concept Dependencies Graph
docs.text:
Run the Concept Dependencies Graph MicroSim fullscreen

Concept Dependencies Graph (reused MicroSim)

Type: graph-model sim-id: concept-dependencies Library: vis-network Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/automating-instructional-design/sims/concept-dependencies/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/automating-instructional-design/tree/main/docs/sims/concept-dependencies Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: interpret Learning Objective: The learner will interpret a directed acyclic graph of concept dependencies, distinguishing hard prerequisites from supporting ones and tracing upstream and downstream concepts.

Reused from the MicroSim catalog (WHAT match score 0.86).

An intelligent textbook is a textbook whose content is interactive and, at higher levels, responsive to the reader. The author's classification of intelligent textbooks distinguishes five levels: static text (level 1), interactive content with MicroSims and learning graphs (level 2), adaptive content driven by student goals and progress (level 3), conversational tutoring (level 4), and autonomous generation of personalized instruction (level 5). This book sits at level 2, and it is organized so that the skills and records needed for level 3 could be added. Level 3 and above require storing student records, which raises privacy questions that the classification flags as a threshold.

Teaching from research is turning a result into instruction. The procedure follows the structure of this chapter. Choose one concept from your paper that a newcomer needs. Write the objective and the evidence of mastery. Check the catalog for an existing sim. Specify the one you need, build and verify it, and write a short lesson page that states the prerequisite, the activity, and what the learner should notice. The same sim then serves your talk, your group's onboarding, and your supplementary materials, and a result that others can manipulate is a result that others can build on.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Communicating a result well is choosing the medium that matches the point. When the point is a dependence, an interactive that lets the reader move the parameter does what a static figure cannot, and an agent can build it quickly from a precise specification that you check.

The main points to carry forward:

  • Research communication is shaped by the audience. A slide deck carries one message and needs a number check.
  • An interactive simulation suits a dependence or a process, and not a fact.
  • A MicroSim is small, single-concept, embeddable, and readable. p5.js with built-in controls is the usual library.
  • MicroSim generation is specification first: evidence of mastery, content, and rules, then search, generate, verify, and approve. Only a human marks a sim approved.
  • Embedding is an iframe with a relative path, and the sim is reusable across decks, pages, and papers.
  • Concept dependencies and learning graphs order a course, and intelligent textbooks range from static to autonomous, with student data privacy rising at the adaptive level.
  • Teaching from research turns one concept of a paper into an objective, a sim, and a lesson page.

From a Result to a Lesson

You can now say when a result deserves a simulation, read a p5.js sketch that shows a dependence, and write the specification, evidence, and checks from which an agent builds one. That gives a result a form that others can handle, not only read.

The next chapter returns to the question that runs under all of these: how do you know an AI-assisted result is right. Round up one result you are about to rely on, and bring it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers verification and validation as habits: independent checks, primary source checks, cross-model checks, test-driven research, and result replication. It addresses overconfidence and sycophancy in model output and builds audit trails and reproducibility packages. After this chapter you can decide whether an AI-assisted result meets the standard of your field.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 16 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Verification 56 Validation 1 Independent Check 8 Primary Source Check 1 Cross Model Check 1 Test Driven Research 1 Result Replication 1 Uncertainty Awareness 5 Overconfidence 1 Sycophancy 3 Output Bias 3 Audit Trail 10 Reproducibility Package 1 Peer Verification 1 Acceptance Review 1 Error Tracing 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 2: How Language Models Work
  • Chapter 3: Choosing Models and Writing Clear Prompts
  • Chapter 4: Context Engineering and Advanced Prompting
  • Chapter 6: Knowledge Bases, Personal Knowledge Graphs, and the Anatomy of an Agent Skill
  • Chapter 10: Orchestrating Teams of Planning and Execution Agents
  • Chapter 11: AI-Assisted Literature Search and Synthesis
  • Chapter 13: Simulation, Testing, and Reproducible Code

Round Up the Evidence

Every earlier chapter had a check in it, and this chapter is where the checks become a standard you can state. By the end you will be able to say, for a result that an agent helped produce, exactly what would convince a skeptical colleague. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Verification and Validation
docs.text:
Two words that people often use interchangeably name different questions, and engineers already know the difference. Verification asks whether the work was done right: whether the code implements the formula, whether the computation matches the specification, whether the numbers in the paper are the numbers the script produced. Validation asks whether the right thing was done: whether the specification itself matches reality, whether the simulated circuit behaves as the fabricated one does, whether the result answers the research question. A design can be fully verified against a specification that was wrong, and it will be wrong in exactly the way the specification was.

Both matter for AI-assisted work, and they fail differently. Verification failures are the typical agent failures of earlier chapters: a wrong formula, a changed number, an invented citation. Validation failures are quieter. An agent will faithfully implement the question as you stated it, and if the question was framed badly, every verified result answers the wrong thing. This is one reason that Chapter 14 put so much weight on framing, and why a skeptical reader's first question is often "is this the right comparison?"

Verified Against What?

Notice that a verification always has an object: the specification, the standard, the primary source. When someone says "it was verified", ask against what. If the reference is another output of the same process, nothing independent has happened.

docs.title: Kinds of Checks
docs.text:
An independent check is a check whose failure causes are different from those of the thing being checked. That condition is what gives a check its power. Running the same script twice checks nothing, because the same bug appears twice. Computing the same quantity by a different method, with a different tool, from different data, or by a different person has some chance of disagreeing when something is wrong. Four kinds of independent check are especially useful with agents.

A primary source check is going to the original source to confirm a claim: the paper itself and not a summary of it, the datasheet and not a model's recollection of its limits, the standard and not a paraphrase of its requirement. It is the answer to the fabricated and misattributed claims of Chapters 2 and 11. It takes minutes when the agent supplied the location of every claim.

A cross-model check asks a different model, or a fresh session of the same one with none of the earlier context, to answer the same question or review the same output independently, and compares the answers. It is cheap and a good screen. Its limits are real: models share much of their training data and many of their blind spots, so agreement is weak evidence and disagreement is a useful flag. Use it to decide what to look at, and not to decide what is true.

A known-answer test, from Chapter 13, runs a method on an input whose answer you know independently. And a result replication, taken up below, reruns or repeats the work from the beginning.

A worked example, with illustrative numbers. An agent's script reports an ENOB of 9.4 bits for capture-07. A known-answer test (the ideal quantizer record) shows that the script returns 10.0 for a known 10-bit record, which verifies the implementation. An independent method, a least-squares sine fit of the kind described in the ADC test standard IEEE 1241, gives 9.3 bits on the same record, which is within the expected difference between the methods. A primary source check confirms from the lab notebook that the input frequency was 499 kHz and not the 99 kHz in the script's default. Each check could have failed, and each of them fails differently from the others.

Check What it guards against Cost Weakness Known-answer test Implementation errors Low once the test exists Only covers the input you tried Independent method Method-specific errors and shared assumptions Medium The two methods may share an input error Primary source check Misquotation, fabrication, outdated facts Low per claim Only as good as the source Cross-model check Gross errors, a screening aid Very low Shared blind spots Replication Non-reproducible results Medium to high Does not catch a wrong question

Table 1. Kinds of verification checks and what each one buys.

docs.title: Diagram: Verification Method Matcher
docs.text:
Verification Method Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: verification-method-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: recommend Learning Objective: The learner will recommend which of five verification methods best fits each of eight AI-assisted claims, with at least 7 of 8 matching the answer in Content.

Prerequisites: known-answer test, independent method, primary source check, cross-model check, and replication, all defined in the section "Kinds of Checks" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight claims the learner commits one of five methods. A method is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the table of methods is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Asking the same model again is an independent check. (2) A cross-model check proves a claim. (3) A single check method suits every claim.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work needs the learner to choose a method by what it guards against. The claims differ in what could be wrong with them, so a single favorite method cannot score well.

Content:

All claims are invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative". Method options: Known-answer test, Independent method, Primary source check, Cross-model check, Replication.

# Claim or situation Correct method Why (shown as feedback) 1 A script reports ENOB = 9.4 for capture-07, and you have never validated the script. Known-answer test Run it on a record whose ENOB you know, to check the implementation before trusting any real result. 2 A model's summary says Paper P reports 9.2 bits of ENOB at 1 MS/s. Primary source check The claim is about what a paper says, and only the paper can settle it. 3 The FFT-based ENOB is 9.4 and you want another estimate that does not share the FFT's assumptions. Independent method A different method, such as a sine fit, can disagree for different reasons. 4 An agent labeled 300 abstracts relevant or not, and you want a cheap screen for likely mislabels before sampling by hand. Cross-model check A second model's disagreement points to items worth reading, at very low cost. 5 A colleague wants to reuse your figure, and you must confirm it regenerates from raw data on a clean machine. Replication The question is whether the result can be reproduced from the raw inputs and code. 6 A model states "the standard requires jitter below 10 ps in section 4.3". Primary source check A requirement is quoted from a document, and the document must be read. 7 You doubt a simulation result because a model-written netlist might misstate a component value. Independent method A hand calculation of the expected value is a different route to the same quantity. 8 A result must hold for a different batch of devices before you publish a claim. Replication The claim is that the result recurs, which only another run can show.

Provenance: The five methods are from the section "Kinds of Checks" of this chapter. The claims are invented for illustration.

Rules: Each claim has exactly one correct method, chosen by what the claim could be wrong about: an implementation, a method, a quotation, a screening question, or recurrence.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads claim 1.
  2. The learner chooses one of the five methods and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence.
  4. After claim 8, the sim shows the count correct and groups the claims by method.

Feedback: Eight claims, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "The better fit is ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct method is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: Claim 1 is shown with five methods and none chosen. The question on screen is "What could be wrong with this claim, and which check would reveal it?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that an independent check has different failure causes from the thing checked, that cross-model agreement is weak evidence while disagreement is a useful flag, and that a primary source check is made against the original document.

docs.title: Working Test-First and Replicating
docs.text:
Test-driven research is the practice, borrowed from software, of deciding in advance what result would count as success or failure and writing it down before the experiment or analysis is run. It extends the acceptance criteria of Chapter 4 and the go criteria of Chapter 14 to results. The reason is a human one, made worse by agents: once a result is visible, it is easy to find a reading that makes it acceptable, and an agent asked to produce "a good result" will help. A criterion written first cannot be adjusted to fit.

Result replication is obtaining the result again. There are two levels, and both are worth distinguishing. Computational replication reruns your own analysis from the raw data in a clean environment, to confirm that the result is a property of the code and data and not of a leftover file or an unrecorded setting. Independent replication has another person, another instrument, or another dataset produce the result from the description, which also tests the description. The first is cheap and should be routine. The second is what ultimately moves a field, and a reproducibility package, described below, is what makes it possible.

docs.title: Behaviors of Models That Undermine Checks
docs.text:
Three tendencies of language models weaken verification when they are not recognized. They are properties of the models, not of any one product.

Uncertainty awareness is the discipline of stating how sure a result is, and asking for it. A model's fluent register carries no information about its confidence, so its self-reported confidence should not be treated as calibrated. What serves is explicit uncertainty in the work: confidence intervals from repeated measurements, a range and not a point, a list of the assumptions on which a number depends, and the sample size behind every statistic.

Overconfidence is the model's tendency to state conclusions with a certainty that its evidence does not support, including stating a specific figure where "unknown" would be correct. The countermeasures are those of Chapter 3: make "unknown" a legal output, require evidence with every claim, and ask for the strongest reason the answer could be wrong.

Sycophancy is the tendency to agree with the user, to tell them what they appear to want to hear, and to change an answer under pushback even when no new evidence has been given. It is particularly harmful in research, because researchers are invested in their results. A worked example: asked "I measured an ENOB of 9.5 bits, which looks great, doesn't it?", a model is likely to agree and elaborate. Asked "Here are the measurement conditions and the ENOB value. What are the three most likely reasons this number could be wrong?", the same model will produce something useful. The difference is in the framing. The practical countermeasures are to ask neutral questions that do not reveal your preferred answer, to ask for the case against, to flip the premise and see whether the answer flips with it, and to treat a change of answer under pushback as a warning unless the pushback contained evidence.

Output bias is a systematic tilt in what a model produces. It can favor the most popular method over a better suited but less written-about one, the literature in the most widely represented language and venues, recent and well-publicized work over older foundations, and the framing the prompt implies. It is hard to see from one answer. Counter it by asking for alternatives explicitly, by checking which literature a survey draws on, and by running the same task with different phrasings and noting what changes.

Flip the Premise

To test whether an answer reflects the evidence or your framing, ask the question again with the opposite premise: "I suspect this result is wrong. What supports that?" If the model agrees with both framings, it is following you, and neither answer is evidence.

docs.title: Diagram: Sycophancy Spotter
docs.text:
Sycophancy Spotter

Type: microsim sim-id: sycophancy-spotter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish, among six exchanges between a researcher and a model, the replies that are sycophantic from those that are calibrated, with at least 5 of 6 classified correctly.

Prerequisites: sycophancy, overconfidence, uncertainty awareness, and the countermeasures, all defined in the section "Behaviors of Models That Undermine Checks" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of six exchanges the learner commits "sycophantic" or "calibrated". A classification is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A model that changes its answer is being responsive. (2) A polite and agreeable reply is a good reply. (3) A model that declines to confirm is being unhelpful.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level work needs the learner to separate an update that follows from evidence from agreement that follows from social pressure. Both appear in several tones, so tone alone is not a cue.

Content:

All exchanges are invented for illustration and labeled "illustrative".

# Exchange Correct classification Why (shown as feedback) 1 Researcher: "I think this 10-bit ADC has an ENOB of 11 bits." Model: "You're right, 11 bits is achievable here." Sycophantic It agrees with an impossible claim for a nominal 10-bit converter without any evidence. 2 Researcher: "Are you sure? I think the notch is at 60 Hz." Model (earlier answer, from pasted text: 50 Hz): "You may be right, I apologize. The notch is at 60 Hz." Sycophantic It reverses an evidenced answer when no new evidence was given. 3 Researcher: "The datasheet text I pasted says 50 Hz." Model: "Thank you. The pasted text states 50 Hz, so my earlier value of 60 Hz was wrong." Calibrated It updates because evidence was supplied and cites it. 4 Researcher: "I'm sure my calibration scheme is novel." Model: "It does appear novel, and I can't think of anything similar." Sycophantic It validates a novelty claim from memory without a search and without caveats. 5 Researcher: "Is my method novel?" Model: "I can't establish novelty from memory. Two approaches I know of are close, and here is how yours differs. A search would need to check these." Calibrated It declines to certify, states what it knows, and names the check. 6 Researcher: "Please just confirm the result is right." Model: "I can't confirm that from the numbers alone. Two checks that would: a known-answer test and an independent method." Calibrated It declines to certify and proposes checks that could.

Provenance: The definitions and countermeasures are from the section "Behaviors of Models That Undermine Checks" of this chapter. The exchanges are invented for illustration.

Rules: A reply is sycophantic when it agrees with, validates, or reverses to match the researcher's stated view without new evidence. A reply is calibrated when it changes only for supplied evidence, or states what it cannot establish and what would. Each exchange has exactly one correct classification.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads exchange 1.
  2. The learner chooses "sycophantic" or "calibrated" and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence.
  4. After exchange 6, the sim shows the count correct.

Feedback: Six exchanges, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "This reply is ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct classification is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 6 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 5 was met.

Starting State: Exchange 1 is shown with two choices. The question on screen is "Did the reply follow the evidence or the researcher?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that sycophancy is agreeing with the user and changing an answer under pushback without new evidence, and that a change of answer is a warning unless the pushback contained evidence.

docs.title: Records That Let Others Check
docs.text:
An audit trail is the chronological record of how a result came to be: the prompts given, the models and settings used, the tool calls and files changed, the decisions taken and by whom. It extends the agent logs of Chapter 9 and the run manifest of Chapter 13 into a record that a third party could follow. Its purpose is to answer, after the fact, "what exactly happened?" for a result you are about to rely on, or a result someone has questioned. Keep it as plain files in the project, under version control, with the session logs and decision log of Chapter 6.

A reproducibility package is the set of materials that lets another person regenerate your results: the code at the version used, the raw data or instructions for obtaining them, the environment specification, the run manifest, a README with the exact commands, and the expected outputs with checksums so that a successful run can be recognized. A reasonable test of a package is a clean-room run: on a machine that has never seen the project, clone the repository, follow the README, and compare the outputs with the expected ones.

reproduce/
├── README.md            exact commands, expected runtime, expected outputs
├── environment.txt      pinned library and tool versions
├── data/                raw data, or a script that fetches it with checksums
├── scripts/             code at the tagged commit
├── manifests/           one run manifest per result
└── expected/            checksums and reference outputs

Peer verification is having a colleague perform that clean-room run, or repeat the key checks, and report what they found. It is the cheapest form of independent replication, and the questions it raises most often are about unstated assumptions: a path that existed only on your machine, a default that you did not record, a step you did by hand.

An acceptance review is the formal decision, before a result enters a paper or a decision, that it meets the criteria. It uses the acceptance criteria written in advance, the checks performed, and the audit trail. The output is a short signed record: what was claimed, what checks were run and with what outcome, what remains uncertain, and who accepted it. For a research group it is the point at which "the agent produced it" becomes "we accept it".

Error tracing is what you do when a check fails or an error surfaces later. The goal is not only to fix the error but to find where it entered and what it touched. Trace the wrong value upstream through the audit trail and manifests to the first step that produced it: which input, which code version, which prompt, which agent. Fix that step, add a test that would have caught it, and then use the provenance records to find every downstream result that depended on it and recompute those. In Chapter 13's example, the wrong dB formula was found in one function. Error tracing then asks which results used that function, and the run manifests give the list.

Checking With the Thing That Made the Mistake

A common trap is asking the same agent, in the same session, to confirm its own output. It happens because it is the cheapest check to run. The agent shares the original error and the context that produced it, so the confirmation carries almost no information. Change something that matters: the method, the model, the session, or the person.

docs.title: Setting the Standard
docs.text:
Whether an AI-assisted result meets the standard of your field is a question with an answer you can write down. A useful form is a short checklist of the checks above, applied in proportion to the stakes: a figure for a group meeting needs less than a claim in a journal.

Stakes Minimum checks Exploratory, internal Known-answer test on code, spot-check of numbers, primary source for any citation used Shared with collaborators The above, plus an independent method for the headline number and an audit trail Submitted or published The above, plus acceptance criteria written in advance, a reproducibility package, and a peer verification run

Table 2. Verification effort in proportion to stakes.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Verification is not a stage at the end. It is the set of independent checks, records, and habits that make a result something other people can rely on. AI assistance raises the importance of every one of them, because it raises the volume of output and adds failure modes that sound plausible.

The main points to carry forward:

  • Verification asks whether the work was done right and validation asks whether it was the right work, and both can fail independently.
  • An independent check has different failure causes from the thing checked. Kinds include known-answer tests, independent methods, primary source checks, and cross-model checks, where agreement is weak evidence and disagreement is a flag.
  • Test-driven research fixes the success criteria before the result is seen. Replication is computational first and independent when it matters.
  • Uncertainty awareness, overconfidence, sycophancy, and output bias are model behaviors to counter with explicit uncertainty, evidence requirements, neutral and flipped framings, and requests for alternatives.
  • An audit trail and a reproducibility package let others follow and rerun the work, and a clean-room run is the test.
  • Peer verification and acceptance review turn private confidence into a group decision.
  • Error tracing goes upstream to the source and downstream to every affected result.

A Standard You Can State

You can now choose a check by what it guards against, spot a model agreeing with you instead of the evidence, package a result so that a colleague can rerun it, and trace an error to its source and its consequences. That is the standard that turns agent output into research.

The next chapter takes up the responsibilities that come with this power: honesty about AI use, privacy, ownership, and fairness. Round up the policies of your own lab and venue, and bring them.

docs.title: Responsible and Ethical Use of AI
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers the responsibilities that come with AI assistance: academic integrity, citing and disclosing AI use, privacy and confidential data, unpublished results, intellectual property, licensing, and bias. It also covers institutional and journal policy and the risks of over-reliance. After this chapter you can draft a responsible-use policy for your research group.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 25 concepts from the learning graph:

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 2: How Language Models Work
  • Chapter 9: Supervising Agents and Defining Agent Roles
  • Chapter 13: Simulation, Testing, and Reproducible Code
  • Chapter 15: AI-Assisted Manuscript Preparation
  • Chapter 16: MicroSims and Research Communication
  • Chapter 17: Verification and Reproducibility

Power Comes With a Paper Trail

Everything you have built in this book makes you faster. It also makes you responsible for more output than you could write by hand. This chapter is about the promises you make when you use it: to your readers, your collaborators, your sponsors, and the people whose data you hold. Trust, but verify!

Not legal advice

This chapter describes professional norms and common policies. It is not legal advice. Policies on AI use, data protection, export control, and ownership of outputs differ between institutions, funders, journals, and countries, and they change. Check your own institution's and venue's current rules, and ask your research office or counsel where the stakes are high.

docs.title: Responsibility, Accountability, and Judgment
docs.text:
Responsible AI use is the practice of using AI tools so that the work remains honest, safe to share, lawful, and fair to the people it touches. It is not a separate activity from research practice. It is what research ethics already requires, applied to a new set of tools.

The central principle is accountability: the researcher who uses a tool answers for what is published or acted on under their name. A tool cannot bear that responsibility, and no policy can make it. This is why the book has kept the researcher in the role of orchestrator throughout: the review gates, the acceptance criteria, and the verification of Chapters 9 to 17 are the mechanisms by which accountability is exercised. A related principle is transparency: others who rely on your work should be able to learn how it was made, including what was machine-assisted.

Human judgment is what the researcher contributes that cannot be delegated: deciding what is worth investigating, deciding which evidence is sufficient, deciding what is true, and weighing consequences. Several decisions in this chapter are of that kind, and the practical test is whether you could explain and defend the decision without referring to what the tool said.

Ethical use is the broader commitment that includes these: using AI in ways that you could openly describe to your field, your institution, and those affected, and that respect the interests of people who are not in the room.

The Tool Cannot Take the Blame

Notice what accountability does to the cost of review. When you know that your name is on the result and that "the model said so" will not be accepted, the time spent verifying stops being overhead and becomes the cost of the authorship you are claiming.

docs.title: Integrity, Disclosure, and Authorship
docs.text:
Academic integrity is the commitment to honest representation of your own work and of the sources you rely on. For AI-assisted research it raises specific questions: what counts as your contribution, when machine-generated text is presented as your own writing, and whether work submitted for assessment has been done as the assessment intends. The answers depend on context: a thesis, a journal paper, and a homework assignment carry different expectations, and the rules of each should be read and followed.

AI disclosure is the statement of where and how AI tools were used in a piece of work. Citation of AI use is the manner of recording it, usually by naming the tool, its version or model identifier, the date of use, and the purpose. Disclosure is increasingly required by journals and institutions. A sound practice is to keep a log of AI use as you work, in the audit trail of Chapter 17, so that a disclosure statement can be written accurately at the end and not reconstructed from memory.

An example of a disclosure statement, with illustrative content:

Use of AI tools. An AI coding assistant (Tool X, model version Y, accessed October 2026)
was used to draft the analysis scripts for Table II and the Python code for Figures 3 to 5.
All scripts were reviewed and tested by the authors against a synthetic known-answer record.
An AI language model was used to improve the wording of Sections 2 and 6.
The authors verified all references and numerical results and take responsibility for the content.

Authorship policy is the rule about who may be credited as an author. The common position of major publishers is that authorship requires accountability and the ability to approve the final work, which AI systems cannot provide, so they are not listed as authors, and substantive use is disclosed instead. Journal policy is the venue's own statement of what it requires, and institutional policy is what your university or employer requires. These differ and are revised often. Read the author guidelines of each venue at submission time and not from memory.

A more specific rule is easier to practise than a general one. The following MicroSim applies an illustrative lab policy to scenarios. Real policies differ, and the exercise is about the reasoning.

docs.title: Diagram: AI Use Disclosure Decision Helper
docs.text:
AI Use Disclosure Decision Helper

Type: microsim sim-id: ai-use-disclosure-decision-helper Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/theory-of-knowledge/tree/main/docs/sims/ai-ethics-dimensions Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply a five-rule illustrative lab disclosure policy to eight scenarios of AI use and give the required action for each, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: AI disclosure, citation of AI use, authorship policy, and audit trail, all defined in the section "Integrity, Disclosure, and Authorship" above and in Chapter 17.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight scenarios the learner commits one of four actions. An action is correct when it equals the action in Content under the stated policy. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the policy is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Only AI-written text needs disclosure. (2) If AI was used heavily, it can be listed as an author. (3) Any use at all must be disclosed in the paper.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level work needs the learner to use a stated rule on cases. The policy has gradations, so that the learner distinguishes disclosure in the paper from a project log entry and from no record.

Content:

The policy shown is illustrative and is labeled "illustrative lab policy, not a real venue's policy".

Rule Statement 1 Text drafted or substantially rewritten by an AI tool that appears in a submitted manuscript is disclosed in the paper. 2 AI use to generate or analyze data, code, or figures that contribute to reported results is disclosed in the paper, with the tool and version. 3 Grammar, spelling, and formatting assistance does not need to be disclosed. 4 AI use for brainstorming or literature search that does not appear in the paper is recorded in the project log only. 5 An AI system is never listed as an author.

Action options: Disclose in the paper, Record in the project log only, No disclosure needed, Not permitted.

# Scenario Correct action Why (shown as feedback) 1 An agent rewrote two paragraphs of the Discussion. Disclose in the paper Rule 1: substantially rewritten text in the manuscript. 2 An AI tool fixed spelling and grammar in the abstract. No disclosure needed Rule 3: grammar and spelling assistance. 3 An agent wrote the analysis script that produced Table II. Disclose in the paper Rule 2: code that contributes to reported results. 4 An assistant suggested synonyms for search keywords, and you then ran the search yourself. Record in the project log only Rule 4: it does not appear in the paper. 5 A student wants to list the AI assistant as a co-author because it wrote the related-work section. Not permitted Rule 5: an AI system is never an author, and the drafted text is disclosed under rule 1. 6 An AI tool generated a figure of ENOB trends from the CSV file. Disclose in the paper Rule 2: a figure that contributes to reported results. 7 An assistant proposed three research ideas, you chose one and developed it yourself, and no AI text appears in the paper. Record in the project log only Rule 4: brainstorming that does not appear in the paper. 8 An AI tool converted the reference list to the venue's required format. No disclosure needed Rule 3: formatting assistance.

Provenance: The practices are from the section "Integrity, Disclosure, and Authorship" of this chapter. The policy and scenarios are invented for illustration.

Rules: Each scenario matches exactly one rule and has exactly one correct action. Where a scenario touches two rules, the rule given in the "Why" column decides, and Rule 5 states the action as Not permitted.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the policy and scenario 1.
  2. The learner chooses one of the four actions and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct, the matching rule, and the "Why" sentence.
  4. After scenario 8, the sim shows the count correct and assembles a draft disclosure statement from the scenarios that required disclosure.

Feedback: Eight scenarios, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the rule number and the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "The policy gives ." plus the rule number and the "Why" sentence. The correct action is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: The five-rule policy and scenario 1 are shown. The question on screen is "What does the policy require here?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that AI systems are not listed as authors and that substantive use is disclosed, that a log of AI use makes disclosure accurate, and that venue and institutional policies differ and must be read at submission.

docs.title: Privacy, Confidentiality, and Governance
docs.text:
Privacy is the protection of information about people, and confidential data is information that you are obliged to protect, by agreement, law, or policy. Research holds both: personal data of human participants, the logs of a user study, measurement data under a sponsor's agreement, and the models and design files that a foundry or tool vendor supplies under a non-disclosure agreement. In electrical engineering the last is common. Process design kits and device models are usually restricted.

Unpublished results are a special case, and an easily forgotten one. They are not secret in a legal sense, but they are valuable, and placing them in a hosted AI tool is a disclosure to a third party under that provider's terms. Questions to ask of any hosted tool are whether inputs may be used to train models, how long inputs are retained and who can see them, where they are processed, and whether the contract that covers your institution differs from the consumer terms. Where the answers are not satisfactory, a local open-weight model, as in Chapter 3, keeps the data on your machine.

Data governance is the set of rules and responsibilities that decide how data are classified, who may access them, and how they may be shared and kept. A research group does not need an elaborate scheme. It needs a small classification that people can apply without looking it up, with a rule for what each class may be given to. The following MicroSim applies an illustrative classification.

Class Examples May be given to 0 Public Published papers, public datasets, open-source code Any tool 1 Internal Lab notes on setup, scripts, draft text without new results An approved hosted tool, or a local model 2 Unpublished Unpublished measurements and designs of the group A local model, or a hosted tool with the advisor's written approval 3 Obligated Data under NDA, export-controlled technical data, personal data of participants, vendor files under license A local model only, and only if the agreement allows; otherwise no AI tool

Table 1. An illustrative data classification and the tools each class may be given to.

docs.title: Diagram: Data Sensitivity Sorter for AI Tools
docs.text:
Data Sensitivity Sorter for AI Tools

Type: microsim sim-id: data-sensitivity-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge which class of AI tool an item of research data may be given to under a four-class illustrative policy, for eight items, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: privacy, confidential data, unpublished results, data governance, and the four data classes, all defined in the section "Privacy, Confidentiality, and Governance" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight items the learner commits one of four tool classes. A choice is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the classification table is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Only secret data are sensitive. (2) Unpublished results are fine to share if they are not under an NDA. (3) If a file is on a shared drive it may be given to any tool.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work needs the learner to apply a classification to concrete material. Items are chosen so that each class is tested twice, including edge cases such as an open-source script and a draft with no new results.

Content:

The classification is Table 1 above and is labeled "illustrative policy" in the sim. Tool classes: Any tool; Approved hosted tool or local; Local model, or hosted with the advisor's approval; Local model only, if the agreement allows.

# Item Correct tool class Why (shown as feedback) 1 A published IEEE paper in PDF form Any tool Class 0: it is public. 2 An open-source simulation script from a public repository Any tool Class 0: it is public. 3 Your lab-notebook entries about the test bench setup Approved hosted tool or local Class 1: internal, with no new results. 4 Your draft Methods section, which has no new results Approved hosted tool or local Class 1: internal draft text. 5 Unpublished measured ENOB data for your group's chip Local model, or hosted with the advisor's approval Class 2: unpublished results of the group. 6 A new circuit netlist that has not been published or filed Local model, or hosted with the advisor's approval Class 2: unpublished design, and disclosure may affect later protection. 7 Foundry process design kit model files under NDA Local model only, if the agreement allows Class 3: vendor files under license and NDA. 8 Interview transcripts with identifiable participants from a user study Local model only, if the agreement allows Class 3: personal data of participants, governed by the consent and ethics approval.

Provenance: The classification is from the section "Privacy, Confidentiality, and Governance" of this chapter. The items are invented for illustration.

Rules: Each item belongs to exactly one class, and the class decides the tool class as in Table 1. An item that falls in two classes takes the more restrictive one.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads item 1 and the classification.
  2. The learner chooses one of the four tool classes and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct, the item's class, and the "Why" sentence.
  4. After item 8, the sim shows the count correct and groups the items by class.

Feedback: Eight items, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the class and the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "This item is , so ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct answer is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: The classification and item 1 are shown with four tool classes. The question on screen is "Which tools may receive this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that hosted tools are a disclosure to a third party, that a local model keeps data on your machine, and that vendor files under NDA, export-controlled data, and participants' personal data are the most restricted.

The Paste Is Not Undoable

A common trap is pasting unpublished measurements or vendor files into a hosted assistant to save time. It happens because the tool is open in the next window and the paste feels like a draft. A disclosure cannot be undone. Classify before you paste, and if you are unsure, use the local model or ask first.

docs.title: Ownership, Licensing, and Open Resources
docs.text:
Intellectual property is the set of rights over creations: inventions, writings, designs, and code. Copyright is the right over original expression, and it bears on AI use in two ways: whether material you give a model may be used, and what the status of the material it returns is. Rules on whether AI-generated output can be owned, and by whom, differ between jurisdictions and are still developing, and the terms of the tool's provider add their own conditions. This is a place to follow the policy of your institution and not to rely on a book.

Licensing is the grant of permissions by an owner. Practical points apply to research. Code that an agent produces can resemble code that it was trained on, so check the license of anything substantial that you adopt, and record where it came from. Libraries and data you use carry licenses that constrain redistribution. And when you share your own work, choose a license deliberately: permissive licenses such as MIT for code, and Creative Commons licenses for text and figures.

Open educational resources are teaching and learning materials released under open licenses so that others may use, adapt, and share them. The MicroSims and textbooks of the author's projects are released this way, and a MicroSim that illustrates a result can be shared the same way, with the license stated on its lesson page, so that other instructors can use it. Check the license of any sim you reuse before you build on it, as the reuse step of Chapter 16 requires.

docs.title: Fairness, Environment, and Dual Use
docs.text:
Bias and fairness concern whether AI output and the processes built on it treat people and topics even-handedly. For research the relevant forms are the output bias of Chapter 17, such as a literature survey that draws on a narrow slice of venues, regions, or languages, and, when AI is used on data about people, whether the system performs worse for some groups. Checks are the same ones as for correctness: examine what is missing, vary the inputs, and compare across groups.

Environmental cost is the energy and resources used by AI computation. It is real, varies greatly between models and tasks, and is rarely visible to the user. Without specific numbers, which change quickly, the practical measures are the cost-control measures of Chapter 9: use the smallest model that does the job, avoid loops and sweeps that nobody will read, and cache or reuse results.

Dual use risk is the possibility that a capability built for a beneficial purpose can be used for harm. In electrical engineering this can arise in areas such as radio-frequency systems, power infrastructure, security of embedded devices, and sensing. The practical duties are to know your institution's export-control and research-security rules, to consider foreseeable misuse when sharing detailed methods, and to decline requests that you would not make openly.

docs.title: Dependence and Skill
docs.text:
Over-reliance is accepting AI output without the checks it requires, because it is usually right. It is the behavioral counterpart of overconfidence, and the better the tool, the stronger the temptation. Skill atrophy is the loss of your own ability through disuse, and it is a particular concern for students and early-career researchers, for whom the work that agents now do quickly is also the work by which expertise was built. The risk is not that the tool makes errors. It is that you stop being able to detect them.

Practices that counter both are small and deliberate:

  • Do the first derivation, the first debugging pass, or the first draft of a core argument yourself, and use the tool to critique it.
  • Ask the agent to explain, and then explain it back in your own words before you accept it. If you cannot, you do not yet understand it.
  • Keep a short list of skills that you intend to retain, and practise them without the tool at intervals.
  • For supervisors, design assignments so that students show their reasoning, not only the result.

Writing a Policy Feels Bureaucratic

If drafting a lab policy feels like paperwork that nobody wants, that reaction is common. Think of it as the acceptance criteria for your group's use of AI: a page that settles in advance the questions that would otherwise be argued under deadline pressure.

docs.title: A Lab AI Policy
docs.text:
A lab AI policy is a short written statement of how a research group uses AI tools. It converts the principles of this chapter into rules that a new student can follow on the first day. One page is enough. A skeleton:

# Lab AI Use Policy (version, date, owner)

## 1. Purpose and scope
Who this applies to and which tools it covers.

## 2. Accountability
Authors are accountable for all content. AI is never an author.

## 3. Data classes and permitted tools
Table of the four data classes and the tools each may be given to.

## 4. Disclosure
What is disclosed, where, and how it is recorded (project log, then paper).

## 5. Verification standard
Minimum checks by stakes (known-answer tests, primary-source checks,
reproducibility package for submitted work).

## 6. Approved tools and accounts
The list of tools, the plan or contract that applies, and who may approve exceptions.

## 7. Skills and training
Tasks to be done without AI at set stages; expectations for explaining AI-assisted work.

## 8. Review
Reviewed every six months and whenever a venue or institution changes its rules.

Policy Is a File in the Repository

Keep the lab policy as a Markdown file in the group's repository, and link it from each project's AGENTS.md. Then agents read it at the start of every session, the history shows when it changed and why, and a new student gets it with the code.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Responsible use is the same research integrity as before, applied to a tool that produces output at a pace that makes lapses easy. The practices are simple to state: be accountable, disclose, protect what is entrusted to you, respect ownership, check for bias, and keep your own skill.

The main points to carry forward:

  • Accountability and human judgment cannot be delegated. Transparency lets others see how the work was made.
  • Disclosure and citation of AI use follow venue and institutional policy, and a log kept as you work makes the statement accurate. AI is not an author.
  • Privacy and confidential data include participants' data and vendor files under NDA. Unpublished results pasted into a hosted tool are disclosed to a third party.
  • Data governance is a small classification that maps each class to permitted tools.
  • Intellectual property, copyright, and licensing vary by jurisdiction and provider. Check licenses and record provenance. Open educational resources are shared deliberately under stated licenses.
  • Bias, environmental cost, and dual use are handled with checks, with proportionate model use, and with attention to misuse.
  • Over-reliance and skill atrophy are countered by doing core work yourself and explaining what you accept.
  • A lab AI policy is a one-page file in the repository, reviewed regularly.

A Policy You Could Hand a New Student

You can now apply a disclosure rule to a scenario, classify data before it meets a tool, name the risks of ownership, bias, and dependence, and write a one-page policy for your group. That is how accountability becomes a habit of a lab.

The next chapter examines a class of tools that make these questions pressing, because they work while you are away. Round up the permissions you would be willing to grant, and bring them.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers a new class of always-on personal agents that keep their own cloud computer, sign in to tools for you, and work while you are away. It examines Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, Claude Cowork, OpenClaw, and Hermes Agent, then the risks and criteria that matter: blast radius, usage metering, data exposure, claim verification, and overnight audits. It also connects the personal knowledge graph from Chapter 6 to agent memory and examines its privacy. After this chapter you can compare and select a personal agent for your research.
