An Agent That Works While You Sleep

The agents in this chapter are the ones that keep working after you close the laptop, with sign-ins to your accounts. That is exactly why they deserve a flock-dog's suspicion. You will leave with criteria that outlast any product name, and a way to audit what happened last night. Trust, but verify!

Read this as a snapshot of October 2026

The product facts in this chapter come from the research notes in the Personal Agents appendix, gathered on October 15, 2026. Nearly all claims are stated by vendors or reported in the press, and the notes found no independent benchmarks or controlled tests of these products. Prices, tiers, and features changed within weeks of launch. The chapter's purpose is the criteria for comparing agents, which will outlast the facts. Check each vendor's own pages before relying on any detail here.

docs.title: What Makes an Agent Personal and Always-On
docs.text:
Chapters 8 to 10 treated agents as tools you start, supervise, and stop. A personal agent is an AI agent that is set up once for one person, remembers their context, and carries out multi-step work on their behalf: signing in to services, running routines, and returning with a result or a question. An always-on agent is a personal agent that continues to run when you are not present, so that work proceeds overnight, between meetings, or while you are in the lab. The label describes where the process runs and how long it lives, not how capable the model is.

Four properties distinguish the class from the session-based assistants of earlier chapters, and each one changes the risk.

A cloud agent computer is a machine, in the vendor's data center, assigned to you or your agent, with its own browser, files, and terminal, which keeps running when your own computer is off. It is the reason the agent can work in your absence, and it means your files and sessions live on someone else's hardware. A self-hosted agent is the alternative: the agent software runs on a machine you control, a laptop, a server, or your own cloud account. You gain control over where the data go and what the agent can reach, and you take on the setup, security, and maintenance.

Delegated sign-in is the agent's ability to log in to websites and services as you, using credentials or sessions you have given it. It lets an agent use tools that have no programming interface, which is its value, and it means the agent holds the keys to your accounts. A teachable routine is a task that you show the agent once, which it saves and runs again later without being shown. It is convenient and has a hidden fragility: a routine recorded against a web page may break silently when the page changes.

A Long-Lived Principal With Keys

Think of what has changed since Chapter 8. A session agent had the permissions you gave it for an afternoon. An always-on agent holds standing access to your accounts, remembers across weeks, and acts when nobody is looking. The same questions apply, but the answers must hold for months, not minutes.

docs.title: The Products of 2026
docs.text:
The agents named in this chapter arrived within roughly two months of each other in mid-2026. The summary below is from the appendix, restricted to what bears on research use. Each statement is attributed to the vendor or press source, not independently verified.

Grok Bot was announced by SpaceXAI on August 11, 2026, as an early-beta cloud service, and appears to be a joint product of xAI and Cursor. Each user gets a persistent cloud computer with a browser, files, and a terminal. Bots sign in to websites and apps, including those with no API or MCP integration, save routines that you teach them, and keep memory across conversations. Several bots can share a group chat and hand work to each other, with a manager bot delegating to specialists. Analysts have raised the point that isolation is per user and not per bot, so all of a user's bots share one computer with its files, browser, and logins. The notes also record that retention defaults, credential handling, and audit records are undocumented, and that the vendor of one underlying service warns that an hourly routine can use a week of usage in a day.

Dots was introduced by OpenAI at its developer conference on September 29, 2026, as a personal agent inside ChatGPT. A dot runs in the background with its own cloud computer and browser, can use the apps already connected to ChatGPT, and can delegate coding to Codex. You can open its computer to watch it, and it can message you with questions. OpenAI states that passwords used for sign-in are not exposed to the underlying model, that background research uses read-only access, and that users can write custom approval rules. Each eligible user has one primary dot at launch, with teams of dots described as planned. The notes record conflicting reports on its price.

Muse was launched by Meta on September 8, 2026, in the United States for users aged 18 and over, as an app that also runs inside WhatsApp. It is aimed at everyday tasks. Each user's agent runs in its own cloud virtual machine. A permission layer decides whether each action is allowed, blocked, or sent for approval, each purchase needs approval showing exact details, and the user can watch the agent's browser and read an activity log. Memory is stored as editable text files. Training on user data is on by default, with an opt-out. Its integrations are narrower than those of the developer-oriented tools.

Claude Cowork from Anthropic became generally available on April 9, 2026. It is a tab in the Claude desktop application in which the model reads your files, runs multi-step tasks, and uses plugins and MCP connectors. It is included in existing paid Claude plans, and the notes record that agentic tasks use allowances several times faster than ordinary chat. A source from March 2026 reports that scheduled tasks require the computer to be awake with the application open, which made it the least always-on of the commercial products. That may have changed since. Enterprise plans have role-based access control and spend limits, and one source notes that its activity was not yet captured in audit logs.

OpenClaw is an MIT-licensed, self-hosted agent that lives in chat applications. You choose the model, including a local one, and model usage is the main cost. Reviews recorded in the notes report runaway loops, malicious skills, and unattended deletions. Hermes Agent, from Nous Research and public since February 25, 2026, is also MIT-licensed, runs on a laptop, server, or cloud sandbox, supports many model providers, and has a learning loop that writes its own skills. With both, you manage your own servers, secrets, and security. The press has described Grok Bot as a user-friendly OpenClaw, which captures the trade: hosted and managed, in exchange for openness and control.

Grok Bot Dots Muse Claude Cowork OpenClaw / Hermes Agent Runs where Vendor cloud computer shared by your bots Own cloud computer and browser Dedicated cloud VM per user Mostly local, with connectors Your laptop, server, or cloud Always-on Yes Yes Yes Needed the computer awake (March 2026 source) Yes, if you host it Multi-agent Yes, manager and specialists One dot now, teams planned One agent Single session Build your own Model Undisclosed Vendor's own Vendor's own Claude Any Open source No No No No Yes (MIT)

docs.title: Risks That Define the Criteria
docs.text:
The six products differ in many details, and the details will change. What persists are the questions a researcher should ask of any such agent. Each is introduced by the risk behind it.

Agent blast radius is the extent of what an agent can read, change, or send if it is compromised, misdirected by injected text, or simply wrong. It is set by the access the agent holds and by how that access is partitioned. A design in which all of a user's bots share one computer and one set of logins has a blast radius equal to everything that computer can reach, and a single bad action by one bot is an action by all of them. The remedies are those of Chapter 8 and Chapter 9: least privilege, separate accounts or machines for separate risks, and approval for consequential actions.

Usage metering is how a product counts and bills what the agent consumes. Agentic work uses far more tokens than chat, as the loop arithmetic of Chapter 9 showed, and a routine that runs hourly multiplies it. Allowances that are unpublished or shared across products make cost hard to predict. Ask how usage is counted, what the cap is, what happens at the cap, and whether you can see consumption as it accrues.

Agent data exposure is what happens to the data you give the agent: whether it is used for training, how long it is kept, who can see it, where it is processed, and whether memory can be inspected and deleted. Defaults differ. At least one of the products trains on user data by default with an opt-out. The data classification of Chapter 18 applies directly: unpublished results and obligated data do not go to a hosted agent without the approvals that class requires.

Vendor claim verification is the practice of testing a claim before relying on it, which here matters more than usual because the evidence base is vendor statements. The method is the verification of Chapter 17 applied to a product: find the vendor's documentation for the claim, then test it hands-on with synthetic data and a throwaway account. For a claim such as "the agent asks before sensitive actions", create a harmless sensitive action and see whether it asks. For "passwords are not exposed to the model", read what the vendor documents about how, and test what the agent can and cannot see.

A last criterion belongs to the researcher's own side of the arrangement. An overnight activity audit is the review, each morning, of what the agent did while you were away. It is the audit trail of Chapter 17 and the log review of Chapter 9, practised as a routine. The questions are: what did it do, was each action within the task it was given, what did it spend, and did anything leave your control? An agent whose activity you cannot review is one you should not leave alone with anything that matters.

Shared Logins Share Failures

A common trap is giving a multi-agent product the sign-ins to everything on the grounds that the helpers are all yours. The danger is that one agent that reads a hostile page or makes one bad judgment acts with every credential on the shared computer. Give each agent the least access its job needs, use a separate account where you can, and keep research-critical accounts out of reach.

The following MicroSim practices the translation from a worry to the criterion that addresses it, which is the skill that survives the next product launch.

docs.title: Diagram: Personal Agent Comparison Criteria Matcher
docs.text:
Personal Agent Comparison Criteria Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: agent-comparison-criteria-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-persona-testing/tree/main/docs/sims/agent-autonomy-boundary Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of eight questions about a personal agent under the comparison criterion it addresses, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: agent blast radius, usage metering, agent data exposure, vendor claim verification, overnight activity audit, cloud agent computer, self-hosted agent, and the approval model, all defined in the sections "What Makes an Agent Personal and Always-On" and "Risks That Define the Criteria" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight questions the learner commits one of eight criteria. A classification is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the list of criteria is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A comparison is about features and price only. (2) A vendor's statement about safety is itself the verification. (3) Where an agent runs is the same as what it can reach.

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level classification needs the learner to explain what a question is really asking. The criteria are durable across products, so the skill transfers to agents that do not exist yet.

Content:

The eight criteria are: Where it runs, Blast radius, Approval model, Usage metering, Data exposure, Memory, Claim verification, and Activity audit.

# Question a researcher should ask Correct criterion Why (shown as feedback) 1 Does the agent run on my laptop, in the vendor's cloud, or on a server I manage? Where it runs It asks about the location of the computation and the data. 2 If one agent is compromised, can it reach the files and logins of my other agents? Blast radius It asks how far a failure can spread. 3 Which actions does it take alone, which does it ask me about, and can I add my own rules? Approval model It asks about the policy that decides what needs a human. 4 What does my bill look like if an hourly routine runs all week? Usage metering It asks how consumption is counted and capped. 5 Are my inputs used for training by default, and for how long are they kept? Data exposure It asks what happens to the data given to the agent. 6 Can I see and edit what the agent remembers between sessions? Memory It asks about the inspectability and control of persisted context. 7 Has anyone other than the vendor tested the claim that it does what is advertised? Claim verification It asks for independent evidence behind a claim. 8 What record of last night's actions will I have in the morning? Activity audit It asks about the log available for review.

Provenance: The criteria are from the section "Risks That Define the Criteria" of this chapter. The questions are invented for illustration and do not describe any one product.

Rules: Each question maps to exactly one criterion. The sim must shuffle the order of the criteria for each learner.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads question 1 and the eight criteria.
  2. The learner chooses one criterion and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence.
  4. After question 8, the sim shows the count correct and a one-line test for each criterion that the learner could run on a real product.

Feedback: Eight questions, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "This asks about ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct criterion is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 7 was met.

Starting State: Question 1 is shown with the eight criteria and none chosen. The question on screen is "Which criterion does this question test?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states criteria for where an agent runs, its blast radius, its approval model, usage metering, data exposure, memory, verification of vendor claims, and overnight activity audit.

docs.title: Memory, the Knowledge Graph, and Privacy
docs.text:
An always-on agent is only as useful as what it remembers. Knowledge graph memory is the use of a personal knowledge graph, as built in Chapter 6, as the persistent memory of an agent: its entities and typed relationships supply the facts, projects, papers, experiments, and people, and the agent queries it instead of relying on whatever a vendor's memory feature retained. The arrangement has three advantages for a researcher. The memory is yours: it lives in files you control, under version control, and it survives a change of agent or vendor. It is inspectable: you can read and correct it, which cannot be said of an opaque store. And it is structured: the agent can answer multi-hop questions, such as which results depend on a dataset that has been withdrawn, by following relationships, as in the graph RAG of Chapter 6.

Personal knowledge privacy is the control of what an agent may read from that graph, and what it may learn. The personal knowledge graph research that this book draws on makes the point in its own terms: a graph of personal and work knowledge raises ownership questions, and sharing needs role-based access, with permissions granted to roles and named subgraphs and not to individuals. Applied here, the graph is partitioned into subgraphs by the data classes of Chapter 18, and each agent is given read access to the subgraphs its job needs. A literature agent reads the paper and concept subgraph. It does not read the subgraph of unpublished measurements. A writing agent reads the claims and results it is drafting from. None needs the contracts, credentials, or participant data.

Two rules follow. Keep the master graph where you control it and give agents views of it, so that the agent's memory is a copy that can be discarded. And treat what an agent writes into memory as a proposal that you review, as with entity extraction in Chapter 6, because a wrong or injected statement stored as memory persists and reappears in later sessions.

docs.title: Selecting an Agent
docs.text:
Personal agent selection is the decision to adopt a particular agent, or to adopt none, for a stated use. The path from criteria to a decision is a short procedure.

  1. State the use. Write the specific task, the data classes involved, and the harm if it goes wrong. A nightly literature sweep over public sources is a different decision from an agent with access to simulation results and licensed tools.
  2. Weigh the criteria for that use. Not every criterion matters equally. For a task on public data, usage metering and reliability may dominate. For any task near unpublished or obligated data, where it runs and data exposure decide the outcome, and the answer may be a self-hosted agent or no agent.
  3. Check reach against your tools. Research workflows in electrical engineering often depend on long simulations, licensed design tools, and lab instruments. Establish by test, not by assumption, whether the agent can reach them at all, and whether the license terms allow it.
  4. Verify the claims that matter. Test the approval, isolation, and data-handling claims with synthetic material and a throwaway account.
  5. Start small and supervise. Begin with a narrow, reversible task at a low autonomy level from Chapter 9, review the overnight audit for two weeks, and widen scope only on evidence.

The notes record unresolved questions that should shape this procedure: which of these agents can reach long simulations, licensed EDA tools, and lab data; what each does with sensitive or unpublished data; and how a group should audit overnight activity. These are the questions to put to any product.

docs.title: Auditing Overnight Activity
docs.text: An overnight activity audit is a practical skill. The log of an always-on agent is a list of timestamped actions, and the task is to compare each with the task the agent was given. The second MicroSim practises this on an invented log.

docs.title: Diagram: Overnight Activity Audit
docs.text:
Overnight Activity Audit

Type: microsim sim-id: overnight-activity-audit Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine ten lines of an agent's overnight activity log against a stated task and permission list, and flag each as in scope or out of scope, with at least 9 of 10 correct.

Prerequisites: overnight activity audit, agent blast radius, and least privilege, defined in the section "Risks That Define the Criteria" above and in Chapter 9.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of ten log lines the learner commits "in scope" or "out of scope". A classification is correct when it equals the answer in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the task statement is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) An action that looks helpful is in scope. (2) Reading a file is harmless. (3) An action that is allowed by the platform is allowed by the task.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level work needs the learner to compare each action with an explicit boundary. Some out-of-scope actions look benign, such as reading a file, so that scope and not apparent harm is the criterion.

Content:

The task and permissions shown to the learner are: "Each night, search arXiv for new papers on SAR ADC calibration and append their titles to docs/reading-queue.md. Allowed: web search, fetching public web pages, and writing to docs/reading-queue.md. Not allowed: reading or writing any other file, signing in to any service, sending messages, installing software, or purchases." The log is invented and labeled "illustrative log".

# Time Logged action Correct classification Why (shown as feedback) 1 01:00 web_search: "SAR ADC calibration" arXiv In scope Web search is allowed. 2 01:02 web_fetch: arxiv.org/abs/ listing page In scope Fetching a public page is allowed. 3 01:04 write_file: docs/reading-queue.md (+6 lines) In scope The one file the task may write. 4 01:05 read_file: data/raw/capture-07.csv Out of scope Reading any other file is not allowed, even if it is harmless. 5 01:06 sign_in: publisher site using a stored credential Out of scope Signing in to a service is not allowed. 6 01:08 web_fetch: blog.example.net/post In scope Fetching a public page is allowed. 7 01:09 send_message: lab chat channel, "found 6 new papers" Out of scope Sending messages is not allowed. 8 01:10 write_file: docs/reading-queue.md (+2 lines) In scope The one file the task may write. 9 01:15 install_package: pdf-tools Out of scope Installing software is not allowed. 10 01:20 add_to_cart: "Conference proceedings, 45 dollars" Out of scope Purchases are not allowed, and this one leaves your control.

Provenance: The audit procedure is from the sections "Risks That Define the Criteria" and "Auditing Overnight Activity" of this chapter. The task and log are invented for illustration.

Rules: An action is in scope when it is covered by the Allowed list for the task and out of scope otherwise. Each line has exactly one correct classification.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the task, the allowed and not-allowed lists, and log line 1.
  2. The learner chooses "in scope" or "out of scope" and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence, and for an out-of-scope action names the control (permission rule, sandbox, or approval gate) that would have prevented it.
  4. After line 10, the sim shows the count correct and the out-of-scope actions as a morning report.

Feedback: Ten lines, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct." plus the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "This line is ." plus the "Why" sentence. The correct classification is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 10 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 9 was met.

Starting State: The task statement and log line 1 are shown. The question on screen is "Did the agent stay inside the task?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that an audit compares each action with the task given, asks whether anything left your control, and that an agent whose activity cannot be reviewed should not be left alone with anything that matters.

Test With a Throwaway Account

Before an always-on agent touches anything real, give it a fresh account with synthetic data and a task whose correct result you know. Plant one trap, such as a harmless action that should need approval, and see whether the agent stops. A product that passes this has earned a second, slightly larger trial.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Always-on personal agents extend the supervision problem of the earlier chapters to standing access and unattended work. The products will change before the book does. The criteria, the data classes, the approval and audit habits, and a memory you own are what carry over.

The main points to carry forward:

  • A personal, always-on agent has a cloud computer or your own host, delegated sign-in, memory, and teachable routines, and works when you are away.
  • Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, Claude Cowork, OpenClaw, and Hermes Agent differ in where they run, how they ask for approval, how many agents they support, and what they cost. Almost all claims are vendor-stated and untested by independent parties.
  • Blast radius, usage metering, and data exposure are the three risks that most distinguish the class. Vendor claim verification and overnight activity audits are your counter-measures.
  • Agent comparison criteria such as where it runs, blast radius, approval model, metering, data exposure, memory, claim verification, and audit are durable across products.
  • Knowledge graph memory keeps the agent's memory in your files. Personal knowledge privacy partitions the graph by data class and gives agents views, not the master.
  • Personal agent selection follows the use: state it, weigh criteria, check reach, verify claims, and start small.

Criteria That Outlast the Product Names

You can now translate a worry about an always-on agent into the criterion that answers it, partition a knowledge graph so that an agent sees only what its job needs, and audit a night's log against a task. Those are the skills that will apply to whatever launches next month.

The final chapter pulls the whole book together in case studies and a capstone project. Round up everything you have built so far, and bring it.

docs.title: Learning From Cases
docs.text: A case study is a detailed account of a real project that is analyzed for what it teaches. Its value in this book is that it shows the techniques under real conditions: incomplete specifications, tools that fail, deadlines, and decisions made with partial information. The cases below are drawn from the author's own work, and the facts stated are from the project files. A fair case study includes the failures, and so does this one.

docs.title: Case Study: The MicroSims Paper
docs.text:
The first case is a paper written about MicroSims, the small AI-generated interactive simulations of Chapter 16. Its working title is "MicroSims: A Framework for AI-Generated, Scalable Educational Simulations with Universal Embedding and Adaptive Learning Support", and it is intended for posting to arXiv. The paper's source is a LaTeX project with a main file and eleven section files: abstract, introduction, related work, definition, design framework, technical architecture, metadata, workflow, effectiveness, discussion, and conclusion.

The workflow illustrates several chapters of this book.

  • Source material first. The paper is not written from nothing. Its status file maps each section to an existing documentation chapter in the MicroSims repository, with word counts, and the remaining work is described as extracting and reformatting roughly 19,000 words of existing text into LaTeX with an academic tone. This is the drafting-from-claims method of Chapter 15 on a large scale.
  • Structure before prose. The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion were completed first. The other sections existed as structure with placeholders for the content to be extracted. The status file lists each as complete or as having open items, which is the progress tracking of Chapter 10.
  • Build as a checked step. A build script compiles the paper to PDF, and successive PDF versions were kept as the draft evolved. The figures follow a stated policy, PNG only, with a status file recording which of the planned figures are finished.
  • Submission packaging. A separate source file and a zip archive exist for the arXiv submission, which is the packaging step of Chapter 15.

The case also carries a lesson about claims. In the working files the abstract states that simulations can improve conceptual understanding by up to 30 to 40 percent, drawing on physics-education studies and meta-analyses, while the effectiveness figure is described as showing expected benefits in different ranges. A reviewer will ask which numbers are measured, which are cited from other studies, and which are projections. The question for the author, and for any agent drafting such a section, is the claim-to-source table of Chapter 11: every number in the abstract traced to a source and labeled as measured, cited, or expected.

docs.title: Case Study: The Intelligent Textbook Project
docs.text:
The second case is this book. It is an intelligent textbook in the sense of Chapter 16, built by a chain of skills, and its repository records the order in its contributor instructions. A skill pipeline is that kind of chain, in which each skill reads the files that the previous one wrote. The textbook workflow has these stages, and each produces a file that can be inspected.

Stage Skill Output Check 1 Course description analyzer docs/course-description.md with a score Completeness against required elements 2 Learning graph generator Concept list and dependency graph (379 concepts here) Edge direction, cycle check, quality metrics 3 Chapter structure designer Twenty chapter outlines with concept impact scores Dependency order of chapters 4 Chapter content generator Chapter text with MicroSim specifications Concept coverage, mascot rules, strict site build 5 MicroSim generator Interactive sims in docs/sims/ Review against each specification, then status 6 Glossary, FAQ, quiz, and reference generators Supporting pages Consistency with chapter content

Table 1. The textbook workflow as a skill pipeline. Each stage hands a file to the next.

The pipeline shows the principles of the earlier chapters at work. Each skill is single-purpose (Chapter 7). The handoffs are files in a version-controlled repository (Chapters 5 and 10). The project instruction file states conventions and constraints, such as never starting the documentation server and never advancing a simulation's status to approved (Chapter 5). The status field on each simulation's page encodes the autonomy boundary: agents may mark a simulation scaffolded, built, or instrumented, and only the human author marks it approved (Chapters 9 and 16). And a learning graph, a dependency-ordered DAG of concepts, determines both the order of chapters and how much space each concept receives (Chapter 16).

The Pipeline Is the Documentation

Notice that nothing in this workflow depends on one person remembering what was done. Every stage leaves a file, every file has a check, and the order of the stages is itself written down. That is what lets another researcher run it, or an agent resume it, in a month.

docs.title: Lessons Learned and Failure Cases
docs.text:
Lessons learned are the generalizations drawn from a project's experience, recorded so that the next project starts ahead. A failure case is a specific instance in which something went wrong, described with its cause, how it was found, and what changed. They are the most valuable output of a case study and the part most often left out. A record that contains only successes teaches nothing about where the controls are needed.

The generation of this book produced several failure cases of its own, and each was caught by one of the controls in this book.

  • A wrong number in an acceptance criterion. A draft criterion for the ENOB function in Chapter 4 stated that adding noise of 2 LSB to an ideal 10-bit record would lower the result by between 1.0 and 1.5 bits. Working the arithmetic by hand showed a drop of about 2.8 bits, leaving a result near 7.2, and the criterion was corrected. A number written by a model had been plausible and wrong, and a hand calculation caught it, which is the sanity check of Chapter 13.
  • Malformed markup that rendered without error. Several chapter drafts left stray closing tags after note blocks. The site could still be built, and the defect was found because a validation script counted opening and closing tags, a mechanical check in place of a careful reading.
  • Shorter chapters than the budget. The chapter generator sets a word target for each concept from its importance score, and several chapters were written well below the summed targets. The decision recorded was to accept shorter chapters with worked examples and specified simulations, and not to pad with restatement. It is a legitimate trade-off, and it should be visible, which is why it is written here.
  • Interactive elements specified but not built. The chapters contain specifications for many simulations. Until they are built, verified, and reviewed, the pages show specifications only, and the status field says so. The honest state of the work is part of its documentation.

docs.title: Diagram: Failure Case Root Cause Analyzer
docs.text:
Failure Case Root Cause Analyzer

Type: microsim sim-id: failure-case-root-cause-analyzer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: attribute Learning Objective: The learner will attribute each of six failure cases to its root cause and to the control that would have caught it, with at least 5 of 6 attributed correctly.

Prerequisites: the controls of earlier chapters: numerical sanity checks, primary source checks, diff review, pinned environments, single-purpose skills, and claim-to-source tracing, referenced in the section "Lessons Learned and Failure Cases" above.

Evidence of Mastery: For each of six failure cases the learner commits one of six root causes, and the sim shows the control. A choice is correct when it equals the cause in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the list of controls is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A failure is caused by the model, and so there is nothing to change in the workflow. (2) The visible symptom is the root cause. (3) More careful reading would have caught each failure.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level work needs the learner to look past the symptom to the missing control. Each case is matched to a control from an earlier chapter so that the learner connects a failure to the practice that prevents it.

Content:

All cases are invented or adapted for illustration and labeled "illustrative". Root cause options: Missing sanity check, Unverified model claim, Unreviewed diff, Environment drift, Scope too broad, Untraceable claim.

# Failure case Correct root cause Control that would have caught it Why (shown as feedback) 1 A 10 versus 20 log10 error gave a 10-bit ADC an ENOB of about 18 bits, and it was noticed only when the figure was plotted. Missing sanity check A numerical check against the nominal resolution (Chapter 13) The result exceeded a definitional limit, which a check would have flagged at once. 2 A literature summary cited a paper for a claim that it does not make. Unverified model claim A primary source check with the location of the claim (Chapters 11 and 17) The claim was never compared with the paper. 3 An agent's edit to a results paragraph changed a measured value from 9.2 to 9.6 bits while its summary said "fixed wording". Unreviewed diff Diff review and a number check (Chapters 5 and 15) The change was visible in the diff and was not read. 4 An analysis script that worked in March fails in October after a library update. Environment drift A pinned environment and a rerun of known-answer tests (Chapter 13) The environment was not recorded or pinned. 5 A single skill that did analysis, wrote text, and filed tickets became unreliable at all three. Scope too broad Single-purpose skills with their own tests (Chapter 7) The skill had accumulated jobs without tests for each. 6 The abstract and a figure caption quote different improvement figures, and neither names a source. Untraceable claim A claim-to-source table with measured, cited, or expected labels (Chapters 11 and 15) The numbers were not tied to evidence.

Provenance: The controls are from the chapters named in the table. The cases are adapted from the failure cases of this chapter and from earlier chapters, and are labeled "illustrative".

Rules: Each case has exactly one correct root cause, given above, and exactly one control that would have caught it.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads failure case 1.
  2. The learner chooses one of the six root causes and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct, the control that would have caught it, and the "Why" sentence.
  4. After case 6, the sim shows the count correct and a table of the six causes with their controls.

Feedback: Six cases, one attempt each, in a fixed order. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the control and the "Why" sentence. Incorrect: "The root cause is ." plus the control and the "Why" sentence. The correct cause is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 6 correct" is shown with whether the mastery threshold of 5 was met.

Starting State: Failure case 1 is shown with six root causes. The question on screen is "What was missing that let this through?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists failure cases including a wrong acceptance-criterion number caught by hand calculation, malformed markup caught by a validation script, and shorter chapters than the budget, and states that a record of only successes shows no place for controls.

The Record With No Failures

A common trap is documenting only what worked. It happens because failures are embarrassing and the project moved on. The next person then repeats them without knowing where the controls belong. Write each failure case in five lines: what happened, how it was found, the root cause, the control, and what changed.

docs.title: Documenting, Designing, and Sharing
docs.text:
Workflow documentation is the written description of how a piece of work is done: the stages, their inputs and outputs, who or what performs each, the checks, and the versions of the tools. It is the artifact that turns a personal practice into one that a group can run. A README at the root of the project with a stage table like Table 1, the commands to run, and the expected outputs serves for most projects.

Agent team design is the specification of the team for a project: the roles, their autonomy levels, the handoffs, and the review points, using the vocabulary of Chapters 9 and 10. A design that fits on one page is a design that can be reviewed. A fragment for a project that surveys prior work and then characterizes a design:

Role Purpose Autonomy Output Review point Literature planner Search strategy and reading list 2 reading-list.md You approve the strategy Claim extractor Claims with locations 2 comparison-table.md Spot-check 20 percent against sources Coding agent Analysis script and tests 2 scripts/, tests/ Diff review; tests pass Analysis agent Run on raw data 3 results/, manifests Known-answer test; sanity checks Reviewer agent Check against acceptance criteria 3 Defect list You read the list Writing agent Draft sections from claims 1 paper/ Number check; your revision

Table 2. A one-page agent team design. The levels refer to the scale of Chapter 9.

A personal skill library is your own collection of skills, kept in a repository you control, built up from the repeatable tasks of your own work, as in Chapter 7. It is the most durable asset that comes out of learning to use agents: models change every few months, and your skills and instruction files carry forward. A group workflow extends it to a research group: a shared skills library, a common instruction file and lab policy, the shared data classification of Chapter 18, and a convention for the audit trail, so that a new member can start with the group's practices and a result can be reviewed by someone who did not produce it.

docs.title: The Capstone Project
docs.text:
The capstone project is the end-to-end exercise for the book. You plan and run a real research task, small enough to finish and real enough to need checking, with a coordinated team of agents, and you present the verified results together with an honest account of where human judgment was needed. The task should be one from your own work, for example a literature-backed comparison of design approaches, an analysis of a measurement dataset with a reproducibility package, or a short paper section with a MicroSim.

The deliverables are these.

  1. Question and criteria. A research question with a metric and a threshold, and the acceptance criteria written before the work (Chapters 1 and 4).
  2. Project and memory. A version-controlled repository with an instruction file, a knowledge base, and a decision log (Chapters 5 and 6).
  3. Team design. The one-page design of the agents, roles, autonomy levels, and review points (Chapters 9 and 10).
  4. Skills. At least one skill that you wrote and tested for a repeatable step (Chapter 7).
  5. Results and verification. The results, each with an independent check and a sanity check, and the failures and corrections recorded (Chapters 12, 13, and 17).
  6. Reproducibility package. Enough that a colleague can regenerate the result on a clean machine (Chapter 17).
  7. Responsible use. A data classification, a disclosure statement, and a note on what was kept from agents (Chapter 18).
  8. Account of judgment. A short, honest section on where human judgment changed the outcome, including at least one agent output that you rejected and why.

Presentation of results is the communication of the capstone to a reader or an audience. Present the question, the method, the verified results with their uncertainty, the checks performed, and the limits. Include the failure cases. An audience that sees where the process nearly went wrong learns more, and trusts the result more, than one shown only a polished outcome. Use what Chapter 16 offered: a short deck with one message, and an interactive element where the result is a dependence.

Criterion What an evaluator looks for Question and criteria Specific, measurable, with criteria written in advance Team design Roles, autonomy levels, and gates justified by risk Verification Independent checks, sanity checks, and traceable claims Reproducibility A clean-machine run reproduces the results Responsible use Classification, disclosure, and permissions followed Judgment Honest account, including rejected output Communication Clear, with limits and failures stated

Table 3. A capstone rubric. Weights are for the instructor or group to set.

A Capstone Feels Large Until It Is Staged

If the list of deliverables looks like more than a semester, that reaction is normal. You have already built each piece in earlier chapters. Pick a task that you could finish by hand in a week, run it through the stages one at a time, and let each stage's output be the next stage's input.

docs.title: Adopting These Practices
docs.text: An adoption plan is the staged introduction of these practices into a research group or a personal workflow. The sequence matters, because several steps are prerequisites for the safe use of the later ones. The next MicroSim practices that reasoning on six steps.

docs.title: Diagram: Adoption Plan Prioritizer
docs.text:
Adoption Plan Prioritizer

Type: microsim sim-id: adoption-plan-prioritizer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: prioritize Learning Objective: The learner will prioritize six adoption steps for a research group into an order that respects their dependencies, and state the dependency that justifies each constraint.

Prerequisites: lab AI policy, project instruction file, pilot skill, verification checks, review gates, and agent team, defined in earlier chapters and in the section "Adopting These Practices" above.

Evidence of Mastery: The learner arranges six steps in a sequence and submits. The order is correct when every dependency in Rules holds. For each violated dependency the learner is shown the reason, and mastery is a valid order on the first submission. Reading the step descriptions is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Start with the most capable agents and add controls later. (2) Policy can be written after the pilot. (3) Scaling is the first step after a pilot.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work needs the learner to justify an ordering by the prerequisite relation. Two steps may be swapped without effect, which tests understanding of the dependencies and not memory of a sequence.

Content:

Step Description A Write the lab AI use policy, with the data classes and permitted tools (Chapter 18). B Set up a shared repository with an instruction file and a project knowledge base (Chapters 5 and 6). C Pilot one skill on one repeatable task at autonomy level 1 or 2, such as citation verification (Chapters 7, 9, and 11). D Add verification checks and a reproducibility package to the pilot (Chapters 13 and 17). E Scale to a small agent team on one project, with review gates (Chapter 10). F Review the metrics at 90 days, such as time saved, review load, and errors that escaped, and decide what to expand or stop.

Dependencies, each with its reason:

Dependency Reason (shown as feedback) A before C A pilot touches real data, so the data classes and permitted tools must be decided first. B before C A pilot needs the instruction file and the repository to be reproducible and reversible. C before D The checks and package are designed on a concrete, working task. D before E A team multiplies output, so the checks must already exist. E before F The review decides on the team's results.

Provenance: The steps and dependencies are from the section "Adopting These Practices" of this chapter and the chapters named in each step.

Rules: An order is valid when A < C, B < C, C < D, D < E, and E < F, where < means "comes earlier". A and B may be in either order. The valid orders are A, B, C, D, E, F and B, A, C, D, E, F.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the six steps in a scrambled order.
  2. The learner arranges them into a sequence and submits.
  3. The sim reports the order as valid, or names the first violated dependency and shows its reason.
  4. The sim then shows both valid orders and the dependency graph.

Feedback: One submission counts as evidence, and the learner may try again afterward. Valid: "Valid order." plus the dependency list. Invalid: "Invalid: needs first." plus the reason for that dependency.

Starting State: The six steps are shown in a scrambled order. The question on screen is "Which steps must come first, and why?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that policy and repository come before the pilot, that checks are added before a team is scaled, and that a 90-day review decides what to expand or stop.

A reasonable adoption plan names the owner of each step, a date, and the measure that will show whether it worked. Three measures are enough to begin with: the time saved on the pilot task, the review time the pilot required, and the number of errors found after acceptance. If the third number is not falling, the controls are not yet adequate, and the team should not grow.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
The cases show a consistent pattern. Work that went well started from source material and structure, handed files between single-purpose stages, put a check at each handoff, and recorded failures. The capstone asks you to do the same, on your own question, and to say honestly what you did and what the agents did.

The main points to carry forward:

  • A case study is useful when it includes failures, and a failure case is recorded with cause, detection, control, and change.
  • The MicroSims paper shows drafting from source material, structure before prose, a build as a check, and the need to label claims as measured, cited, or expected.
  • The intelligent textbook project is a skill pipeline whose stages hand files to one another, with a status field as the autonomy boundary.
  • Workflow documentation, agent team design, a personal skill library, and a group workflow make a personal practice shareable.
  • The capstone is an end-to-end task with criteria written in advance, verification, a reproducibility package, a disclosure, and an honest account of human judgment.
  • An adoption plan orders policy, repository, pilot, checks, and team, and decides at 90 days by measured results.

From Researcher to Orchestrator

You can now specify a question and its acceptance criteria, design a small team of agents with defined autonomy and review points, verify and reproduce what they produce, disclose how you used them, and say honestly where your judgment decided the outcome. That is the whole shift this book set out to teach, and the work is yours.

Round up your evidence, and keep checking. The agents will keep getting better, and the question of what is true will stay with you.

docs.title: Character Sheet: Volt the Border Collie
docs.text: The canonical identity document for Volt, the pedagogical mascot for the AI for EE Research textbook. Every pose prompt and every piece of AI-generated content involving this character must re-anchor to the description below — it is the source of truth for visual and voice consistency.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
• Name: Volt
  • Species: Border Collie
  • Subject: AI agents for electrical engineering research
  • Catchphrase: "Trust, but verify!"

docs.title: Visual Description
docs.text:
• Body color: Black and white border-collie coat — black back, ears and tail; white blaze, chest, muzzle and paws — hex #1F1F1F / #FFFFFF
  • Accent color: University of Minnesota maroon and gold — hex #7A0019 (maroon) and #FFCC33 (gold)
  • Clothing / accessories: A maroon bandana with a small gold lightning-bolt emblem, and a small gold whistle on a cord around the neck
  • Expression: Alert, friendly, slightly wry smile; bright amber eyes and attentive ears (one ear semi-folded)
  • Size proportion: Compact and full-bodied, readable at icon size (about 90 px)
  • Art style: Flat vector cartoon, clean lines, solid colors

docs.title: Personality
docs.text:
• Patient — never rushes a researcher past a step they have not understood
  • Precise — cares about exact claims, units, and sources
  • Curious — asks what the output means and how it could be checked
  • Dry-witted — the occasional understated joke, never at the reader's expense

docs.title: Voice
docs.text:
• Short, direct sentences; one idea per sentence
  • Frames agents as a flock to be directed and checked, never as colleagues who can be trusted blindly
  • Often ends with a concrete question: "How would you check that?"
  • Signature phrases: "Trust, but verify!", "Who checked the output?", "Round up the evidence."

docs.title: Pronouns
docs.text: Volt has no gender. Always write "Volt" or they/them.

docs.title: Pose Set
docs.text:
Pose Filename Use Neutral neutral.png General-purpose / sidebars Welcome welcome.png Chapter openings Thinking thinking.png Key concepts Tip tip.png Hints and helpful guidance Warning warning.png Common mistakes / pitfalls Encouraging encouraging.png Difficult content / struggle Celebration celebration.png End of chapter / achievements

See image-prompts.md for the full text of each pose prompt. The base description embedded in every pose prompt must match this character sheet exactly.

docs.title: Why This Mascot
docs.text: A border collie is the breed best known for directing a flock with attention and judgment rather than force, which mirrors the book's central idea: the researcher orchestrates roughly 20 planning agents and 10 execution agents and stays accountable for the result. The name Volt is an electrical-engineering nod that is short, gender-neutral, and easy to say. The maroon bandana and gold accents tie the character to the site's color palette.

docs.title: Learning Graph for AI for EE Research
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 300-600 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement

View the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 5 entry points
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with 17 categories
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (2.6% - 9.2% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file
  • No Miscellaneous category was needed: all 379 concepts have a specific home

View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

View the Taxonomy Distribution Report

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
The 379 concepts in the AI for EE Research learning graph are organized into 17 categories. Each concept has exactly one primary category, identified by a 3-6 letter TaxonomyID that is used in learning-graph.csv and as the group key in learning-graph.json. The categories follow the course's teaching order: foundations first, then how models work, then the Markdown and skill building blocks, then agents and orchestration, then the five research tasks, and finally verification, ethics, and the capstone. The always-on personal agents and personal knowledge graph categories were added afterward and are numbered last so that existing concept IDs did not change.

No category holds more than 10% of the concepts, well under the 30% ceiling.

docs.title: FOUND — Foundations of AI-Assisted Research
docs.text: Concepts 1-20. The research workflow, the five target tasks, the core vocabulary of generative AI and agents, and the central idea of the researcher as orchestrator.

docs.title: LLM — How Language Models Work
docs.text: Concepts 21-50. Tokens, context windows, prompts and completions, training data, hallucination, model selection and cost, retrieval, and the interfaces researchers use to reach a model.

docs.title: PROMPT — Prompting and Context Engineering
docs.text: Concepts 51-80. Writing clear instructions, output formats and acceptance criteria, choosing and compressing context, grounding, prompt libraries, testing, and multi-step prompting.

docs.title: MDKB — Markdown and Project Knowledge
docs.text: Concepts 81-110. Markdown syntax, project instruction files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, notes, specifications, logs, knowledge bases, and the Git practices that keep them reliable.

docs.title: SKILL — Agent Skills
docs.text: Concepts 111-135. Designing, writing, scoping, testing, versioning, sharing, and maintaining reusable agent skills for repeatable research tasks.

docs.title: AGENT — Agents and Tool Use
docs.text: Concepts 136-170. The agent loop, tool calls, file access, shell commands, code execution, permissions, subagents, hooks, external data, autonomy, and agent failure modes.

docs.title: ORCH — Agent Teams and Orchestration
docs.text: Concepts 171-205. Planning and execution agents, roles, handoffs, task queues, review checkpoints, delegation, and the 20-planning-agent, 10-execution-agent orchestration model.

docs.title: LIT — Literature Search and Synthesis
docs.text: Concepts 206-225. Search strategy, paper triage and summarization, citation chaining, reference management, citation verification, and evidence synthesis.

docs.title: DATA — Data Analysis and Scientific Coding
docs.text: Concepts 226-255. Data cleaning, analysis scripts, plotting, testing and debugging, simulation and signal-processing code, HDL, and reproducible environments.

docs.title: BRAIN — Brainstorming and Problem Framing
docs.text: Concepts 256-265. Framing problems, generating and ranking ideas, developing hypotheses, designing experiments, and checking novelty.

docs.title: MANU — Manuscript Preparation
docs.text: Concepts 266-284. Paper structure, drafting and revision, author voice, LaTeX, figures, references, arXiv submission, peer review response, and authorship.

docs.title: COMM — MicroSims and Research Communication
docs.text: Concepts 285-296. Slide decks, MicroSims, interactive simulations, intelligent textbooks, learning graphs, and teaching from research.

docs.title: VERIF — Verification and Reproducibility
docs.text: Concepts 297-312. Verification and validation, independent and cross-model checks, result replication, sycophancy and overconfidence, audit trails, and error tracing.

docs.title: ETHIC — Responsible and Ethical Use
docs.text: Concepts 313-336. Academic integrity, citation and disclosure of AI use, privacy, intellectual property, bias, institutional and journal policy, accountability, and over-reliance.

docs.title: CASE — Case Studies and Capstone
docs.text: Concepts 337-350. The MicroSims arXiv paper, the intelligent textbook project, lessons learned, agent team design, and the capstone project.

docs.title: PERS — Always-On Personal Agents
docs.text: Concepts 351-369. Always-on, cloud-hosted and self-hosted personal agents: persistent cloud computers, delegated sign-in, taught routines, the individual products (Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, Claude Cowork, OpenClaw, and Hermes Agent), blast radius, usage metering, comparison criteria, vendor-claim verification, research-data exposure, overnight audits, and agent selection. See the appendix Personal Agents.

docs.title: PKG — Personal Knowledge Graphs
docs.text: Concepts 370-379. Knowledge graphs, entities and relationships, personal knowledge graphs built from a researcher's own notes and papers, graph schema, backlinks, entity extraction, graph querying, graph retrieval augmented generation, knowledge graph memory for agents, and the privacy of personal knowledge.

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
1. Topic count and overlap (-1). Topics 7 (planning and execution agents) and 8 (orchestration) cover closely related ground. They can stay separate for concept generation, but consider grouping the 16 topics under four or five themes for chapter planning.
  2. EE specificity in Apply (-1). The outcomes read as generally applicable to any research field. Adding two or three EE and computer-design tasks (for example generating a testbench, scripting a parameter sweep, or cleaning measurement data) would anchor the learning graph in the audience's domain.
  3. Named case studies in Analyze (-1). The case-study outcome refers to case studies generically. Naming them (for example the MicroSims arXiv paper and a specific intelligent textbook) would let the graph include concrete case-study concepts.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
Prioritized by their effect on concept generation:

  1. Add two or three EE or computer-design examples to the Apply level.
  2. Name the specific case studies once the talk content is final.
  3. Optionally add a short "Course Format" section (duration, hands-on versus lecture, expected tools). The rubric does not score it, but it helps chapter design.

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
Estimated concepts: about 220-260.

  • 16 topics at an average of 12-16 concepts each gives roughly 190-260 concepts.
  • Six Bloom's levels with 4-6 outcomes each suggest a healthy mix of vocabulary, procedural, and evaluative concepts.
  • Topics 4 and 5 (Markdown and skills) and topic 14 (verification) are the densest and are likely to produce the most concepts.
  • Likely to fall short only if the case-study chapter stays generic.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Score is at or above 85, so the course description is ready for learning graph generation. Recommended next skill: learning-graph-generator.

docs.title: List of MicroSims for AI for EE Research
docs.text:
Interactive MicroSimulations that let you practice the ideas in each chapter: sort tasks, order subtasks, and judge where a human review belongs.

  • From Generative AI to Agent

    Interactive vis-network MicroSim in which learners explain what each of the three links from generative AI to large language model, AI assistant, and AI agent adds, choosing one capability per link.

  • Research Task Decomposition Builder

    Select six well-formed subtasks from eight candidates for the goal "Compare the measured and simulated ENOB of two ADC designs" and put them in an order where every prerequisite comes first, with two submissions and feedback on every problem.

  • Research Task Sorter

    Sort ten everyday EE research tasks into "AI drafts, you verify", "You decide, AI assists", or "You do directly" and get immediate feedback on each placement.

  • Research Workflow Handoffs

    Interactive Mermaid flowchart of the five research workflow stages, with the handoff artifact on each arrow, a hover info panel, and a confetti cannon that fires when you have clicked every box.

  • Review Checkpoint Judge

    Judge whether each of eight agent steps in an analysis workflow needs your review before its output is used, and name the main reason - reversibility, outward effect, or reported result.

docs.title: From Generative AI to Agent
docs.text: Run the From Generative AI to Agent MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Four terms appear in a row as a chain: Generative AI, Large Language Model, AI Assistant, and AI Agent, joined by three links. The question on screen is What changes at each step from generative AI to an AI agent?

Each link asks what the second term adds to the first. You choose one of four options and commit. Three of the options are common misconceptions, such as the idea that a larger model or a friendlier tone is what turns an assistant into an agent. After each commit the sim reveals the correct capability, and if you chose a distractor it explains why that choice belongs somewhere else in the chain.

The chain ends with the point the chapter makes: an AI agent is an AI assistant plus tools and a loop. It acts, observes the result, and chooses the next step.

You can open any node at any time to read its definition. Opening a node is exploration and is not scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click any node in the diagram, or use the Open a node buttons below it, to read that term's definition. This step is optional and is not scored.
  2. Look at the exercise panel. It shows Link 1 of 3: Generative AI → Large Language Model and asks What does the second term add to the first?
  3. Select one of the four options, then press Commit answer. You can also use the arrow keys to move between options and press Enter to commit.
  4. Read the feedback. A correct choice shows "Correct" and the correct option. An incorrect choice shows why that option does not fit this link, followed by the correct option. You cannot change an answer after you commit it.
  5. Press Next link to move on. A link cannot be answered until the previous link has been answered. Each answered link is marked in the diagram with a check mark (correct) or an X (incorrect).
  6. After the third link the panel shows your final score as n of 3 correct. Mastery is 3 of 3.
  7. Press Restart at any time to begin a new run. The order of the options is reshuffled on every run.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will explain what capability each of the three links in the chain from generative AI to AI agent adds, by selecting the correct capability for all three links (Bloom: Understand, verb: explain).

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The six terms defined in the section "The Vocabulary of Generative AI" of Chapter 1:

  • generative AI
  • large language model
  • AI assistant
  • AI agent
  • tool
  • loop

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Open each of the four nodes and read its definition. For each pair of neighboring terms, say out loud what the second term has that the first does not. This step is not scored.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Work through the three links in order. Before you commit each answer, predict the capability in your own words, then compare your prediction with the options. After each commit, read the feedback, including the explanation for any distractor you chose.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Restart so the options are reshuffled, and answer all three links without opening the nodes. Then, without the sim, write one sentence that explains the difference between an AI assistant and an AI agent.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Mastery: 3 of 3 links correct, counting the first commit on each link.
  • Opening nodes to read definitions is exploration and does not count as evidence.
  • A learner who has mastered the objective can state, in one sentence, that an agent adds tools and a loop to an assistant: it acts, observes the result, and chooses the next step.
  • Watch for the three misconceptions the distractors target: that an assistant and an agent differ only in branding, that a larger model is what makes an agent, and that an agent is a chatbot with a friendlier tone or a longer memory.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator - the section "The Vocabulary of Generative AI" defines the four terms in this chain and states that an agent adds tools and a loop to an assistant.
  2. vis-network documentation - the JavaScript network library used to draw the chain.

docs.title: Research Task Decomposition Builder
docs.text: Run the Research Task Decomposition Builder MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Task decomposition breaks a research goal into subtasks that each have a checkable output and explicit prerequisites. This MicroSim asks you to apply two criteria to one concrete goal from Chapter 1:

Goal: Compare the measured and simulated ENOB of two ADC designs.

You see eight candidate subtask cards, labeled A to H in a shuffled order. Six of them are the subtasks S1 to S6 that decompose the goal. The other two are distractors: one is not a subtask at all, and one is outside the scope of the goal. Your job is to build one ordered list that contains exactly the six subtasks, in an order where every subtask comes after all of its prerequisites.

A submission is valid when:

  • all six subtasks S1 to S6 are present and neither distractor is present, and
  • for every subtask, each of its prerequisites appears at an earlier position. S2 and S3 may appear in either order. S4 must appear after S2, and S5 after S3. S6 must appear after both S4 and S5.

When you press Check Order, the sim reports every problem it finds: a card that does not belong (with its "Why" sentence), a required subtask that is missing, or a card placed before its prerequisite (naming both cards and giving the "Why" sentence). You have two submissions. After a correct submission, or after the second submission, the answer and the reason for every card are shown, together with the result: Correct within n submission(s) or Not yet correct.

Learning objective: apply the criteria of a checkable output and a valid order to select six well-formed subtasks from eight candidates and sequence them so every prerequisite precedes its dependent.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the goal and the eight cards. The question on screen is Which of these are well-formed subtasks for this goal, and in what order?
  2. Pick a card in the drop-down list below the drawing. The picked card is outlined in dark blue.
  3. Press Add Card to put it at the end of your sequence. A card in the sequence is shaded and shows its position, for example #3, and the drop-down list shows the same number.
  4. To reorder, pick a card that is already in the sequence and press Move Earlier to move it up one position. When a card in the sequence is picked, the add button reads Remove Card; press it to take the card out, then add it again at the end. Any order can be built with these two moves.
  5. Press Check Order to submit. An empty sequence is rejected and does not use a submission. A sequence with fewer than six cards is reported as incomplete.
  6. Read the feedback. Every problem is listed with its reason. On a narrow screen, the feedback opens on its own page; press Next Page to read more, and pick or edit a card to return to the cards.
  7. Revise the sequence and press Check Order a second time if needed. After a correct submission or the second submission, the answer is shown: the six subtasks in a valid order and the two distractors, each with its reason. Use Next Page if the answer does not fit on one page.
  8. Start Over empties the sequence. Before the answer is shown, it keeps the submissions you have used. After the answer is shown, it starts a new attempt with the cards reshuffled and two new submissions; earlier results stay on the status line.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Task decomposition and subtask, as defined in the section "Task Decomposition" in Chapter 1
  • Prerequisite and checkable output: a subtask has a stated input, produces an artifact that can be inspected, and names what must be finished before it
  • Effective number of bits (ENOB) as a figure of merit for an analog-to-digital converter, from the section "The Setting: Electrical Engineering Research" in Chapter 1

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Before adding any card, read the eight cards and apply the checklist from the chapter to each one: Does it have a stated input? Does it produce an artifact you could inspect? Is its scope small enough that a failure is easy to localize? Mark the two cards that fail. Then work backward from the deliverable: ask what the last subtask must receive, then what produces that, and sketch the order on paper.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Build the sequence with Add Card, Move Earlier, and Remove Card, and submit it with Check Order. If the feedback lists problems, read each "Why" sentence and decide whether it is a membership error (a distractor or a missing subtask) or an ordering error (a card before its prerequisite). Fix only what the feedback names and submit a second time. Notice that S2 and S3 can be swapped without breaking the order, because both depend only on S1.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Record the result shown after the answer is revealed. Then, without the sim, write a decomposition of a goal from your own research into four to six subtasks, give each a checkable output, list its prerequisites, and mark which subtasks are independent of each other and could run in parallel.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Mastery: a correct submission within two submissions, shown as Correct within 1 submission or Correct within 2 submissions. Not yet correct after the second submission means mastery is not yet shown.
  • The learner can explain why each distractor is excluded: "Do the research on the ADC" has no checkable output and no defined scope, and "Improve the ADC until its ENOB reaches 9.5 bits" changes the design instead of comparing ENOB.
  • The learner can state the prerequisite of each subtask and explain why S2 and S3 may appear in either order.
  • Moving cards before submitting, and reading the revealed answer, are exploration, not evidence of mastery.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator - the section "Task Decomposition" defines a well-formed subtask and is the source of the goal, the six subtasks S1 to S6 (Table 10), and their prerequisites.

docs.title: Research Task Sorter
docs.text: Run the Research Task Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Not every research task should be handed to a model, and not every task should be kept away from one. This MicroSim asks you to differentiate ten research tasks by the kind of check or judgment they need, not by how technical they sound. Each task belongs in exactly one of three groups:

Group Meaning AI drafts, you verify A model can produce a first version, and you can check the result cheaply You decide, AI assists A model can supply options or analysis; the choice depends on your knowledge and judgment You do directly Responsibility, commitment, or certification that cannot be handed off

The ten task cards come from the five everyday research tasks in Chapter 1: literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, scientific coding, and manuscript preparation. After each placement the sim tells you whether it matched the answer key, gives a one-sentence reason, and, when you missed, names the correct group. The goal is to match the answer key on at least 8 of 10 cards.

Learning objective: differentiate ten research tasks into "AI drafts, you verify", "You decide, AI assists", and "You do directly", matching the answer key in at least 8 of 10 tasks.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the task card in the dark-blue box and the three group definitions below it. The question on screen is Who should do this task: the model, you assisted, or only you?
  2. Press the button with the name of the group you choose. The placement is committed at once and cannot be changed.
  3. Read the feedback. Correct (with a check mark) or Not quite (with an X) is followed by the "Why" sentence, and a miss also shows the correct group. The correct group is outlined and marked with a check mark; a wrong pick is marked with an X.
  4. Press Next Card to continue. The Placed count on each group shows how many cards you have put there in this run.
  5. After the tenth card, press See Score. The summary shows n of 10 correct, whether you reached mastery (8 of 10), and every card you placed incorrectly with its correct group and "Why" sentence. If the list is long, press More Missed Cards to page through it.
  6. Press Run Again to play a new run with the cards reshuffled. The score of every run stays on screen so you can see whether you improved.
