docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The five everyday research tasks (literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, scientific coding, manuscript preparation) from the section "The Five Everyday Research Tasks" in Chapter 1
  • The definitions of the three groups "AI drafts, you verify", "You decide, AI assists", and "You do directly"
  • Basic familiarity with lab measurement, simulation, and paper-writing workflows in electrical engineering

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Before placing any card, read the three group definitions and write down, in one phrase each, the test you will use to tell them apart (for example: "Can I check the output cheaply?", "Does the choice depend on what only I know?", "Does it carry my signature or commitment?"). Then play one run without stopping to think too long, and note which cards surprised you.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Review the list of missed cards on the summary screen. For each miss, read the "Why" sentence and decide which of your three tests you applied incorrectly. Compare two cards that sound similar but fall in different groups, such as "Draft an abstract from a table of measured results" (AI drafts, you verify) and "Certify before submission that the reported measurements were taken and not generated" (You do directly), and explain in a sentence what separates them.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Press Run Again and sort the reshuffled cards. Record both run scores. Then write one new task from your own research that would belong in each group, and justify each placement with a sentence in the style of the "Why" feedback.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Mastery: at least 8 of 10 placements match the answer key on the first run. The score of the second (reshuffled) run shows whether the criteria transferred.
  • The learner can state, for any missed card, why the answer-key group is correct, using the distinction between cheap verification, judgment that depends on the researcher's knowledge, and responsibility that cannot be delegated.
  • The learner's three self-written tasks are each placed in a defensible group with a one-sentence justification.
  • Reading the feedback and reviewing the missed-card list are exploration, not evidence of mastery.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator - the section "The Five Everyday Research Tasks" defines the three groups and is the source of all ten task cards and their answer key.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This diagram turns Table 1 of Chapter 1 into a flowchart. The running example follows a doctoral student designing a low-power SAR ADC through five stages. Each box is a stage, and each arrow carries the artifact that the stage hands to the next one. The example is illustrative and not drawn from a published study.

docs.title: Workflow Steps
docs.text:
1. Find what is known takes a topic and a gap and produces a reading list with citations.
  2. Frame the question turns the reading list and a design goal into one falsifiable question statement.
  3. Build and measure uses the question and a design to produce netlists, scripts, and raw data files.
  4. Analyze turns the raw data files into result tables and plots with uncertainty.
  5. Communicate turns the result tables and plots into manuscript source and figures.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Hover over any box to see its input, output, and handoff artifact in the right panel.
  2. Hover over an arrow label to read what that artifact is and which stages it connects.
  3. Click each box. A clicked box gets a green outline, and the counter above the panel shows how many of the seven boxes you have clicked. With the keyboard, press Tab to reach a box and Enter or Space to click it.
  4. Click all seven boxes to fire the confetti cannon once. It does not fire before then, and it does not fire again. Confetti is skipped if your system requests reduced motion.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will describe the input, output, and handoff artifact of each of the five research workflow stages (Bloom: Understand, verb: describe).

docs.title: Activity
docs.text: Cover the right panel and name the handoff artifact on each arrow from memory. Then hover to check. For one arrow, say what would go wrong downstream if that artifact contained an unnoticed error.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Can the learner name the artifact passed between each pair of adjacent stages?
  • Can the learner explain why a handoff is where quality is either confirmed or silently lost?

docs.title: Review Checkpoint Judge
docs.text: Run the Review Checkpoint Judge MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An agent that can act on your files, send messages, and compute results will take many steps you did not individually approve. Asking for approval on every step teaches you to click through requests; asking for none lets an irreversible or public mistake through. This MicroSim asks you to judge where a human review checkpoint belongs, using three criteria from Chapter 1 that stay on screen the whole time:

Criterion Question Reversibility Is the action irreversible? Outward effect Does the output leave your control by being sent, published, or used to commit resources? Reported result Does the output become a result you will report?

A step requires review when at least one criterion applies.

You see eight agent steps from an analysis workflow, one at a time and in a new shuffled order on every run. For each step you commit two things together: a judgment, Review required or No review needed, and the main reason, which is one of the three criteria or No criterion applies. Choosing the reason separates a correct decision from a correct guess. Four of the eight steps require review and four do not.

Learning objective: judge, for each of eight agent steps in an analysis workflow, whether a human review checkpoint is required before its output is used, agreeing with the answer key on at least 7 of 8 steps.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the three criteria at the top and the agent step in the dark-blue box. The question on screen is Does this output need your review before it is used?
  2. Choose the main reason in the drop-down list below the drawing: Reversibility, Outward effect, Reported result, or No criterion applies. If you press a judgment button without choosing a reason, the sim asks you to choose one first and nothing is recorded.
  3. Press Review required or No review needed. The judgment and the reason are committed together and cannot be changed.
  4. Read the feedback. Correct means both the judgment and the reason match the answer key. Right decision, different reason means the judgment matches but the reason does not; the correct reason is shown. Not quite means the judgment does not match; the correct judgment is shown. The "Why" sentence appears after every commit, and the criterion that is the main reason is marked Main reason with a check mark.
  5. Press Next Step to continue. After the eighth step, press See Score. The summary shows the score as n of 8 (it counts judgments only), whether you reached mastery (7 of 8), and every step judged incorrectly with its "Why" sentence. If the list is long, press More Missed Steps to page through it.
  6. Press Run Again to judge the eight steps again in a reshuffled order. The score of every run stays on screen.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Graduate students (MS and PhD) in electrical engineering, computer engineering, and computer design, plus postdocs and faculty who want practical AI skills for everyday research (AI for EE Research)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Human in the loop: the three positions of a person relative to an automated process (in the loop, on the loop, out of the loop), from the section "Human in the Loop" in Chapter 1
  • Reversible and irreversible actions
  • Output that leaves your control by being sent, published, or used to commit resources
  • Output that becomes a reported result
  • The idea of an agent as an assistant with tools and a loop, which can take actions you did not individually approve

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Read the three criteria and restate each one as a yes/no test you could apply in under ten seconds. Then judge the first step without hurrying, and read the "Why" sentence and the marked main reason before pressing Next Step. Reading the criteria is exploration, not evidence of mastery.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Finish the run. On the summary screen, for each step judged incorrectly, name the criterion you applied (or failed to apply) and explain the miss using the "Why" sentence. Compare two pairs that look alike but are judged differently: the agent sends an email versus drafts the same email and leaves it unsent, and the agent overwrites the raw measurement files versus renames a column header in a copy of the data file. Write one sentence for each pair saying which criterion separates them.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Press Run Again and judge the reshuffled steps. Record the first-run and second-run scores and how many steps showed Right decision, different reason. Then describe one agent step from your own research workflow, judge it, and name its main reason in the style of the "Why" feedback.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Mastery: at least 7 of 8 judgments match the answer key on the first run. The score counts judgments only.
  • The learner names the correct main reason for each step that requires review (Reversibility, Outward effect, or Reported result) and gives "No criterion applies" for the four steps that do not. A "Right decision, different reason" result shows a judgment that is not yet backed by the right criterion.
  • The learner explains, for any missed step, why the answer-key judgment is correct using the three criteria.
  • The learner's own example step is judged with a defensible reason.
  • Common misconceptions to listen for: every agent action needs review, so review is never a choice; a step that looks harmless needs no review even when it is irreversible; a step that only drafts something is safe to send without review.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator - the section "Human in the Loop" states the three review criteria (reversibility, outward effect, reported result) and is the source of the eight agent steps and their answer key.
